Economic Programme—Support for New Zealand Families

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I had a significant number of
complaints yesterday about the level of noise through question time. We cannot allow it
to be at the same level as it was yesterday.
1. JAMI-LEE ROSS (National—Botany)  to the Minister of Finance : How is the
Government supporting New Zealand families through the economic recovery?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Despite large deficits, the
Government is committed to supporting families through uncertain times. For instance,
households earning less than $60,000 per a nnum, which is around 50 percent of all
households, pay no net tax; that is, they  get more in inco me and accommodation
support, paid parental leave, Working for Families, and welfare support than they pay in
tax. We have also focused assistance on those most in need, with $190 million for the
next stage of welfare reforms to get peop le off benefits and into work; $100 million
insulating 215,000 homes; $41 million extra for early childhood education for the most
vulnerable; $24 million for rheumatic fever prev ention, which is, again, focused on the
most vulnerable families; and the KickStar t Breakfast in schools programme, which is,
again, focused on the most vulnerable families.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: What changes has the Government  made to income tax rates and
other taxes, to help families get ahead?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The 2010 tax switch reduced taxes on work and savings and
increased taxes on consumption and property speculation across all income levels. That
2010 Budget also provided for better targeti ng of Working for Families. Two-thirds of
the value of the income tax cuts in 2010 went to reducin g the bottom two tax rates.
Someone on the average wage of around $50,000 was immediately $15 a week better
off as a result of the tax changes. Three-qu arters of taxpayers now face a top personal
rate of 17.5 percent.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: What effect is the Government’s approach having on inequality, and
how is the Government working to ensure households get a fair deal?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Ministry of Social Development tracks household
incomes, and reports that income inequality is falling slightly after peaking in the mid-
2000s, so we are starting to undo some of the damage done by the previous Labour
Government to New Zealand’s equality. There are a variety of reasons for this. The tax
and redistribution system favours the bottom 50 percent of households. Our investments
in welfare, health, and education have been focused on the most disadvantaged.
13682 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Sep 2013
Whereas the previous Government focused on subsidies to people on middle incomes,
we are focusing on solvi ng long-running problems of welfare dependency, poor
educational achievement, ill health, and family violence.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: What progress is the Government making in supporting more people
into work, improving health care, and education outcomes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member does not really need to ask this question,
because you can track progress by going to the Government website and looking at the
Better Public Services results. As at 30 June this year, the number of people
continuously receiving a working-age benefit for over 12 months has fallen by almost
3,000. In March this year 89 percent of 8-month-olds had been immunised, and M āori
immunisation rates are for the first time ever  as high as mainstream immunisation rates,
and, in fact, in some parts of the country are higher than among P ākehā children. The
proportion of 18-year-olds with National Certificate of Educational Achievement level 2
has increased to 77 percent from 74 percent the previous year.
Hawke’s Bay Water Management—Departmental Submissions on Plan Change
Proposal
2. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Has he or his Office sought an assurance from  the Minister of Cons ervation that he did
not know about the existence of the draft submission prepared by the Department of
Conservation in early July relating to the Ruataniwha Dam, before 17 September 2013;
if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No; an assurance was not
required, because the Minister had advised this House in his answers to a number of
questions that he had not seen the leaked draft submission until Tuesday, 17 September,
and I take the Minister at his word. The Mi nister was aware that the Department of
Conservation was working on a submission. He  was not aware of the content of the
leaked draft submission until Tuesday, 17 September. My office was advised by the
Minister’s office on Tuesday, 17 September th at the leaked draft submission was never
sent to the Minister.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Why does he take at his word the Minister of Conservation’s
statement from Tuesday last week: “I di d not know that this draft document even
existed until this morning.”; if that were just  proven to be incorrect, what action will he
as Prime Minister take?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As I said, I take the member at his word. It would not be
unusual for a Minister to ask to see a departmental submission.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Is the Prime Minister concerned about reports that an official
working on the Department of Conserva tion’s Ruataniwha Dam submissions has
resigned as a result of his Minister’s involvement?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There is no evidence that that claim is true.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Exactly why does the Prime Minister think that the Director-
General of the Department of Conservation or  senior managers would email senior staff
that the Minister is “concerned” with the s ubmission, given that hi s Minister said in
answer to whether he had raised concerns: “Did I give an indication? No, I did not.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Minister receives weekly de partmental reports. This is
not unusual. In that departmental report, I am advised, there were two sentences in it
regarding lodging a submission in the name of  the director-general. The Minister asked
to see a final submission before it was made. On Wednesday, 31 July the Minister
received a full briefing on the final submi ssion. The leaked draft report appeared on
Tuesday, 17 September, which was the first time the Minister had seen the leaked draft.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he stand by his statement “I expect high standards from
my Ministers … if they don’t meet the standards I set then obviously I will take action if
25 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13683
necessary”; if so, will he ask the Minister of  Conservation, Nick Smith, to resign if it is
proven that he indicated to the Department of Conservation that it should change its
submission, or if it is shown that his statements to this  House or to the media are
incorrect?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Whatever the details the member thinks he is going to
release or divulge, I would hope  that at the same time he will divulge the final version
of his CV.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Is it true that a draft submissi on from the Ministry for Primary
Industries expressed concerns over the economics of the Ru ataniwha Dam but that the
final submission reversed this finding; if s o, why was this 180-degree turn made, and
which Ministers and/or their staff were involved in any way?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have no advice on that matte r. I think the member can be
reassured, though, that all issues around the Ru ataniwha Dam will be dealt with by the
statutory processes that apply to a large project that has environmental and economic
impact.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Can the Acting Prime Minister explain to the House how it was
possible for Nick Smith to say that he did not know the submission even existed until 17
September, yet the briefing note from 29 July  includes a discussion of the very same
submission?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As I understand it, as Dr Smith has answered in the House,
the note on 29 July said that the department  was making a submission. He then asked to
see the final submission, which is a legitimate, perfectly normal activity by any Minister
of any department.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Can the Prime Minister explai n how it is possible to have a
discussion about a submission—a nd the evidence s hows that there was a discussion on
29 July—yet the Minister says that he did not know that the submission even existed
until 17 September? How is it possible to ha ve a discussion about a submission you do
not know exists?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Again, as I understand it, the departmental weekly report
said that the department was making a s ubmission. The Minister had not seen that
submission. When the department showed him a submission a couple of days later, as
the final submission, he saw that submissi on. The draft the member is referring to
appeared some time later on 17 September, which was the leaked draft submission, not
the final submission. It does not matter how  hard the member digs, there is no
conspiracy here. It is pretty straightforward. The Minister asked to see a submission and
he saw it.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I know that it may seem a
fine point, and so you may not agree with my point of order, but there is a difference
between whether you have seen a copy of it or whether you know—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, I have h eard quite enough. The memb er can use further
supplementary questions if he wants further detail from the Acting Prime Minister. The
question was whether the Prime Minister can  explain, and the Acting Prime Minister
attempted to explain.
Better Public Services Targets—Justice Sector
3. ALFRED NGARO (National)  to the Minister of Justice : What recent Better
Public Services results for the Justice Sector has she announced?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The latest results to June 2013
show the justice sector is well on track to meet all of its Better Public Services targets
by 2017. Total crime is down by 12 percent, violent crime is down by 8 percent, and
reoffending is down by 11 percent. Youth crime has reduced by a huge 19 percent. As a
13684 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Sep 2013
result, the Better Public Services target for reduction in youth crime has been reset to 25
percent by 2017. I am delighted that the justice sector is working so well together, and I
thank the Ministry of Justice, the New Zealand Police, and the Department of
Corrections for their achievements and commitment to reducing crime, making New
Zealand a safer place than it ever was under a previous Government.

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: How will the revised youth crime Bette r Public Services target assist
in further reducing youth crime?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Targeting youth crime is a major focus for this
Government. We know that the earlier young people begin offending, the greater the
chances are that they will reoffend and the hard er it is to turn them away from a life of
crime. The Government has a range of initiatives aimed at ensuring young people get
the best possible opportunity to lead positiv e, fulfilled lives. This includes improving
health and education responses for at-r isk youth, improving sc hool attendance and
engagement, and improving yout h mental health pathways. The youth crime target was
an interim target of 5 percent and measures the number of youth appearing in the Youth
Court. These are the most difficult young reoffenders, for whom family group
conferences and other programmes have not worked.

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: What other initiatives will help the justice sector reduce crime?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The justice sector board, made up of chief executives of
justice, police, and corrections, are conti nually monitoring progre ss against our justice
sector targets of reducing crime, reducing violent crime, reducing youth crime, and
reducing reoffending. Across the justice se ctor, supporting work  is under way,
including: Addressing the Driv ers of Crime, Prevention First, Policing Excellence,
improved corrections rehabilitation and rein tegration programmes, alcohol and other
drug treatment courts, the Hutt Valley Innov ation Project, and expanding safe@home,
to name just a few.
District Health Boards—Resourcing and Service Delivery
4. Hon ANNETTE KING (Labour—Rongotai) to the Minister of Health: Has the
increase in health funding for 2013/14 been suffi cient to stop cuts in health services and
staffing?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The increase in available health funding
for this year and for the next 4 years, averaging around $400 million a year, has actually
been sufficient to improve, not reduce fr ont-line services a nd staffing, like the 2,700
more nurses and 1,300 more doctors employed in our public hospitals. The Government
is, however, very aware that there are alwa ys pressures on providers, such as on some
general practices offering low-cost doctors visits to some in our most vulnerable
communities. Consequently, although we have  already increased the very low-cost
access scheme subsidy to these practices by $11 million over the last 5 years—that is,
by 33 percent—it is clear that some are finding  it difficult to remain viable, and later on
this afternoon the Government will be a nnouncing an increase of a further $16 million
over 4 years, or an 8 percent increase, to help these practices out.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If district health boards ha ve sufficient funding, why has
Waitematā District Health Board now confirmed it is cutting mental health charge
nurses in mental health units by 50 percent, why has it told staff that it intends to slash
the numbers of mental health administrato rs by 14, and why is it removing cars from
public health and community nurses because of “continuing cost pressures coupled with
lower funding growth” ?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: My understanding is that the Waitematā District Health Board
is continuing to invest more money in its  mental health serv ices, and that would
25 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13685
certainly meet with the fact that we put an extra $31 million into the Waitemat ā District
Health Board in this year’s Budget.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If the funding is sufficient, why is the Waitematā District Health
Board proposing to cut 10 docto rs from the emergency depart ment, not for clinical or
quality reasons but to save money; and does this not make a mockery of his letter of
expectation to district health boards where he said they need to “improve clinical staff
retention”?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: T h i s  i s  s o r t  o f  w h a t  w e  h a v e  c o m e  t o  e x p e c t  f r o m  t h i s
member, because—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. It wa s a straight question.
There is no need to have the beginning of his answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I agree. Would the Minister just answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: My understanding is there is a c onsultation that will see that
staffing mix at the Waitemat ā emergency department change to reflect the staffing mix
at Auckland - Counties Manukau. But I cannot believe that the Opposition would ask a
question about the North Shore’s Waitemat ā District Health Board emergency
department when under its watch old people waited for 3 days on hospital trolleys under
bright florescent lights and they do not do that any more.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer is quite sufficient.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: What progress is being made to improve health services on the
West Coast?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I am pleased to advise the member that later this afternoon the
Government will announce that it has given th e green light for a brand new West Coast
hospital to be built at Greymouth, at an estimated cost of around $60 million. This new
development will replace Grey Base Hosp ital with new wards, an emergency
department, and new operating theatres. It will also include an integrated family health
centre that will co-locate general practice on the Grey Base Hospital site. The Grey
Base Hospital’s facilities have significan t seismic issues, so this announcement is
important for the 32,000 people who live on the West Coast and it gives them
confidence in the future of their health services . Site work is expected to begin late next
year, with the new hospital a nd facilities to be complete d by the end of 2016. Even in
the most difficult of economic times, this Government has found $60 million for that
member’s electorate’s hospital.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of that answer, can he guarantee that with the building
of the new Greymouth base hos pital, Reefton Hospital will not be closed and patients
shifted to Greymouth?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: What I can tell that member is—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Well, I give this assurance to the people of Greymouth. We
are putting $60 million in, and once more I can say that there will be a further
announcement this afternoon on a further investment on the West Coast, and I say to the
member “Wait for that”.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that the—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Give up, old girl.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I beg your pardon, Attorney-General? Did you hear that, Mr
Speaker?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That type of interjection is tota lly unhelpful to the order of this
House. Would the honourable member start—[ Interruption] Order! Would the
honourable member start her question again. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: He just did it again, Mr Speaker.
13686 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Sep 2013

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I did not catch where that  interjection came from, but—
[Interruption] Order! We are getting to the stage now where, unfortunately, I am going
to be asking members who constantly interject to leave. That is a warning I am giving to
all members on both sides of this House. I ask the Hon Annette King to continue with
her line of questioning.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that the emergency department at Waitakere
Hospital is being discussed at a closed board session today; if so, will he guarantee that
the emergency services at this hospital will  not be compromised by a lack of funding
and staffing?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Waitemat ā District Health Board’s budget has increased
by $30 million this year. There are 268 more  nurses and 114 more doctors. What I can
say regarding this Government’s record w ith the Waitakere emergency department is
that we have improved that service beyond whatever existed under the previous Labour
Government, which is opposite. We now have 24-hour emergency department services
at Waitakere Hospital, far more than that party opposite ever delivered to those people.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Did he raise the amount of f unding Waitemata District Health
Board received when he phoned the chair and the chief executive officer to pressure
them after being questioned about proposed cuts in Parliament 2 weeks ago, and did
they tell him that under his watch the addi tional funding this board has received in
2013-2014 is half what it received in 2007- 2008, which might account for its current
financial situation? He might like to have a look at this graph, which shows that the
level of increased funding he is crowing about is now halved.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I just have to say that I am glad the member has admitted
finally that this Government increases heal th funding, because she c onstantly paints the
picture that we have reduced health fundi ng. We have increased it year on year, by an
average of $500 million. I can tell this to the people of Waitemat ā: because of our
investment in a 24-hour emergency department  at Waitakere and tens of millions of
dollars in a new emergency department at North Shore, they are getting faster and better
emergency department care than was ever o ffered when that member was the Minister
of Health.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table a copy of the Minister of Health’s letter of
expectation, which is not readily available, saying that he wants district health boards to
improve their staff retention.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table an expect ation letter from the Minister. Is
there any objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table a copy of  the consultation document from
Waitemata District Health Board on mental  health services, of 26 August this year,
which states that cost pressures and lower funding growth are the reason for cuts.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is that document freely available?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: No, it is not available, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table the cons ultation document. Is there any
objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table a graph of  additional funding per year at
Waitemata District Health Board—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Is that the graph the member was using?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: It is. Here is the—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am not prepared to put that leave. [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Can I please know why you
would not let me table a graph that comes from district annual plans?
25 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13687

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am happy to catch up with the memb er and deal with her later. It
is a Speaker’s ruling. If the member is seek ing leave to table a graph that has been
prepared for a political point, it is not—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The graph in question comes
from the Waitemata District Health Board planning department and from its annual
planning process, so it has not been prepared for any purpose other than for the
Waitemata District Health Board, and I think you should put the leave.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have already ruled that I am not putting the leave.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: A fresh point of order?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: No, I want to table another document. I seek leave to table an
email sent to John Key, Campbell Live, and myself from a constituent from North Shore
about the lack of proper care at North Shore Hospital becau se doctors and nurses have
said—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that part icular email. Is there objection?
There is objection.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I do think we need some
clarity from you around what the basis of th e ruling is. I accept that there may be a
Speaker’s ruling that we are not aware of, but it would be good to know because there
will be other occasions we want to table documents like this.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: There will be, and I suggest the member look at a page full of
Speaker’s rulings 148.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. A page full of rulings will
have about half a dozen different reasons. I think what my colleague was asking was for
the reason—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member now is dispu ting my ruling, which will lead to
disorder. There are a number of rulings there.  I am suggesting he read them all, which
would help him.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am on my feet. Is this a fresh point of order? Because any
attempt to dispute a ruling that has been made—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: It is seeking clarity from you.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is it is any way disputing a ruling I have made?

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: No, it is not disputing; it is seeking some clarity.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear from Chris Hipkins.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Thank you. I am relatively familiar with the issue of  the tabling of
documents, because you will be aware that  it was raised by the Standing Orders
Committee of the last Parliament, and signi ficant changes were made to reduce the
scope for the tabling of documents. But the cr itical issue there was that the Standing
Orders Committee did not want to in any way cu rtail a member’s right to seek leave; it
wanted to provided further clarity as to what was legitimately to be tabled. Information
that is not publicly available is a legitimate thing for a member to seek to table, and the
Standing Orders Committee was very careful not to overly restrict what sort of format
that might be in. So I just want to get so me clarity. Annette King indicated that the
document she sought to table was not publicly available, or may not  be available to
members. The principle behind the tabling of do cuments is that it is in order to provide
members with information that they might not have readily available to them, and it
seems to me that without hearing a prope r description of the document and without
actually putting it to the House, we cannot j udge whether the House would like to have
that information.
13688 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Sep 2013

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member for his point. The issue I think that may be of
confusion to me is the authenticity of th e document. If it has been prepared by the
member for the point of making a political point , then I will not be prepared to put the
leave. If the member rises and says that it has not been prepared by the member and is
of an authentic source, the easiest way forward—[ Interruption] Order! The easiest way
forward, once I am convinced of that, is that  I will put the leave.  I am asking the Hon
Annette King for clarification.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: The data is sourced from the Waitemat ā District Health Board’s
annual plans for 2008, 2009—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I did not ask where the data came from; I asked for the
authenticity of the graph. Is it a graph that the member has prepared herself?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Yes, but—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is all I need to know, thank—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker . It is a point of clarification.
Could you please explain to the House—[ Interruption] Well, I am entitled to ask for a
point of order—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: —in silence.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Would the member please continue with her point of order.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Could you please explain to the House when sources of
information that come from an independent source are a political item?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

Economy, Rebalancing—Productivity
6. Hon SHANE JONES (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he agree with
the Productivity Commission that the “growing gap in labour productivity has been the
main driver of an increasing disparity in GDP per capita between the two trans-Tasman
economies,” and given double-digit house price inflation in Auckland, doesn’t this show
the Government’s efforts to rebalance the economy towards productive exports and jobs
has failed?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In answer to the second part of the
question, no. The commission’s full comment refers to New Zealand’s relative decline
since the mid-1970s. The Government understands those issues and has a programme in
place of tax reform, upgrading educational achievement and skills training, building
more infrastructure, rolling out ultra-fast  broadband—perhaps some 10 years ahead of
when it would have turned up in the market—and getti ng the Government back to
surplus. We believe that this program me and hundreds of other initiatives will
contribute to closing the productivity gap with Australia.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Why does he believe the Government’s current economic settings
are correct, when the Productivity Commissi on says that New Zealand’s productivity
performance shows no evidence of catching up to other countries?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We have looked at that evid ence pretty hard, and we believe
that the programme the Government has outlined will make a difference. I must say that
in trying to turn round pr oductivity decline dating back to  the 1970s, it will take
persistence over time, with sens ible policies and public support.  That is the recipe that
this Government is following. We welcom e suggestions from the retread economic
spokespersons on the Opposition front bench that will assist in that project.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: When did the New Zealand economy  first show signs of imbalance
in the current economic cycle?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, between 2001 and 2007 house prices doubled. By
2007 first mortgage interest rates were at 10 pe rcent. They are currently half of that. In
the 5 years to 2008 public spending increased by  50 percent. The result of that was that
in 2005 the export sector in New Zealand went into recession, when the rest of the globe
was enjoying an economic boom. It was a pretty amazing achievement.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What is the outlook for the New Zealand economy and how does
that compare to the situation in 2008?
25 Sep 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13691

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The current economic outlook is for 2 to 3 percent growth
over the next 3 years, with export growth of  2 to 3 percent, once the effects of the
drought are over. The Government is expe cted to be in surplus in 2014-15. This
compares favourably to th e situation in 2006 to 2008, when the housing market was
booming, first mortgage interest rates were at 10 percent, but the export sector had
already been in recession for a couple of years. In the next 2 or 3 years New Zealand
will be one of the fastest-growing developed economies and one of a handful in surplus,
but there is a lot of work to do yet, particularly on productivity.

items.text: Given that the Productivity Commission’s report shows that the long
hours New Zealanders work have not helped  improve wages or productivity, will he

work rather than the completely deregulated  system we have now, where some workers
are working dangerously long hours?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No workers should be put in the position where the hours of
work they have are dangerous. If that is the situation, then their employers are breaching
their statutory responsibilities.  I know the member has, for instance, been supporting a
campaign around the forestry industry, whic h I think has had some impact on that
industry, that is positive for workers in reducing the dangers posed by long hours.

items.text: What alternative economic proposals has he seen and what effect
would those proposals have on productivity and the tradable sector?

items.text: I have seen a number of propos als over recent weeks, which
I think come from somewhere in the 1960s and 1970s, around how to try to legislate for
a stronger economy, with higher taxes, more  spending, and bigger Government. I have
also seen a number of proposals to shut  down the dairy industry, close down the
smelter, prevent all mining, and stop any ne w irrigation, at the sa me time as people are
proposing more jobs and regional development. It clearly does not make sense.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Does he agree that the 2.5 percent decline in productivity
recorded by Statistics New Zealand in th e fishing and forestry industries since 2008—
the first productivity decline in those crucial regional sectors since records began—is
directly linked to his Government’s cuts to regional training; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I certainly do not agree wi th that, although  the reasons
for that decline are not well understood. My colleague Minist er Joyce and the Ministry
of Business, Innovation and Em ployment are doing a lot of sectoral work to understand
changes in productivity. In respect of training schemes, we are still cleaning up the mess
left by the last Government of billions of dollars of wasted spending—misleading
young New Zealanders that they were getting tradable skills when they were not. But
the clean-up is almost over and help is on its way for those young New Zealanders who
do want better skills.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: How will he achieve his promise to close the wage gap with
Australia, when the Productivity Commissi on says that under his current economic
settings New Zealand’s productivity performance shows no evidence of catching up?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As I said before, the Governme nt has outlined its plan. It is
all set out in deta il in the Business Growth Age nda, which has been thoroughly
discussed with business, with iwi, with tertiary instituti ons, and with industry groups.
And if the member has another suggestion or  two to add to the 300 policy initiatives,
they are most welcome.

are scheduled to become part of the throat-swabbing campaign by October 2013. The
campaign, which aims to reduce the incidence of rheumatic fever by two-thirds by June
2017, received an additional $21.6 million ove r 4 years in Budget 2013, bringing the
total Government investment to $45 million.

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison

rheumatic fever?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Local communities and health providers are working together
in at-risk communities that experience the highest rates of disease, such as Auckland
and Porirua. Soon the Associate Minister of Health the Hon Tariana Turia will
announce details of the free sore throat rapid response clinics that will target families
whose children do not attend schools with throat-swabbing services, and an Auckland-
wide healthy homes initiative will addre ss poor-quality housing and overcrowding,
which are contributors to this disease, part icularly in Auckland. Other initiatives, like
research into a rheumatic fever vaccine a nd a targeted awareness campaign, will also
help families understand how to protect thei r children from this very serious Third
World disease.

items.text: It must be a good Government
when the biggest issue of the day, of the second week of the new leader’s career, is
whether the Minister of Conser vation saw a draft report before  he knew it existed. That
is the biggest issue, and I think it does show how out of  touch the pale, male, stale
Labour Party is.
One of the bigger issues is actually housing, and I just want to outline the
Government’s programme of work towa rds resolving New Zealand’s housing
affordability issues. In the last economic cycle, up to 2007-08, housing in New Zealand
became less affordable than it had ever bee n, driven mainly, actually, by the policies of
the current Leader of the Opposition, where we ended up with first mortgage rates at 10
percent at a time when house prices had doubled in less than a decade.
Back in early 2011, when house prices had ac tually been falling and were flat, this
Government decided that it was an issue that needed to be dealt with. At that time we
announced the first inquiry of the new Productivity Commission. The first inquiry of the
25 Sep 2013 General Debate 13703
new Productivity Commission was into housin g affordability. That commission did a
very good job, because what it did was show that, in fact, the supply of housing was a
critical determinant of the pr ice of housing. I have to say th at before then, when this
Government had advanced that proposition, it was roundly criticised, particularly by
local government, and also by the Opposition and by pretty much any commentator who
thought they knew much about it.
The Productivity Commission did its inquiry and released its report in April 2012. In
October 2012 the Government released its response to that report, and then we
proceeded to take action because housing affo rdability is an issue that affects every
New Zealander. We started intensive discussions, particularly with Auckland Council,
because this is about the interaction of local decision-making and regulation, along with
its impact on macroeconomic settings and, pa rticularly in New Z ealand, on our export
sector.
Of course, the Opposition s hould have understood the re al risks of a runaway
housing market, because the runaway housing market under Labour was so bad that in
2008 it, and then we, had to back a sovere ign guarantee of the New Zealand banking
system with a contingent liability of over $100 billion. So we should all be aware of the
risks of having a runaway housing market alongside any kind of financial disruption.
It had never happened before that a New Zealand Government had had to underwrite
our banking system, which is driven primarily by housing loans. So of course we set out
to take action to ensure that those circumstances could not arise again. As a result of our
intensive negotiations with Auckland Council, we have come to an agreement—I might
say, a historic agreement—that the Govern ment and Auckland will work together on
increasing the supply of housing going into that market, where prices have been
growing by 12 to 15 percent.
That agreement is backed up by an innovativ e legislative solution, which, I have to
say, took an enormous amount of work from the previous and the current Minister of
Housing and was put through the House in pretty  quick time. It still took 6 or 8 months
to get it through, because that is the time it takes.
The housing cycle, of course, has taken off—there is no doubt about that—and it is
fortunate that this Governme nt 3 years ago set off down the path of dealing with
housing affordability. Now we are ready, alongside the Auckland Council, to consent
thousands—thousands—of new houses, including affordable houses.

determined to pursue its irrigation agenda, regardless of the environmental effects.
What we know from the Ruataniwha scheme is  that it is massively subsidised by the
taxpayer—both the ratepayers in the Hawke’s Bay as well as central government, which
will be kicking in a lot of money—w e know it will have a huge downstream
environmental effect of massive nitrogen cont amination as a result of this dam project,
if it is to go ahead; and we know that th e only Government department with the
13704 General Debate 25 Sep 2013
statutory responsibility to stand up for the envi ronment, to speak out for it, and to make
a submission into this process is the Depart ment of Conservation, and that is why the
Minister of Conservation ha d to censor his department a nd prevent it from putting in a
submission that was critical of this dam project.
The Department of Conservation’s original  submission simply stated the science.
The science around this is very clear. Wh en you have a massive irrigation project—
hundreds of millions of dollars this proj ect will cost—and then you have tens of
thousands of hectares of intensified agricu lture as a result, you get massive downstream
nitrogen pollution, with all the problems that causes, not on ly to the native fish in that
river system but, of course, to the recreational trout fishery, as well. It is the
fundamental destruction of the New Zealand environment.
The Department of Conservation was simply going to put in a submission pointing to
these basic scientific facts, but it was unacceptable to the Government that the
department should tell the truth about the freshw ater science, so it had to be suppressed.
It was just the same as when the Governme nt got rid of the democratically elected
councillors in Canterbury. Prior to the earthquake it got rid of the elected councillors in
Canterbury. They were standing up to the irrigation agenda of  this Government, so they
had to go. That is why the Department of Conservation had to be  suppressed and its
submission had to be suppressed. It was not allowed to go into this process.
The Ministry for Primary Industries, of c ourse, was allowed to put in a very large
submission in favour of the dam project, but the Department of Conservation was
blocked. What this means is that we are heading down an economic path where we kill
the goose that lays the golden  egg. New Zealand’s clean, gr een, and safe reputation, the
foundation of our primary sector, is being destroyed by the Government while it seeks
short-term profits and simply an increase in more and more milk solids. The last drop of
milk from the last blade of grass could describe this Government’s economic strategy.
Instead of having investment in research and development and innovation making us
an innovative economy that makes money from our brains, we are simply becoming an
economy that digs stuff up and grows milk and sells it to the rest of the world, and in
the process completely destroying the natu ral environment that underpins our primary
food export sector. As the Riddet Institute—tha t is, the agrifood institute that is an
expert in this—pointed out, the Government is  determined to destroy the clean, green,
and safe brand that underpins our primary sect or, rather than saying that what we need
to do is build on that brand, get value out of that brand, control more of the value chain
from that brand, get to know our customers,  do the research and development so we
make more money out of it, and at the same time invest in research and development in
more innovative industries that can complement  the primary sector, so we do not build
an economy entirely dependent on cows a nd mining, as this Government thinks we
should do.
That is the fundamental economic strategy i ssue that is at stake in this argument
around the Ruataniwha dam. It  is a fundamental divergence of views between the
National Party, which wants to keep headin g down this strategy of daft, dirty, and
heartless, and the Green Party, which says that we need a smarter, greener, more
compassionate strategy, and a smarter, green er economic strategy th at actually adds
value and makes us more pros perous and richer, rather than simply degrading the
natural environment on which our economy depends. That is the fundamental
contradiction.
When Nick Smith had the motive to get in the way of the department’s report, he had
the opportunity, and the evidence is that he in terrupted the report. The reason why he is
doing that is not just some accidental reas on; he is doing it in order to support the
25 Sep 2013 General Debate 13705
Government’s irrigation agenda, which is fundamentally undermining the New Zealand
economy.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I am sure the House is very grateful
for that lesson in business, re sting on the vast experience in the real world of that
member, Russel Norman. I am sure we have enjoyed that. I do challenge such members
to check some of their facts around the job creation side of what he has just been talking
about.
Anyway, every time the far-left socialist coalition members over there speak and
welcome socialism with open arms, as does the new leader of the Labour Party—and
congratulations to the new leader—every time they open their mouths, New Zealand
mortgages suffer. After that speech right then, and the Leader of the Opposition’s
speech, New Zealand mortgages will suffer if, in fact, those members are ever to get
near the Treasury benches. The programme of multibillion-dollar borrowing from
overseas that the three cont estants in the Labour Party leadership contest have
committed their party to if Labour become s the Government will mean that New
Zealand mortgages will be so much higher than they are now. The Opposition cannot
wait to get its sticky fingers on the Reserv e Bank. Its members cannot wait to get the
independence of monetary policy out of the clutches of the world-renowned Reserve
Bank here in New Zealand. The moment they ta lk about that, as with the moment they
went there the last time they were in G overnment, in 2008, with an inquiry—actually,
New Zealand mortgages will go higher if, in fact, those members ever get anywhere
near implementing that policy.
The results of the Better Public Services  prudent management of our economy are
starting to be enjoyed by more and more Ne w Zealanders all the time. There are lower
mortgage rates—half of what  they were under Labour in 2 008, in spite of the global
financial crisis and in spite of the effort s we are having to do around the Christchurch
and Canterbury earthquake trag edies. I must note that we should contrast where we are
now with 2008, the source of data bei ng the 2008 pre-election fiscal update—the
document that introduced the decade of defic its to our country. I do note that one of the
Associate Ministers of Finance was one Mr David Cunliffe in 2008, when the decade of
deficits arrived in New Zealand.
In 2008 under a Labour Government New Zealand had been in a recession for over 1
year. Under National right now there is some of the highest growth in the OECD. Under
Labour, when one Associate Minister of Fi nance was one David Cunliffe, we had 10
percent floating mortgages. Under Nationa l right now we have  5 percent floating
mortgages. Under Labour, when Mr Cunliffe wa s an Associate Minister of Finance, we
had only 4 percent real wage growth over 9 years. Here under the National Government
over just 5 years we have had 22 percent grow th in after-tax wages. Inflation when Mr
Cunliffe was an Associate Minister of Fi nance was nudging 5 percent, destroying the
financial assets of New Zealand and pumping up an ongoing housing boom. Under
National it is 0.5 to 1.5 percen t—under control. In 2008 under Labour exports had been
in recession for many, many years. Under National manufacturing and all export sectors
are growing and having a brighter future. Under Labour, when Davi d Cunliffe was one
of the associate finance spokesmen, the tax take went up 50 percen t. Taxes went up 50
percent. National in 2013 is rebalancing the tax system to target those who speculate on
property. Under Labour in 2008 there was an explosion of loss attributing qualifying
companies—nobody really hears about them a ny more—a product of the distorted tax
system of the Labour Government backed by the Greens, when Mr Cunliffe was one of
the associate finance spokesmen.
13706 General Debate 25 Sep 2013
After 5 years of National in Government, New Zealanders are better off. There is no
better proof than the mortgage rates that Ne w Zealanders are paying, which are half of
what they were under the Labour Government.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Over the years New Zealand
First has raised a number of issues in this Parliament and over the years we have had
our credibility attacked by certain people in  the press gallery and around the country
who do not seem to have much of an unde rstanding of how facts are assembled. The
reality is that over the years we talked a bout things as wide as the wine-box inquiry,
New Zealand Rail, the leaking of secret documents, the Bank of New Zealand scandal,
the Māori loans affair, and, time after time, we have had the effrontery to be faced by
journalists and people in the Opposition who say that what we are arguing is not true.
I want to say about Wh ānau Ora that the allegations be ing made here in the last 2
days are true, and that what the Minister for Wh ānau Ora has been telling the House is
not true. That is demonstrably obvious to ev erybody here, in respect of those questions.
Yesterday she was asked a question on whethe r or not she had ever offered resources
and staff, such as report writers, to prepare Wh ānau Ora commissioning agency bid
documentation. All the evidence for that has b een placed before this House. Instead, the
Minister gets up here and seeks to vacillat e and argue and, by being deliberately obtuse,
get away from what used to be a House wh ere things were transparent and members of
Parliament were accountable. This is a di sgrace, and all over this country there are
people writing in—I am sure even to you, Mr Speaker—to say what a disgrace they
think it is.
The fact is that John Key said that Wh ānau Ora contracts would be focused on
results, meaning that the providers would be  held accountable for what they achieved
with Government funding. When did that happ en in the last 2 days? She was asked a
simple question: did this or did this not happen, and 2 days later you have got officials
in this Parliament and members of Parlia ment and certain people in the media, who
would not know a M āori if they fell over one, havi ng the effrontery to challenge
someone whose information is based on documentation and Māori information as well.
This is the “bro-rocracy” of the “Brownta ble”—to transfer hundreds of millions of
dollars from worthy social causes to th e elite mates and supporters of the M āori Party.
They have been caught out yet again with their pork and pūhā politics. It is a blatant and
barefaced use of public money to fund a comp letely separate system—a blatant attempt
to sideline pan-M āori and urban M āori authorities for their own preferred ancient
mediaeval mechanism. It is a giant leap back  to the worst excesses of ancient tribalism
and it does not fit in with the modern democratic society.
Whānau Ora, medieval in pur pose, does not empower M āori. The M āori Party most
certainly does not empower M āori. Democracy does empower M āori, and all the great
progress and achievements came with the democratic system to this country, and every
time we let that system down in this Parliament we sell our nation and democracy short.
It is a giant leap backwards. They star ted with $30 million, then $43 million, then $50
million, and now it is $53 million a year sin ce 2010-11. It is a gold-plated gravy train,
and the latest twist is that now there are three non-governmental agencies in the mix—
the so-called commissioning agencies.
Remember when we said that they were giving money to M āori gangs and selling
drugs? Remember when we said that they we re giving money to a rape crisis centre
with not one client? Remember when we sa id they gave $65,000 for a weekend hui at a
rugby club, as some sort of attempt to get connection amongst M āoridom? She opposed
that—[Interruption] What does that mean, Mr Speaker?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: One minute.
25 Sep 2013 General Debate 13707

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, I thought you were saying it was wonderful.
Sorry, Mr Speaker. Tariana Turia, in this House and outside it, denied it, in the face of
the media. I want to tell the New Zealand media that it does Māoridom no good—or this
nation any good—if it thinks it can take sides and that somehow this issue will go away.
It will not. The fact is that the Minister ha s been caught out. I have lodged a breach of
privilege. If we have got justice in this country, it will find favour. The Minister said—
not once, but twice over 2 specific days —on the question as to whether she was
involved in any sort of res ourcing of these agencies, “No.”, over, and over, and over
again. That is a breach of privilege, and that Minister should go.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: As I rise for this general debate
today, I do so knowing that the feedback I am  getting from the people of my Rangitata
electorate is that they are so  grateful to have a Government that has its eye on the ball;
that has its eye on the things that really matter to New Zealanders. So it is not what is
the matter with New Zealanders; it is what matters to New Zealanders.
One of the most important things to them is that the Government has assisted their
households and their families through the gl obal financial crisis and through the tough
times, and they have come to understand that it has their interests at heart. So it is about
responsibly managing the Government’s fi nances. As I often say to people, I
understand, as does this Nati onal Government, that when we talk about Government
spending, it is actually their spending. It is their taxpayer money that we are spending. It
is not Government money. It came out of the pockets of hard-working New Zealanders.
It is actually about a more competitiv e and productive economy, because that is
about jobs, that is about raisi ng incomes, that is about rais ing the standard of living for
the households of New Zealand. That is the so rt of stuff where, in fact, the average
household understands that it is spending so much less on its mortgage under this
National Government than it ever did und er the previous Government. They can
certainly get their heads round how that has helped them through this time.
It is about the confidence th at the people of Canterbury understand. They know that
this Government is backing them and is back ing getting the rebuild done. Canterbury is
firing on all cylinders. I can tell you that unemployment is low there. I can tell you that
in my part of Canterbury we are now sufferi ng from unease about skills shortages. So I
would say to people in the rest of New Z ealand to come on down—we have got a job
for you. We will look after you down our end of the country.
The thing I want to concentrate on today is  the Better Public Services targets. You
see, this Government does not shy away from  setting itself tough targets—targets that
will not be easy to achieve and that are not simply window dressing. Our Government
and New Zealanders understand that it is  not about spend, spend, spend—spend for the
sake of spending. It is actually about get ting some value for the money we spend. It
really is. We are certainly delivering. We are reducing crime. We do have measurable
improvements in the health of New Z ealanders. We are reducing educational
underachievement and long-term welfar e dependence. But long-term welfare
dependence is something that the members on the other side of the House depend upon.
They actually depend upon it to stay there and support them.
In fact, the targets we have actually set are quite hard to  achieve. We have actually
had to take some risks. On this side of the House, we have had to take some—

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: We’re over here.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Welfare dependence is over ther e, is it? Welfare dependence
is over there, since that is what I am act ually talking about at the moment and the
member calls out “We’re over here.” So, th e number of long-term beneficiaries has
fallen by almost 3,000, to 75,300. That is 3,000 in the past year.
13708 General Debate 25 Sep 2013
As for the Social Workers in Schools scheme, they are now implemented in decile 1
to 3 schools—72 percent of low-decile schools. That is making a real difference in those
schools. Not only have we got social workers in schools but we have got social workers
in every single district health board hospital. That makes a real difference. That makes a
real difference.
So if we want to look at some statisti cs that are truly, truly scary, 3,044 children
experienced substantia l physical abuse in the year to March 2013. But, actually, the
good news is that that is a reduction of 3.5 percent. So we are seeing—

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: That’s margin of error.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Oh, the member is dreaming. The Vulnerable Children Bill
received universal, unanimous support across the House, so that is something that we
can actually all agree on. But what we did not see under the previous Government is any
jolly improvement on that, or on any tough things. So when we went out around the
country with a green paper, we said that we wanted to hear the tough things that people
thought we should do to protect vulnerable children. We are having fantastic success
when it comes to immunisation, elective surgery, cancer treatmen t—results, results,
results under this Government—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is always extraordinary
to follow Jo Goodhew, the only Minister of Wo men’s Affairs ever to vote in this House
against paid parental leave. That is an unbelievable record that she will leave behind in
this House.
It is movie time for Nick Smith. We are up to the sequel in the series. The first
movie, as most people will know, was entitled “ Fatal Attraction: The Bronwyn Pullar
Affair”. That is how things began. For those who do not recall the details of that case, it
concerned Nick Smith writing a letter on a mi nisterial letterhead as Minister for ACC
and intervening in that case. I might say that there was a guest star in that movie—
Judith Collins. While we are discussing that , we still do not know who leaked the email
out of Judith Collins’ office. We still do not know that today. There are some suspicions
around, but she was certainly a guest star in that movie.
Now we have reached the sequel. The se quel is a remake of  a well-known film, The
Dam Busters—or, in this case, “The Accidental Dam Buster”, with Nick Smith. What is
not well-known about the Dam Busters movie is that it is actually based on an operation
in World War II called Operation Chastise. It w ould be fair to say th at there has been a
great deal of chastising going on, on the other side of the House. Nick Smith is very
grateful for the fact that Gerry Brownl ee and Steven Joyce are not here, because
Operation Chastise was taking place in the Beehive earlier this week.
Nick Smith just cannot stick to one story about what has happened. What Nick Smith
told us on 17 September is: “I did not give the department an indication of what that
submission would be.”

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: “I did not have sex with that woman.”

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: He also said: “I did not know that this draft document
even existed until this morning.” As my colleague Annette King says, there are echoes
here of “I did not have sex with that woman Ms Lewinsky.” Nick Smith cannot keep his
story straight in this matter.
What we are seeing here from Nick Smith is  a continuation of his form, his complete
lack of respect for any kind of due process, and a conti nuation of the crony capitalism
that is now the mark of this Government. Nick Smith has the ACC case. He also has the
Canterbury Regional Council case. It is importa nt to remember that when Nick Smith
was asked why he cancelled the Canterbur y Regional Council elections in 2010, he
said: “Because I’m worried about the outcome.” That is what he told New Zealanders.
25 Sep 2013 General Debate 13709
His lack of respect for democracy is so great that he cancelled those elections. So he has
form in this. He also has form in the funding of the Mackenzie Basin consultative
process on behalf of Jacqui Dean, where he overrode the Ministry for the Environment’s
funding processes to put in funding for his pet project.
This National Government does not believe in  the old “one rule fo r all” saying that
we used to hear from Don Brash—no, it does no t. There is one rule for National Party
Ministers. They can intervene. They can me ddle. They can show up on behalf of their
cronies, because that is the kind of Governme nt we have now. It is a Government that
works in the interests of its mates and not in the interests of ordinary New Zealanders
and the people who work every day to earn a living in this country.
There should be a third film in this series, and that is Gone with the Wind—or “Gone
with the River ”, because that is what Nick Smith should be. If John Key has any
standards for ministerial behaviour, Nick Smith should be gone. He has misled this
Parliament. He has misled New Zealanders. He has intervened in a process that the
Department of Conservation legitimately wa nted to be involved in. We stand here
today, with a staff member having resigne d from the Department of Conservation
because of this Minister’s interference.
John Key needs to say to Nick Smith that his time has gone—there has been one too
many breaches of what New Zealanders woul d see as the standards of ministerial
behaviour. John Key is letting it go because  his Government is on the ropes. Nick
Smith’s behaviour has fallen well short of the expectations of New Zealanders. This is a
continuation of the cronyism, of the meddling, of a Government on its way out.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I am wearing a gerbera, which is
the symbol for Arthritis New Zealand, to ac knowledge and celebrate the organisation’s
wonderful work with the many New Zealanders  who are living with that deb ilitating
and often painful condition. I also want to acknowledge those who are out collecting in
their annual appeal this w eek—in pretty inclement condi tions in many parts of the
country. I am always so proud of the genero sity of New Zealande rs in responding to
such good causes.
I am also very proud to be a member of a Government that is doing such a good job
focusing on the challenges and the issues that matter to New Zealanders, and is
succeeding. One of the four key planks of our current term of office, as was mentioned
by the Hon Jo Goodhew, is delivering better  public services. That is because New
Zealanders want their Government to spe nd their hard-earned tax dollars wisely, and
they deserve to see positive results for that  expenditure. We have been through very
challenging times since the recession hit at  the end of 2007, and our Government has
had to make many tough decisions to ge t public spending unde r control and the
Government’s books back into surplus. We are succeeding and that is a remarkable
achievement, which has earned admiration from Standard and Poor’s, the IMF, and
many Governments that look on New Zealand with great envy.
The members opposite love to talk of cuts . Frequently they make them up because
the facts do not support the story they are trying to tell . In fact, their constant
misrepresentation of the Government’s fi scal strategy and signi ficant progress is a
major reason for their failure to connect with the electorate at large or to persuade the
public to accept their attempts to rewrite history.
My constituents in Hamilton West know we have had to get Government spending
under control after the reckless approach that  we inherited at the end of 2008, and they
understand that we are following a programme to attract investment in our economy and
job creation. They are unimpressed by th e constant opposition of Labour MPs and
Green MPs to the many options that we ar e suggesting to create new job opportunities
and investment in this countr y. The facts demonstrate that our plan is getting results
13710 General Debate 25 Sep 2013
because the economy is growing, wages are incr easing, and interest ra tes are at record
lows.
More than 65,000 jobs have been created in the past 2 years and our unemployment
rate is lower than that of most developed countries. Business confidence is the highest it
has been this century and our manufactur ing sector has grown 9.2 percent since 2009—
an amazing turn-round from just a year before, when Labour was in office and it
plummeted. Our fiscal outlook has impr oved markedly, our management of the
economy is sound, we are on track to surplus in 2014-15, and we will be one of the few
countries in the world that will not be increasing public debt at that point.
At the start of this term of Government the Prime Minister set some very ambitious
targets for those who are delivering better p ublic services in our country. That is
because we are an ambitious Government and because New Zealanders want to see
better outcomes across health, education, social  welfare, our criminal justice system,
and elsewhere, and in every one of those ar eas we are delivering. Th e recent results are
very good.
Let us consider some of the results. We have committed to reducing child abuse and
neglect in New Zealand because it is a tragic blight on our society. In the year to March
2013 we have seen a 3.5 percent reduction in  the number of New Zealand children who
are experiencing substantiated physical abuse. It is still a major challenge, and I am
absolutely committed to the Children’s Action Plan, which Paula Bennett has rolled out,
because it will deliver further gains and further safety for our children in this country.
Our crime rate is the lowest it has been for 30 years, and our police are doing a superb
job—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How long?

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Thirty years. The police do a superb job on the front line. Most
encouragingly, youth crime has fallen by 19 per cent in just 2 years. We have already
exceeded the Better Public Services target.
As a political candidate, and latterly as an MP, I hammered the need for a much
greater focus on rehabilitating those who are already in ou r criminal justice system,
because there is no point in incarcerating offe nders at great expense to taxpayers if we
do nothing to reduce the likelihood of thei r reoffending on release. That is why I
warmly welcome a raft of initiatives that we  have seen in recent months from the Hon
Anne Tolley. We have seen a new nationwid e reintegration progr amme called Out of
Gate, which will deliver fantastic services to those who are on the point of being
released. It is a fantastic initiative. I really commend it. It will ensure they have much
greater options to get a job at that crucial tim e just before their release, when they could
be at risk of reoffending.
We have seen that there are fewer victims of crime, and there are further reductions
in reoffending rates as a result of the new edu cation strategy that is  being rolled out for
prisoners. The majority of prisoners cannot r ead or write properly.  This is a serious
driver of crime. That is why we are tackling the problem. It is working.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I recognise the Hon Ruth
Dyson.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I would be very disappointed if you
did not, Mr Assistant Speaker. It is a real pleasure to talk in this general debate this
afternoon, but I am really disappointed in my su bject. I have not seen very often in this
Parliament the kind of inconsistencies a nd misleading that the Hon Nick Smith has
indulged in in the last 2 weeks,  and I say that it does a diss ervice to the whole of this
House. The reputation of this Parliament shoul d be important to all of us. If a Minister
ends up doing something that is not right, then I think it is incumbent on that Minister to
front up and say so.
25 Sep 2013 General Debate 13711
But what we have seen is that the Minister  of Conservation was briefed clearly on a
draft submission from the Department of Conservation that it wanted to make—and,
actually, it is its statutory obligation to make—to the board of inquiry looking at the
proposal for plan changes to do with the Ruataniwha dam. It was concerned about it and
it wanted to make a submissi on expressing its concerns, pa rticularly about the water
quality and the impact on native fish. That is  its responsibility. It briefed the Minister.
He has consistently denied knowing of the existence of that submission. How could a
Minister be briefed on a subm ission, raise concerns about it,  ask for a copy of the full
submission before it is submitted, and then deny its very existence? That is not credible.
Today I was very disappointed that the Minister was not able to join us in the House
to answer questions, and I think that my  disappointment was matched only by the
disappointment of Nick Smith’s colleague Tony Ryall, who was clearly disappointed
that he was passed the parcel—an absolute hospital pass—in trying to justify the
inconsistency that I just referred to. Minister  Nick Smith has said that he did not give
the Department of Conservation an indicati on of what its submission should be. Yet the
deputy director-general—not a junior staff member; a competent well-regarded
professional—sent an email out to her seni or colleagues saying: “The Minister has
expressed concern about our submission. He wa nts to see a final copy of it. You should
send it over tomorrow, because I am out of town.” I am quoting from the email, Mr
Assistant Speaker, rather than referring to  you. Then she said: “He has expressed
concern and might want us to let the determ ination about the water quality be made by
the EPA.” It was a clear indication from th e Minister about what  should be in the
submission and what should not, and, again, we have had the Minister denying that.
The denial of knowing about the submission is clearly not credible. The Minister had
a briefing, he expressed concer n, he asked for a full copy, and then he said that he did
not know of the existence of the draft submi ssion. That is just totally unbelievable. It
just cannot be true. He then said that he did not have any influence on that submission at
all. As I have just said, if you line that st atement up against the statement of the deputy
director-general from the email that wa s sent, which is now on the department’s
website, that statement clearly is not credible either. And this afternoon we have had
further revelations of Minist ers riding roughshod over their departments in relation to
this very same proposal, the Ruataniwha dam. Had David Cunliffe been allowed to table
the documents that he sought leave to table, which was denied by the Hon John Banks,
then that would be out in the public domain. I certainly hope he is ab le to table those in
the future.
The Ministry for Primary Industries, a nother Government department, expressed
concern in its draft about the Ruatan iwha dam proposal about the phosphorus
management, about the lack of industry be st practice, about th e economics of the
proposal, and about the nutrient management system—very similar concerns to those
expressed by the Department of Conservation. The ministry no doubt reported that to its
Minister. What did its final submission say? Its final submission omitted everything
about the water quality and went from the draft submission saying that the economics of
this proposal are very dodgy, very risky, to sa ying that this is a ve ry solid proposal on
economic grounds—a miraculous U-turn.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I would just like to say—and I am sure the
Hon Annette King will join me in saying—t o the Hon Tony Ryall 60 million thankyous
on behalf of the people of the West Coast for the Grey Base Hospital. That is one of the
most wonderful pieces of news that we have  had in recent times. But one of the most
important things to National is—as members opposite know; you can see it in their eyes
that they know—supporting families and households. We are doing it in spades. We are
doing it in spades. We are doing it with our clear plan to take New Zealand forward. We
13712 General Debate 25 Sep 2013
are doing it where it matters, when it matters, and for whom it matters. How are we able
to do this in times of ea rthquakes, global recession, and continuing economic risk? We
do it through having the Prim e Minister we have got. We do it from having the Cabinet
Ministers that we have got, a nd in my view they work extraordinarily hard. And we do
it through having the whole of the Nationa l caucus working with our coalition
partners—

items.speaker: Hon Chester Borrows
items.text: As a team.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: —as a team; as a team, quite right.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: United.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: A united team.
One of the biggest differences between centre- right and centre-left, just to be serious
for a moment, is the size of the Public Se rvice. This is a major divide, in my
observation, in New Zealand politics, and always has been. Each side is equally
determined that their way is best. Labour and the Greens combined believe in big
Government, with big Government departments and lots of civil servants. Ask the real
estate agents in Wellington how much property the Labour Government had leased
before we saw it off the Treasury benches.  There were heaps—heaps of places were
under lease. National-led Governments work on  the basis of judging the use and effect
of Government services—not on the basis of  size, not on the basis of the number of
staff, but on having better public services. Targ ets have been set. Strategies have been
introduced, implemented, reviewed, and a ssessed. There are many indications of
success. We have heard of so many examples t oday from this side of the House. It has
been a pleasure listening to the speeches from my colleagues. It really gives one
confidence that the country is in good condition, in good heart.  Mortgages rates are half
of what they used to be under Labour—half of  what they used to be under Labour, the
“Shylock Party”.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: What about Christchurch?

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Christchurch is getting re built. The economy is growing.
Jobs are being created, weekly wages are incr easing, and interest rates generally are at

employed in New Zealand now in paid work th an ever before, more than at any other
time. New Zealand has a proud history. Othe r countries look at our managed success
with understandable envy—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Sorry to interrupt the
honourable member, but there were two memb ers who do not have the floor who are
interjecting on each other, and that is not permitted.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Thank you so much for introducing an element of control
on the side benches—a constant risk to the—[ Interruption] I am not going to repeat
that, but they are a constant  risk to the integrity of good government. However, I had
not actually noticed them. I had not actually heard them. But it really is interesting to

Our Prime Minister has been doing a great job overseas, putting our credentials before

But one of the achievements of this Government that I am particularly proud of is in
the health portfolio—in the health portfoli o. I remember when we were in Opposition
when Pete Hodgson was Minister of Healt h. Do you remember “Screeching Pete”? I
remember when the Hon Tony Ryall pick ed up the portfolio and shook it like a
