people stuck in corridors and all that sort of thing. I know that Annette King was very
disturbed as well. When we became the G overnment, the Hon Tony Ryall transformed
25 Sep 2013 General Debate 13713
the health services and the National-led Government committed to growth in health
services—committed to growth in health se rvices. I have been stopped by doctors and
medical practitioners at servic e stations, in the street, in  a number of towns throughout
New Zealand, where people say “Please tell Tony he is doing a wonderful job.”, and he
is.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member must
use the Minister’s full name or title.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I will say it again—

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: Climate scientists and officials are assembled
in Stockholm this week to go through the firs t part of the Inter governmental Panel on
Climate Change’s fifth assessment report. Th e focus is on the scientific findings of
climate change. We know from the media that  the report is confirming the scientific
forecasts of climate change that were put  forward generally in 2007. The difference is
that the scientists are now affirming this  with greater confid ence. Although this is
reassuring, it does not alter the terrain for policy makers in terms of the need for
prescribed policy. In fact, we have known for two decades now of the need for an
economic transformation. The first Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report
of 1990 concluded that scientis ts were virtually certain th at emissions resulting from
human activities are substantially increas ing the atmospheric concentration of
greenhouse gases. Based on then current em issions, global warmi ng would be about 3
degrees by 2100. That was in 1990. The panel’s four subsequent reports have simply
reaffirmed what we largely knew 23 years ago.
This scientific insight, you might hope, would be matc hed with rational discussion
and insightful policy. Given the stakes involv ed—the bio-integrity of the planet, the
health of the global economy, the quality of life of our children—you might think we
would act on the basis of the precautionary principle we proclaimed at the Earth
Summit back in 1992. But rationality and insight have been attacked by vested interest
and a weird form of scepticism. That has de layed action, to a point  where we now face
catastrophe if urgent action is not undertaken.
The World Bank president, attending Stoc kholm, said yesterday: “Decades of
progress are now in danger of being rolled back, because of climate change … This is a
‘make-or-break’ decade fo r action on global warming. The time to address the
interlinked challenges of climate change and ending extreme poverty is now.”
There is a difference between the scien tific method and political gaming. Science
requires, by its nature, cont estation of hypotheses advanced and conclusions reached.
Political gaming allows the undermining of th at process through tac tics of defamation
and selectivity of fact. Let us listen to the scientists in the past 24 hours. They are saying
a few things about the confidence thing. They are saying that they are about as certain
that global warming is a man-made threat as they are that cigarettes kill. They are
saying that they are as sure about climate change as they are about the age of the
universe. They are more certain about clim ate change than about vitamins making you
healthy.
George Gray used to be the chief scientist in the Bush administration. He said:
“There’s a group of people who seem to think that when scientists say they are
uncertain, we shouldn’t do anything … That ’s crazy.” A new group of international
leaders, headed by former Irish president Mary Robinson, has just issued an appeal. She
said: “The time for radical leadership on climate change is now … for the sake of
generations to come,”.
So the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s fifth assessment view,
according to the media, is that atmospheric carbon dioxide has increased 40 percent
since 1750, half of that in the last half cen tury. Temperature rises are pretty much as
13714 General Debate 25 Sep 2013
projected back in 2007, most likely around 2 de grees plus, perhaps almost 5 degrees.
The fifth Intergovernmental Panel on Climat e Change report on climate science will be
another wake-up call for humanity. It will in form us on the related issues that must
follow—an assessment of impact and mitigation measures.
And what will New Zealand have to say? Wh at might we ask of the Minister? He is
attending trade talks in Asia right now, largely indifferent to the real global issues of the
day in the Swedish capital. What emission reduc tions have been achieved as a result of
his Government’s radical lead ership in the emissions trading scheme? What is our
projected emissions level for 2020, the end of  the make or break decade for action on
global warming? Is he satisfied that the 5 percent unconditional target set by New
Zealand for 2020 is enough, is a fa ir share in global radical l eadership for this critical
decade? Why do he and the John Key Government  not show greater concern for what is
happening around them?

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is always interesting to follow a
Green member in a debate such as the general debate—one where we have doom and
green gloom, ad nauseam.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: What?

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Doom and green gloom. The Green vision for New Zealand is
like the Amish without the Bibles . It is back to the horses a nd the carts. It is back to
doom and gloom, and, frankly, we on this side of the House have a far more optimistic,
a far more positive, a far more aspirational view of the world. Ours is a Government—
led so ably by the Rt Hon John Key—that has a vision and a view of New Zealand that
is going to create the brighter future that we have already set in place for all folk in our
country. Our plan is about responsibly managing the Government’s finances so that
taxes are spent wisely and services are provided well.
Over the last 48 hours my electorate of Coromandel has been buffeted by high winds,
by heavy seas, and by heavy rain. That is no  doubt all due to th e climate change, Dr
Graham?

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: The member says it is no doubt due to all the climate change. It
is probably more to do with the annua l spring equinox, actually. It has been going on
since time immemorial. It has probably got to  do with nothing more than just the spring
equinox. Trees are down, roads have been clos ed by slips, and there have been high
tides all around the electorate. Roads have been closed, and electricity, I am told, is still
off in some parts of the electorate. So my  good wishes and concerns go to the hard-
working, stoic, diligent people of the Coro mandel, who are putting things to right,
getting on with the job, and cleaning up after the storm. I want to particularly mention
and thank our emergency services on the pe ninsula, most of which are volunteer
emergency services. They have done a great job.
Better public services are what  this Government is abou t. Yesterday during question
time I had the opportunity to ask our very capab le Minister of Justice, the Hon Judith
Collins, about the conviction and sentencing statistics for the 2012-13 financial year. I
am delighted to say that she was able to confirm to the House that the figures just
released show that the number of adults ch arged in our courts has decreased a further 7
percent in the last 12 months—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: 7 percent.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a further 7 percent. Si nce the 2008-09 financial year the
total number of people charged with criminal  offences has been reduced by a massive
23 percent. That is 23 percent. The number of  people charged with criminal offences in
our justice system has reduced by this massive 23 percent.
25 Sep 2013 General Debate 13715
Clearly, the justice sector is working well, and in my capacity as chair of the Justice
and Electoral Committee I am very pleased to be able to work with National’s justice
team. That involves the Minister of Justice, Judith Collins, the Minister for Courts, the
very capable Chester Borrows, the Minister of Police and the Mini ster of Corrections,
Anne Tolley, and, of course, the Attorney-G eneral, Chris Finlays on. Together they are
doing a great job. Altogether it means that ther e are fewer people in our criminal justice
system, because this is a Government that  is committed to maki ng New Zealand a safer
place for all so that we have fewer victims in our community. It is absolutely important
that we do have that.
These statistics show that our initiatives across the sector ar e having very positive
results. The crime rate is down to its lowest  in more than 30 years—the lowest crime
rate in more than 30 years. And it gets better because under National, youth crime, in
particular, has fallen 19 percent in just 2 years—19 percent down in 2 years. This means
that we have already exceeded the Better Public Services target to reduce youth
offending by 5 percent by 2017. So what have  we done? We have upped the challenge.
We have upped the challenge and we have incr eased the target so that it is now set at a
25 percent reduction by 2017. The number of  young people appearing in court is
dropping as well. Child and youth prosecution statistics show that the number of
children and young people being charged in court is at its lowest in 20 years.
So collectively this National Government is bringing better public services to New
Zealand, and in the justice sector we are really excelling. That means there are fewer
victims and fewer New Zealanders who are fe eling unsafe in their homes and in their
workplaces. Together, this is a good Government doing an exceptionally good job,
which is making the justice sector a hallmar k of success in terms of our better public
services. This is a good G overnment doing a great job,  and I am privileged and
delighted to be working with such capable colleagues on this side of the House.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
NEW ZEALAND MISSION TRUST BOARD (OTAMATAHA) EMPOWERING
BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: I move, That the New
Zealand Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Em powering Bill be now read a first time.
Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. Ka nui te mihi ki a koe i tēnei rā.
[Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I appreciate you hugely today.]
I nominate the M āori Affairs Committee to consider the bill. Ka nui taku mihi ki a
koutou e whakarongo mai n ā i roto o Tauranga Moana i t ēnei w ā. Ko te t ūmanako ia
kua aro mai koutou ki te ia o t ēnei o ng ā k ōrero. Te tikanga ia ka whakahokia t ēnei
wāhanga whenua ki ētahi ō koutou, hoi an ō, koinei te mihi o te ng ākau ki a koutou
katoa. Tēnā koutou.
[My huge appreciation to you co llectively listening in from Tauranga at this point in
time. The hope is that you have taken aboard the tenor of this of the speeches. It means
essentially that this parcel  of land will be returned  to some of you, and so an
acknowledgment from the heart to you all. Well done.]
As I stand to open the discussion on this bill, the New Zealand Mission Trust Board
(Otamataha) Empowering Bill, I want to  first acknowledge Albert Puhirake Īhaka, the
chair of the Ōtamataha Trust and promoter of th e bill. I think his leadership and
perseverance in bringing this bill to fr uition should be commended. In achieving this
significant moment in the statute, recognition must also go to Mr Alan Tate, the trust
administrator who has managed the preparator y work to get here today. He has liaised
13716 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otama taha) Empowering Bill 25 Sep 2013
with the Department of Internal Affairs, Land Information New Zealand, Trinity Wharf,
Te Pīhopa o Aotearoa, the registrar-general, the Solicitor-General, and Crown Law—all
agencies that have a direct interest in this bill.
I want to also acknowledge all of the trustees: M ōrehu Ngātoko Rahipere, Desmond
Matakōkiri Tata, Joanne Ng āpeeti Gear, Peri R āweti Kohu, Sylvia Hemoata Willison,
Rena Uruhina Bennett, Raewyn Ngakum āmā Keith, and William Charles Retireti
McGuigan. I first met the trustees in Se ptember 2009 to discus s their proposal to
introduce a private bill to vary the terms of a trust affecting land at Dive Crescent in
Tauranga Moana. Of course, 4 years later it is  a great day today to see this bill finally
come before the House.
But if I thought that 4 years appears to be  a significant time to wait, it pales into
insignificance with the 117 years that these people have had to wait. This bill, in
acknowledging and recognising the mana of Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi Tamar āwaho, also
appreciates their status over land that ha s been held by the New Zealand Mission Trust
since 1896. The bill transfers land in Tauranga and other property from the New
Zealand Mission Trust to the Ōtamataha Trust so that it can be used for the beneficiaries
of the Ōtamataha Trust rather than of the 1896 trust. At the heart of the bill, then, we are
talking about two trusts. The Ōtamataha Trust was es tablished by the hap ū of Ngati
Tapu and Ngai Tamar āwaho to own and manage land and other property acquired
through those historical common interests of those hapū in Tauranga Moana.
The New Zealand Mission Trust Board is a body incorporated under the Religious
Charitable and Educational Trust Boards Incorporation Act 1884. The purpose of that
Act was to hold the assets of the board in trust for the spiritual benefit and spiritual
instruction of M āori people in the North Island or, failing that, the evangelisation of
heathen races in any part of the world. We ha ve to remember that we are talking here
about 1884, and that the Mission Trust Board itself was a by-product of the Church
Missionary Society. The Church Missionary So ciety was formed out of the global goal
to send the missionaries to “Africa and the re st of the heathen worl d” to “propagate the
knowledge of the Gospel among the Heathen.”
It would be a little b it remiss of me as th e co-leader of the M āori Party to avoid the
obvious, which is to comment on the use of the word “heathen” to marginalise, oppress,
and discriminate against Māori as the other. It fits within the context of political, social,
economic, and cultural discrimination of the day—a time in which tangata whenua were
described in other comparable terms, su ch as “the noble savage” and other terms
denoting an immoral status.
It was anticipated that the introduction of the Gospel to indigenous people would
transform them from this supposedly heat hen state to a world of civilisation. The
process of converting indigenous  populations to the doctrin e of Western Christianity
was meant to achieve beneficial return fo r the native congregati on. It is outside the
scope of this bill to pass any judgment on th e Church Missionary Society other than to
note its role in the land in question.
The Church Missionary Society was esta blished in Tauranga in 1835. In 1838 and
1839 the society purchased two blocks of land at Te Papa—the Te Papa Peninsula being
the site of central Taura nga today. The 1838 purchase wa s carried out by deed by Rev.
Alfred Nesbit Brown on behalf of the Church  Missionary Society. He was charged with
purchasing land at Tauranga, including Ōtamataha, from tangata whenua. The 1838
transaction, however, has never been accepted by tangata whenua as a sale of the land to
the Church Missionary Society, and therein lies the genesis of this bill.
The core issue at the heart of this bill is to recognise that the awarding of the Crown
grant in 1852 was, in itself, contrary to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. In 2004
the Waitangi Tribunal, in Te Raupatu o Tauranga Moana: Report on the Tauranga
25 Sep 2013 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill 13717
Confiscation Claims , after considering the manner in  which the Crown grant for the
land was awarded to the Church Missionary Society, concluded “we find that Godfrey
failed to ascertain and acknowle dge the conditional nature of the transactions under
Maori customary law and that  he wrongly concluded that  the [Church Missionary
Society] had fully and fairly purchased the whole of the area. The Crown, in accepting
Godfrey’s recommendation and finally awar ding the [Church Missionary Society] a
Crown grant for the whole area, was therefore in breach of the Treaty principle of active
protection.”
Fifteen years after the awarding of the Cr own grant, in 1867 th e Church Missionary
Society gifted the Crown four-fifths of the land, and military settlers were settled on it.
On 28 September 1896 the residue of that land, including Ōtamataha, was transferred by
the Church Missionary Society to the New Zealand Mission Trust.
Fast forward a century and in 1996 the New Zealand Mission Trust Board handed
back control of the land to the new trus tees appointed by Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi
Tamarāwaho. That all appears to be very posi tive, but there was a catch. Although the
new trustees had control of the land, they ar e still obliged to use the land with the new
Sebel Hotel built on it. The trust would collect  the ground rent from that hotel. It has
always been the intention of the two trusts  that it be changed so that the two hap ū can
benefit from it directly.
So 2 years after the control of the land was passed over in a deed dated 20 September
1998, the then trustees of the New Zealand Mission Trust Board, in recognition of the
manner and the process by which the land wa s acquired from tangata  whenua, resigned
as trustees. They were immediately repla ced by the trustees representing the hap ū of
Ngāti Tapu and Ngāi Tamarāwaho. This bill, then, puts right a wrong that occurred over
a century ago.
In the letter that Albert Īhaka wrote to the Clerk of th e House of Representatives in
submitting this bill, he summed up the purposes  in one clear statement. He said: “The
reason for this bill is to enable property to be used for the be nefit of people and hap ū
from whose t ūpuna that property  was originally derived.” That property will be
transferred from the charitable trust that cu rrently holds that property to a new common
law trust. The beneficiaries of this new trust and, indeed, this bill will rightfully be the
descendants of the tūpuna from which the property was originally taken.
So, ultimately, the history and the context of this bill rest with the mana of Ng āti
Tapu and Ng āi Tamarāwaho. We look forward to hearing more from these hap ū about
their historical common interests in Taur anga Moana and at Te Papa. That common
interest extends from Tauranga Harbour to  the Waikareao Estuary and includes all of
the land north of that line, including reclaimed land at Sulphur Point and the adjacent
harbour bed. At the select committee we will also learn more about the significance of
their whakapapa to Tapukino, in the case of Ng āti Tapu, and Tahuriwakanui in the case
of Ngāi Tamarāwaho.
My fervent wish is that these people w ho have waited well over a hundred years for
justice to be done will now be able to see th is injustice righted in as quick a time frame
as can be realistically achieved. I commend this bill to the House today.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. My colleague Te
Ururoa Flavell from the M āori Party sums up the New Zealand Mission Trust Board
(Otamataha) Empowering Bill in the nicest lang uage possible. But to  think that in the
year 2013 we are in the House before you fi xing up a rather messy and dirty episode—
one small dirty episode—that  happened in the Tauranga  Moana area some 100 years
ago. Two hundred years ago Samuel Mars den got on a boat and came out to New
Zealand, and that is where his deed—I was going to say “dirty deed”, but it might not be
correct of me because I suppose that in his day his adventure was to go to all corners of
13718 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otama taha) Empowering Bill 25 Sep 2013
the earth and Anglicise everybody he saw, whet her it was right or wrong. That was his
mahi; that was his job. I must say that when  he first came here he had only a couple of
supporters from the indigenous people. It took him a while to get them all signed up to
this new and funny religion at that time, Christianity. He did a good job because by the
time he was sort of moving on in his life, most of M āoridom had signed up for
Christianity.
But as we have seen over our history, esp ecially members of this House in dealing
with Treaty settlements, on occasion—more than one occasion—there have been some
suspicious deals done over landholdings, and none more so than by the Church. It is
pleasing to note that in this enlightened time the Church itself has realised that there
were mistakes and bad deeds done in the name of the Lord, and it is willing today to
help fix those problems that caused so much damage. To Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi
Tamarāwaho I say well done. Well done for waiting fo r the return of land that is highly
significant to you both. If I can be so  bold as to say that both hap ū say it re-establishes
their connection to the water of Tauranga Moana, it provides an income to the hap ū to
finance other activities, including allowing hap ū to participate in the downtown
economy of Tauranga, and it comes just befo re the 150-year anniversary of Gate P ā,
which is next year. I am pretty sure that we will get the bill back into the House and
done and dusted before that anniversary.
The Ōtamataha Trust has been established by the hapū of, like I said, Ngāti Tapu and
Ngāi Tamar āwaho to own and manage land and ot her property just like any other
normal person in this country. That is a great thing. The bill declares the new trustees to
be a leasing authority for the purposes of the Public Bodies Leases Act 1969. The land
being transferred will be subject to a leas e granted under that Act. This enables the
transfer to happen without affecting the lease and le ssee’s rights. The Church
Missionary Society, the CMS,  was established in Tauranga in 1835, and in 1838 the
society bought two blocks from tangata whenua  on the site that is where the city of
Tauranga is today. When I say “bought”, I mean “bought” in i nverted commas; bought
in the language of the day. The transacti on has never been accepted by tangata whenua
as a sale of the land to the Church Mi ssionary Society. In 1867 the Crown acquired by
gift of the Church Missionary Society four-f ifths of the land, which had been vested in
the Church Missionary Society by Crown gr ant in 1852, and military settlers were
settled on it. This land was surrounded by confiscated M āori land that was also settled.
In 1896 the remaining land, including Ōtamataha, was transferred from the Church
Missionary Society to the New Zealand Missio n Trust Board, which held the assets of
the board on trust for the spiritual benefit and spiritual instruction of Māori people in the
North Island of New Zealand—and here is th e bit that I really, really like—or, failing
that, the evangelisation of heathen races in any part of the world. So—

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: There’s still hope for you, Tau.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: There is still hope for me. The interesting thing is that through
the so-called purchase of this little block of land it was not only for the Anglicisation or
the evangelisation of iwi M āori but for the rest of the world as well. So way back then
we were having an effect on the world’ s Christian population. Those people in the
deepest, darkest parts of Africa, Austra lia, America, and England, even, should be
thankful to Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi Tamar āwaho for their contribution to their
evangelisation. In 1996 the New Zealand Missi on Trust Board handed back control of
the land to the new trustees appointed by Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi Tamarāwaho. This was
done in recognition of the manner and process by which the land was originally
acquired from tangata whenua.
I want to mention the Treaty of Waitangi a nd what the Waitangi Tribunal said in its

items.speaker: Te Raupatu o Tauranga Moana
items.text: Report on the Tauranga Confiscation Claims  in 2004,
25 Sep 2013 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill 13719
and echo what my colleague Te Ururoa Flavell said, “… after considering the manner in
which a Crown grant for the land includi ng Otamataha was awarded to the Church
Mission Society in 1852 [it] concluded … : ‘we find that Godfrey failed to ascertain and
acknowledge the conditional natu re of the transactions unde r Maori customary law and
that he wrongly concluded that the CMS had fully and fairly purchased the whole of the
area. The Crown, in accepting Godfrey’s recommendation and finally awarding the
CMS a Crown grant for the whole area, was ther efore in breach of the Treaty principle
of active protection.’ ” The sad thing about that is that th ese people had to go to the
tribunal only to find the tri bunal rule in their favour but that it could not do anything
about it because the land was not in Crown hands; it was in private ownership. And
through the good deeds of various people from then on to this day—and I want to
congratulate my colleague Te Ururoa Flavell on being the member who sees this bill
through the House. Despite this conclusion, s ection 6(4A)(a) of the Treaty of Waitangi
Act 1975 prevented the Waitangi Tribunal fr om making any recommendation affecting
the future ownership of Ōtamataha, because the land, as I said, was not owned or
controlled by the Crown.
It is a good day. I am pleased as the chairperson of the M āori Affairs Committee to
have this before our committee, and can guarantee that we will not only enjoy our work
listening to submissions but make a bit of a pi lgrimage, to coin a phrase, to the area to
listen to those submitters and actually get a feel for what is being handed over. I also
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker. I am pleased to be able to take a call on the first reading of the New Zealand
Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empoweri ng Bill. I also want to endorse the
sentiments of the chair of the M āori Affairs Committee to congratulate Te Ururoa
Flavell on bringing the bill to the House. It is a good example of where issues sit outside
the context of Treaty settlements but where they are included within the context of
Waitangi Tribunal claims. You can find a so lution albeit it takes a long time getting
there. So thank you, Te Ururoa, for the exte nsive history that you have given regarding
Ngāti Tapu and Ngāi Tamarāwaho’s interests in Tauranga Moana.
I had the privilege to be able to sit alongside a member of Ng āi Tamar āwaho and
listen to some of their histor y and connection to raupatu th at occurred over there. Much
of the interests of that particular hapū, as I understand it, actually extend into the central
business district of Tauranga Moana, of Taur anga City Council. So there is a level of
concern that within the contex t of their broader Treaty set tlement claims, the nature of
their interests may not wholly be satisfied by the claims settlement process. We can
only wait and see because the Government is  continuing its negotiations with the
Tauranga Moana claimants. But for the purposes  of this discussion and in the interests
of Ng āi Tamar āwaho, it is a significant interest w ithin the Tauranga central business
district, and I hope that they are able to achieve some greater settlement recognition
come that time.
Te Ururoa made mention of the Ōtamataha Trust, in partic ular, the contribution of
Albert Puhirake Īhaka. I too want to recognise the hard  work and effort that have gone
into preparing the bill and in getting it to a point where the interests of the trust and the
New Zealand Mission Trust Board have been able to converge and present something
that this House can have a level of confidence in. When the bill gets to the M āori
Affairs Committee, I am sure that members around our table will be hearing for the first
time some of the extensive interactions of the missi onaries during the 1800s in
Tauranga Moana, and the impact that they had on the hap ū in that region. There will
probably be a smattering of familiarity thr oughout their story that will be common to
other stories in other regions, as well. But th e point of all that is to ensure that an
13720 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otama taha) Empowering Bill 25 Sep 2013
enduring opportunity to rec ognise the connection of Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi Tamarāwaho
to this area can be achieved, that there is a management structure in place, and that there
will be an ongoing opportunity for the manage ment of the interests and purposes of
what happens on that land that can take place.
When I was reading through the notes on this particular bill, I thought it was of some
interest that the Waitangi Tribunal report was quite clear. Without repeating
contributions of previous members, I thought this particular statement was germane to
how this bill came about. It is taken from the Waitangi Tribunal report on the Tauranga

items.speaker: Moana confiscation claims. It said
items.text: “The Crown acquired the Te Papa lands without
accounting for the implied trust, which it wa s aware of. According to the Crown’s own
records, the land was held in trust for the benefit of Maori.  In ignoring the trustee role
the CMS”—the Church Missionary Soci ety—“had in holding the land, the Crown
further breached the principle of active pr otection.” What we understand throughout the
whole process of Treaty se ttlements, and in the nature of interests that M āori have in
instances like this, is that where the Crown has failed its obligation in the active
protection of interests, there will always be an issue to remedy.
So I am very pleased—very, very pleased—that we have this bill, which will go to
the select committee. It will get a robust hearing that will inform the committee
members of the history of the area, and that will lead to what I predict, hopefully, will
be a larger claims settlement bill that will hopefully come to the House before the end of
the year for Tauranga Moana. I am sure that is the sincere hope of the member for
Waiariki, because the outstanding interests of the iwi in Tauranga Moana still need to be
addressed. Nō reira, ki a koe te mema m ō Waiariki, t ēnei te mihi atu ki a koe i tau mai
tēnei pire i mua i te aroaro o te Whare nei. Tēnā koe, tēnā tātou.
[And so, to you the member for Waiariki I commend you for bringing this bill before
this House. Congratulations to you and to us collectively.]

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I am very pleased to be
able to stand and support the New Zeal and Mission Trust Board (Otamataha)
Empowering Bill at its first reading. As we ha ve heard, it is a private bill that has been
brought to the House by Te Ururoa Flavell. I think it is important to thank him for the
work he has done to bring th is bill here, because these bills are difficult, they are
convoluted, and they have a long history.
The purpose of this bill is to effect the transfer of assets from the New Zealand
Mission Trust to the Ōtamataha Trust so that those assets can be used in future for the
benefit of the hap ū of Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi Tamar āwaho. This bill is an attempt to
unravel the long, complex, and convoluted history of the land near the Tauranga area.
The story started back in London in 1799, wh en the Society for Missions in Africa
and the East was founded by evangelical Chris tians. Their goal was, firstly, to convert
people in Africa and then in the East, but  this organisation became part of New
Zealand’s history when its missionaries met Samuel Marsden in Sydney. They agreed to
give Africa a miss and come to New Zeala nd. They joined him a nd they travelled and
arrived here in 1814.
Their early years in New Zealand were tu multuous, but by the time they had the
arrival of Henry Williams in 1823 they were the dominant group of Anglican
missionaries amongst M āori right throughout the North Island. They were very active
and they worked hard, but by 1830 there ha d been only two conversions. However,
during the 1830s the tide turned and there was a mass conversion of M āori. By 1845 an
estimated 43,000 Māori were attending Church Missionary Society services.
With this expansion they established mission stations throughout the North Island. In
1838 the Rev. Alfred Nesbit Brown, acting on beha lf of the Church Missionary Society,
purchased two blocks of land at Te Pa pa—Te Papa, of course, is now central
25 Sep 2013 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill 13721
Tauranga—and that included Ōtamataha, from tangata whenua. In 1867 four-fifths of
this land was gifted to the Crown, and the Crow n used that to settle  military settlers.
The area where this land was had adjacen t land that had been confiscated from M āori,
and that was used as a settlement, as well. The key point here is that this 1838 purchase
by the Church Missionary Society was never accepted by tangata whenua.
In 1896 the last remaining remnants of the land, including Ōtamataha, were
transferred to the New Zealand Mission Trus t Board, which had held the assets of the
board on trust—and this is the wonderful quote the Hon Tau Henare likes—“for the
spiritual benefit and spiritual instruction of M āori people in the North Island of New
Zealand or, failing that, the evangelisation of  the heathen races in any part of the
world.” It is a fascinating story, and we  look forward to unravelling it in the M āori
Affairs Committee, hearing the full story, and making sure that we do the right thing by
tangata whenua.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. He mihi
ki te Whare. He mihi nui ki te Ng āti Tapu me Ng āi Tamar āwaho o Tauranga Moana.
Tēnā koutou. I would also like to acknowledg e the member Te Ururoa Flavell, who
brought the New Zealand Miss ion Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill to the
House.
This is an important day and it is great to  have a process whereby this issue can be
progressed, given the way that it  has struggled in other foru ms and how important it is
to the people of Tauranga Moana. It is a beautiful area of the country, full of natural
resources, but, regrettably, not shared with  the original tangata whenua, who are still
struggling for basic justice today.
All of my colleagues in the House toda y have clearly outlined some of the
fascinating history around this  very good example of what I would call the three “m”s
of colonisation: the military, the mass, and the missionaries. Those three “m”s have had
an important role in the colonisation process and are intertwined deeply in our history.
The purpose of the missionaries, as described in this bill, was the evangelisation of
the heathens. They managed to get to Aotearoa to carry this out in the 1830s, and they
were sincere in their belief that what they were doing was going to be beneficial. At the
heart of the missionaries—and I have read a number of the diaries of the Williams
families and other missionaries—was a deep-seate d belief that they were superior and a
deep-seated belief that they were bringing something that people who had not heard this
message should hear, but also that they were  superior. That superiority created a lot of
problems for them. It goes right back to Henry Williams and the signing of Te Tiriti o
Waitangi where Henry Williams, who was a fluent M āori scholar, took an interesting
approach to articles 1 and 2.
However, this bill is more specific than that. It is not just about Te Tiriti; it is about
what happened in Tauranga Moana at Te Pa pa and the Tauranga mission station. I read
last night some of the life of Alfred Br own, who was the missionary who came in 1838,
3 years after the mission was established, after he had converted a very famous rangatira
Wīremu Tamihana Tarap īpipi of Waharoa. Alfred had an  interesting life and was very
sincere, but he also pu rported to have purchased  this land from the hap ū, and, as others
have said, his understanding of “purchas e” was deeply framed by the Western
individual property rights view, rather than the understanding of what customary rights,
reciprocity, and land is actually about for the people of that place. So Alfred’s role in
the Tauranga mission station is fraught w ith contradictions, as  are those of many
missionaries around Aotearoa at the time.
Alfred was involved in attempting to mini ster to the wounded and the dead at the
battles of Gate P ā and Te Ranga, and he did attempt to be impartial, it is said, but it is
also suggested that he lost the trust of the local M āori people not only because of this
13722 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otama taha) Empowering Bill 25 Sep 2013
Ōtamataha land issue but because he was deemed to be associating with the enemies. So
he was, as many missionaries were, in an invidious position where he had a particular
set of goals that he failed to carry out . His aims, he said, were to protect M āori from
European influence and convert them into  perfect Christians , which is deeply
contradictory given that he was a European trying to convert them to a European view
of the world. Such is the complex world of the missionaries.
The missionaries in Aotearoa—not necessari ly Alfred, who was quite moderate in
his acquisitions, compared with some; for ex ample, the Williams family—acquired vast
quantities of land, and along the East Coast they still own that land. They certainly
benefited alongside the military and alongsid e the mass who migrated, in obtaining
wealth, power, and privilege. It is only right now that this bi ll begins to redress some of
that.
The Green Party is very pleased to support th is bill. We think it is high time, after
this very long battle, that these people, these hap ū, should actually get complete
authority and control. But as our first speaker said, already the land has been
unutterably altered. There is a hotel on it. They  will get the financial redress, which is a
great thing. However, they will never get what they lost and it will never be returned in
the state it was when they lost it. Money is always helpful, but mana is also important,
which is why, although the Waitangi Tribunal was very clear, they then had to go
through a long process to get to this point that we are at today.
It is really important, and I am quite sorry I am not on the M āori Affairs Committee.
I think it is a privilege to hear these stories.  It is a privilege to be presented with this
information by tangata whenua coming to this  Parliament. I know that they will get a
good hearing at the select committee. I have faith  that this bill will actually take these
people to a better place.  I look forward to the wider issu es that the Hon Nanaia Mahuta
referred to, in terms of the settlement of Taur anga Moana. We fully support this bill, so
that the mass, the military, and the missionaries can no longer dominate anyone’s land
in Aotearoa.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First on
the New Zealand Mission Trust Board (Ota mataha) Empowering Bill, brought to the
House by the member Te Ururoa Flavell. I congratulate him on doing this. There is a
huge amount of history going back hundreds of  years, as we have heard from the
member. This bill is now putting right aspe cts of that in terms of the New Zealand
Mission Trust and the handover to the new trust, which is the Ōtamataha Trust, on
behalf of the hapū of Ngāti Tapu and Ngāi Tamarāwaho.
It is wonderful when you go to Tauranga and you look around this particular area of
the headland and the central business district , because it has a huge amount of history.
To go into the mission house grounds there, w ith the beautiful historic home that is
there, the library, the other buildings, and also the trees and garden that surround it—
this is an important part of New Zealand’ s history, very similar to the mission house at
Waitangi and other mission houses around the countr y. It is very fitti ng, therefore, that
in this Parliament we are able to transfer this over to the new trust, which is part of the
local community, the local hap ū, so that they will administer it and take what was very
old legislation and update it to a modern situation.
This bill is good for the people of Ta uranga. It is good for the local hap ū and local
iwi. It brings the legislation into a modern  context and it allows the trustees to now
move forward with a lot more certainty. New Zealand First certainly supports this going
to the M āori Affairs Committee. We will be s upporting this through. This is a good,
sensible piece of legislation, which the memb er can be proud to have brought to this
House, and we support it.
25 Sep 2013 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill 13723

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Ā, kia ora an ō t ātou. Me k ōrero i te tuatahi i t ō
tātou Reo Māori mō tēnei pire e pā ana ki te hāhi i whakatipungia ai ahau, me te whenua
o ō tātou huanga Māori i roto o Tauranga Moana. Me mahara t ātou, ā te Tīhema te wā o
te Kirihimete, ka pau te 200 tau m ō te ekenga mai o te whak apono ki Aotearoa. Ko te
kaimau mai ko H āmuera Mātenga. Ko te w āhi i tau mai ai ia, ko Ōihi. Ko te kaum ātua
nana ia i whakatau, ko Ruatara. N ā, kīhai rawa r ātou i noho ki t ēnā pito, ki Rangihoua
mō te hia roa, k ātahi rātou ka whakatat ū me neke ki w āhi kē. Nō muri noa nei, ka tae
mai ngā mihinare i raro i te whakahaere ā Te Wīremu. Nā, ko tetahi o ng ā rōpū pēnei i
te H āhi Mihingare i whai pakiaka ai ki ro to o Tauranga Moana hei torotoro, hei
whakawhānui atu i te whakapono.
Arā noa atu wetahi kōrero i puta i te koretake o te hāhi ēngari, kaua tātou e pōhēhē he
kino te katoa o ng ā mahi i oti i te r ōpū nei m ō te iwi M āori. N ā ōku m ātua o roto o
Ngāpuhi a Hongi Hika m ā i whakat ūpato i Te Ao M āori. Ko te kararehe hei
whakamataku i ō tamariki, i ō mokopuna, ko te koti whero, ēhara ko ngā mihinare. Nā,
kia whārikitia e ahau i te tuatahi, e Te Māngai o te Whare, he kōrero pērā.
[Greetings to us once again. But first I must address in our M āori language this bill,
which relates to the Church I was brought up in and relates to the land that belongs to
our fellow M āori relations in Tauranga. We must remember that in the coming
December at Christmas time, 200 years will have passed since the arrival of the faith in
New Zealand. The bearer was Samuel Marsden. Ōihi was where he landed and Ruatara
the elder was the one who welcomed him.  They had not stayed at that end, at
Rangihoua, for any length of time when they decided to move elsewhere. It was later on
that the missionaries arrived under the tutela ge of Williams. One of these missionary
groups like the Church of England establ ished itself in Tauranga, reconnoitred the
area, and expanded the faith.
Much has been expressed about how useless the Church has been, but we must never
be deluded by the fact that what this group did for the Māori people was not all bad. My
elders from within Ng āpuhi—Hongi Hika and others—cautioned M āoridom: the beast
that our children and grandchildren will fear  will indeed be the redcoats and not the
missionaries. And thus I need to lay out a statement like that first.]
This hapū, Ngāi Tamarāwaho, and I have an association that goes back to an incident
involving the library in Tauranga Moana. A chap by the name of Hone Ngata, since
disappeared—passed away, should I say—who wa s married to a leading woman of this
tribe Ng āi Tamar āwaho, a kaum ātua by the name of K ōpū, and a host of others
occupied that particular library. The occupation turned very sour when the police, just to
show that they did not discover their foul ways in the T ūhoe raid, sent the police dogs
into the Tauranga library in order to dislodge the occupiers.  As a consequence, a fire
broke out. Considerable damage was in flicted upon the books, the library, and the
members of that hap ū who were seeking to recover th eir rights that they had lost, I
would say, broadly through the process of colonisation but, more to the point, through
the nexus of Crown action and the Church of England.
I cannot help but think about those people—indeed, one of them, a P ākehā chap who
went to my old school, St Stephen’s School —who made unsuccessful attempts in what
is a pretty conservative area, Tauranga Moana, to push their agenda. That was in the late
1980s. When we pass a bill like this , the New Zealand Mission Trust Board
(Otamataha) Empowering Bill, it is good that we recite a little of the unknown history
so that the efforts and the name s of the members of that hap ū—as I said, most of whom
have moved on—are recorded, because this is the people’s House and we are talking
about a group of people here who have received back from the Anglican Church a small
portion of their former estate. Naturally, I acknowledge Te Ururoa Flavell and follow on
13724 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otama taha) Empowering Bill 25 Sep 2013
from what others have said. I am looking fo rward to hearing what my colleagues on the
Māori Affairs Committee say about this piece of legislation.
We tend to regard the centres of M āoridom in the Bay of Plenty as being T ūhoe, Te
Arawa, and Whakat āne, but there is a proud and rich history that has been eclipsed in
Tauranga Moana, belonging to the tangata whenua, and this makes a small step for—
and I suppose that when you mention the name Ng āi Tamar āwaho to the average
Pākehā, they cannot pronounce it for a start. It  does sound a bit rude if you get the
consonants around the wrong way, but that is another matter. I would say that they are a
truculent group of Māori. Indeed, a number of conservative Māori did not like them, but
we should be here today to support this bill, and we do.

items.speaker: CLAUDETTE HAUITI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. The National Party will
be supporting this private bill, the New Zealand Mission Trust Board (Otamataha)
Empowering Bill, in the name of Māori Party MP Te Ururoa Flavell, going to the Māori
Affairs Committee.
What we are effectively doing here is ame nding a century-old trust. We have heard
the story of the New Zealand Mission Trust, as well as Samuel Marsden. When I hear
the name Samuel Marsden, I recall an area in Sydney, in Parramatta, on New Zealand
Street where Samuel Marsden had his market  gardens. He had a mission there and he
established an agricultural college there. A lo t of our rangatira were encouraged to send
their boys there to learn how to grow kai—as though we, at that time, did not know how
to grow kai. However, three of our tamaiti, our rangatahi, from Ng āpuhi were sent to
Samuel Marsden’s mission in Parramatta, on Ne w Zealand Street. It was during a time
when influenza was running rampant through Australia, and our rangatahi there caught
the flu. Three of our rangatahi, to cool themselves off, placed their feet in the Parramatta
River, and subsequently they passed away. It was not until qu ite a few months later that
their parents were told of  their passing. However, unfor tunately, they were never
brought home. Whether at the time their parents, their papa or their mama, wanted them
returned home or not, I am not sure.
However, in the mid-1990s a very large ope , thanks to Wairua  Tapu Church in
Sydney, was invited by the council in Sydney to bless the area before the building on
the site was demolished and then turned in to a car park. So Wa irua Tapu arranged a
very large ope, and the Māori Women’s Welfare League and the Māori Council brought
iwi from Aotearoa over there to bless the area. What they thought would take a few
hours took, in fact, almost 48 hours—obviously, they had a break—but they felt that the
area was so deep and rich in our history and our  wairua that they were not able to leave
without it being blessed to the extent that they thought it needed to be done.
So that is part of our connection with the Mission Trust. It was not just around
Aotearoa but it extended its arm right across the Tasman to Poih ākena, too. So with the
assistance of Samuel Marsden, we also have  a very deep connec tion to the Kurranulla
people, who are over in Poih ākena. As I said, the New Zealand Mission Trust is a
remnant of the first missionaries in the 19 th century and I think that this deed, the
original deed—and I would like to congratul ate Te Ururoa Flavell, the MP, on his
generosity in stating that it was a deed of its time. This bi ll, therefore, is a bill of its
time, its relevance, and its pertinence today.
We have also got to remember that this bi ll is not a precedent. In fact, there was
something very similar in 1986. A similar i ssue arose, with money and investments
derived from lands held by the Mission Trust in Port Waikato. It was to be transferred to
Ngāti K ārewa and Ng āti T āhina, and the result was th e New Zealand Mission Trust
Board (Port Waikato Maraetai) Empowering Act of 1986. With this bill the return of the
land is highly significant to the hap ū of Ng āti Tapu and Ng āi Tamarāwaho. The hap ū
say that it will re-establish their connec tion to the awa—to the water—and provide
25 Sep 2013 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill 13725
income to the hapū, and, as my colleague said, it comes on the 150th anniversary of Gate
Pā. Kia ora.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: It is my pleasure and privilege to speak
on the New Zealand Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill. I initially want
to mihi to my colleague Te Ururoa Flavell for sponsoring this bill, and also to the
whānau of Ōtamataha Trust, e ngā hapū o Ngāti Tapu me Ngāi Tamarāwaho whānau in
Tauranga Moana, whose lands will be returned to them [ to the subtribes of Ng āti Tapu,
the family of Ng āi Tamar āwaho in Tauranga ]. My contribution really is to highlight
that this continues to be part of New Z ealand’s truth and reconc iliation process. It
highlights our colonisation history from  the perspective of the missionaries’
contribution to creating relationships with tangata whenua, which then eventuated in
lands of tangata whenua being placed in such entities as the Church Missionary Society.
I want to acknowledge that the society was established on 12 April 1799. In fact, its
mission was to spread the word of the Lord and the Gospel, but it was also to go to parts
of the world, including Aotearoa New Zeala nd, and create an asset base and a capital
base that has meant that lands such as the la nd that is being returned via this private bill
was taken so that the Church could establish itself.
When looking at this piece of legislation and th e history, it is interesting to note that
the Church made its first voyage here in 1814, via its representative Samuel Marsden.
Over a period of 30 years what it did was es tablish itself to a point where it developed
the relationship with tangata whenua, which m eant that it could give us blankets, axes,
adzes, trousers, soap, the New Testament, sc issors, spades, looking  glasses, razors,
handkerchiefs, and tobacco. Those were the commodities that it gave us in exchange for
our lands.
What I want to acknowledge in that pr ocess is that from the beginning tangata
whenua never treated it as a transaction. Fo r us, it was part of becoming Christians, and
part of that was having a relationship with th e Church that meant it needed land to build
its churches on. But what quickly happened wa s that we were displaced from a huge
amount of land, and so in terms of this spec ific experience, what happened was that we
are talking about close to 40,000 square metres of central Ta uranga land that, in 1835,
the Church purchased. What happened thereafter was continued dispute with the tangata
whenua. The Crown intervened and in 1852 act ually granted that land to the Church
Missionary Society, and in 1867 the Church Missionary Societ y, in return, gave the
Crown 80 percent of the land that it had taken from tanga ta whenua. I find that really
interesting because what we are talking about  today is the return of 20 percent of the
original piece of land that the Church Mi ssionary Society had. So  the tangata whenua
get 20 percent back by virtue of this private bill, but I am actually interested in the 80
percent that the Crown was gifted in 1867.
But what I do want to acknowledge is that over a period of time the Church
Missionary Society obviously developed a philosophy about this land and the fact that it
needed to give it back to tangata whenua . So I want to acknowle dge that from 1998 it
replaced the trustees of the New Zealand Mission Trust Board with tangata whenua
representatives, and what this bill will do is  ensure that those lands, that property, are
transferred to the Ōtamataha Trust. It will be a tangata whenua trust and it will benefit
the hapū beneficiaries of that particular trust. Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am pleased to stand and
speak on the New Zealand Mission Trust Bo ard (Otamataha) Empowering Bill in its
first reading, and I commend the M āori Party MP Te Ururoa Flavell for bringing it to
the House. This is a private bill in his na me. It seeks to return transferred land in
Tauranga and other property from th e New Zealand Mission Trust to the Ōtamataha
Trust so that it can be used by the beneficiaries of that trust, the hapū of that area.
13726 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otama taha) Empowering Bill 25 Sep 2013
It is going to be interesting as we go through this bill in the Māori Affairs Committee
and as we look at the history of events. I want to make the comment that we do hear
sometimes, I guess, a converged history of what has happened here in New Zealand,
and not all of it, in terms of  the missionary work, is as bad as some people may portray.
As we go to the select committee, I would like to ensure also that the good is
acknowledged as well. I think not particular ly of this area but  of one of my own
forebears, John Hobbs, who, during the Nort hern War in 1845-46, used his influence
with a number of Hokianga chiefs to limit the spread of the fighting, and during other
wars he used his influence among warring entitie s in order to seek to preserve life. I
think that through all of these things, yes, there are things that need to be redressed,
there are histories that have to be acknowledged, and there are things that need to be put
right, but let us be careful and let us also  reflect the good that has happened in our
country in the past. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Te Ururoa Flavell, 5 minutes in
reply.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Firstly, can I acknowledge
all of the statements made by members of the House this afternoon. I appreciate very
much the support, and it sounds like it is across the House for this bill, the New Zealand
Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill. Can I just own up and say that the
work that I did was relatively minimal, and I acknowledge again Alan Tate, who was
the adviser to the Ōtamataha Trust, who basically over the last couple of years has been
the communication person for me, through my office and, of course, through the trust—
so thank you to him.
There are some interesting poi nts I picked up in the disc ussion, and in the couple of
minutes that I have got, just to wrap up, I say that I am sure we will learn a lot of history
when we go to Tauranga Moana and pick up much of the discussion when submitters
present evidence in front of the M āori Affairs Committee. It re minds me of another bill
that we had in the House here not long ago that related to sewa ge pipes and a large
chunk of area of land being handed back to the Tauranga people that was originally
taken for a sewage pond. Those sorts of things, I think, very much stick in the hearts of
Māori people, but I do acknowledge the point  that Jonathan Young has made. Sure,
there were some good things that came with the arrival of the mi ssionaries, but some
things very much stick in the heart, especi ally if you have been hanging out for a long
period of time to get your land back.
This for me is a very important bill because  I do not recall—not that I am the expert
in it—that there are too many times that the Anglican Church has ha nded land back to
Māori people. But in my area, my constituency, the T ūhoe people up at Maungap ōhatu
received some land back from the Presbyt erian Church, I think it was, through Mr
Laughton, who had a close association with Rua K ēnana back in the day. They set the
scene a couple of years ago because they started handing land back, but there is a hell of
a lot of land out there that is still under th e auspices of a number of churches that has
not come back to the M āori people, and I hope that the pr ecedent set with these sorts of
bills is going to be some good news for years to come.
I do not think we can deny, t oo, some of the main thought s of the missionaries as
they came to New Zealand, because they are pretty much set out in a lot of the doctrine
that was set up at the time. I am thinki ng about my old school, St Stephen’s School—
Mr Jones’ school as well—which pretty much had a set charter, if you like, which was
about educating the uneducated and, indeed, young M āori boys. Some of them were
heathen—Mr Jones, well, I am not too sure ab out that, but nevertheless he is all right;
he came good after a couple of ye ars at St Stephen’s, but he  has sort of faded away a
25 Sep 2013 NZ Mission Trust Board (Otamataha) Empowering Bill 13727
little bit since that time. Mr Hone Harawira is another old boy—a sort of similar pattern,
but nevertheless they might come good at some point or other.
I have to say that I do cringe  at times at some of the actions by the Church. When I
was teaching Treaty education we always referr ed to two doctrines of the time, of both
the Catholic Church and the Anglican Churc h. One was called the papal bull, set out by
the Pope, which I suppose set the scene fo r colonisation throughout the world, and the
other one, under the Anglican doctrine, was called the require mento—meaning you
were required to read a certain statement. Both of those statements were about “Take
the land, take the women, and if anybody gets in the road deal to th em, and do it in the
name of God.” Under those circumstances we have got a lot of work  to do to catch up
with those sorts of things.
I do not want to take up too much time, but I think the key point that was made by
Louisa Wall around the reconcili ation process is important—tha t we are on that line, in
particular, with the efforts around settling Treaty settlements, and that the work that has
been done by Mr Chris Finlayson is along th e way. Talking about the other 80 percent,
as Louisa Wall said, it will be interesting to see what the people think about the other 80
percent of land that might come back to them. For those who ar e travelling through
Tauranga Moana, I think the easiest way to find this place is to look for the best fish and
chip shop in Tauranga Moana, down on th e harbour—they are blinking nice fish and
chips from the Palmer wh ānau, I think it is. They look after that fish and chip shop, and
I hope they give me free fish and chips when I go up next time. But also the Sebel Hotel
is sitting right on that land. It has all been reclaimed, I think, right on the harbour. If you
are flying over there, I am sure you cannot miss it.
I look forward to hearing the stories fr om the people up in Tauranga Moana and
congratulate them on advancing this bill. Today I think of the koroua M ōrehu—the old
koroua up there at Ngāi Tamarāwaho. I am sure that he woul d be pretty proud to finally
get this land in their hands. Ka nui te mihi kia ora tātou.
