CONSERVATION (NATURAL HERITAGE PROTECTION) BILL
In Committee

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I seek leave for all provisions to be taken as
one question for the purposes of debate and voting.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is there anyone
opposed to that course of action? It appears not. Leave is granted.
Parts 1 to 6 and clauses 1 and 2

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: The Conservation (Natural Heritage
Protection) Bill amends six of the main Acts administered by the Department of
Conservation. Those Acts are the Conser vation Act 1987, the National Parks Act 1980,
the Reserves Act 1977, the Wildlife Act 1953, the Wild Animal Control Act 1977, and
latterly—and I will come to this later—the Marine Mammals Protection Act 1978.
I would like to outline to th e Committee five key aspects of the changes that are set
out in the bill. The purpose of these changes is to better safeguard New Zealand’s
protected native wildlife, public conservati on lands, and other natural and historic
resources. To do so, the changes seek to create effective deterrents against conservation-
related offending, with a clearly formulated an d consistent penalty fr amework that is in
line with the modern era.
13728 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 25 Sep 2013
The key changes are to provide  significant penalties for illegal activities carried out
for commercial gain of a maximum of 5 y ears’ imprisonment, a $300,000 fine, or both,
and an additional fine of $20,000 a day if the offence is ongoing. This will greatly
reduce the incentive for such offending. Th e bill increases penalties for serious
offending that is not commercially motivated to a maximum of 2 years’ imprisonment, a
fine of $100,000, or both. If the offence is a continuing one, there may also be an
additional maximum fine of $10,000 a day. The bill increases the maximum fines for
offending by bodies corporat e to $200,000, or to $300,000 where the offending is
commercially motivated. It increases the pena lties for breaches of regulations and by-
laws made under these Acts to a maximu m fine of $5,000, or $10,000 in some specific
cases, plus an additional maximum fine of $500 a day if the offence is ongoing. It
improves the courts’ flexibility to tailor appr opriate penalties by enabling the courts to
impose a penalty of imprisonment or a fine, or both, and providing for community work
sentences.
I would note to the Committee that the bill does not amend the Marine Reserves Act.
The Minister of Conservation intends to ame nd penalties in that Act through a separate
legislative process. I want to also note to  the Committee that the additional daily fines
for ongoing offences are amended only where the relevant Act already provides for such
fines. The bill does not propose any new fines of this type.
So these improved penalties and more flex ible sentencing options apply across the
six Acts that I have mentioned. I will go thr ough those Acts. Part 1 of the bill amends
the Conservation Act, as I have describe d. The new penalties primarily relate to
offences committed in places protected under the Conservation Act, but also include
offences involving freshwater fish and their habitat. The bill increases fines for breaches
of regulations only, as the Conservation Act does not provide for by-laws.
Part 2 amends the National Parks Act. Li kewise, it amends the penalties under the
National Parks Act. These will apply to illegal activities in all of New Zealand’s
national parks. The bill incr eases fines for breaches of by-laws only, as the National
Parks Act does not provide for regulations . Maximum fines for breaches of by-laws
involving aircraft in national parks are set at a higher level of $10,000, as such breaches
are potentially more serious.
Part 3 amends the Reserves Act for all reserves, including those administered by the
Department of Conservation, local bodies, boards, and other administering bodies. The
bill increases fines for breaches of both Rese rves Act by-laws and regulations. The bill
sets penalties for national and other reserves at the same level. This is because the new
higher penalties provide better scope for cour ts to take into account factors including,
but not limited to, the status of the particular reserve, th e values contained in that
reserve, and the seriousness of the particular offending.
Part 4 amends the Wildlife Act, as I have described previously, with some variations,
which I will go through. Absolutely and part ially protected native species will have
their protection increased by the higher new maximum penalties of 2 years’
imprisonment or a $100 fine, or both. An existing slightly higher maximum fine of
$250,000 is retained for offences  against absolutely and pa rtially protected marine
species. Offending in wildlife refuges and wildlife management reserves will have a
maximum penalty of 1 year’s imprisonment or a $100,000 fine, or both. Wildlife
sanctuaries have higher status and will attract the 2-year maximum imprisonment
penalty.
Existing additional per head fines are removed, as these are rarely used. The courts
can take the number of animals affected in to account as an aggravating or mitigating
factor—aggravating, I would hope. Penalties for offences involving game birds or
unprotected wildlife, such as introduced spec ies, are not changed by this bill, and
25 Sep 2013 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 13729
neither are the penalties for failing to report  accidentally killing or injuring protected
marine life during fishing. The b ill increases fines for breach es of regulations only, as
the Wildlife Act does not provide for by-laws.
Part 5 amends the Wild Animal Control Act, as I have described. The higher new
penalties apply to offences  such as aerial hunting without landowner permission and
unlawfully releasing wild animals. The bill increases fines for breaches of regulations
only, as the Wild Animal Control Act does not provide for by-laws.
Part 6 of the bill amends the Marine Mamm als Protection Act. Thanks go to Maryan
Street and the Local Government and E nvironment Committee for their work in
bringing this amendment to the bill. I tha nk the member for that good work. Higher
standard penalties apply to offences, incl uding illegally taking  or killing marine
mammals, harassing them, or using a purse seine net w ithout escape panels. An
existing, slightly higher maximum fine of  $250,000 is retained for illegally taking
marine mammals. Changes to the Marine  Mammals Protection Act do not change
penalties for failing to report accidentally ki lling or injuring marine mammals during
fishing.
I have gone through the changes pr oposed in this bill at so me length. I want to thank
the House and the Committee for consideration of this bill and for your support of our
special places and species, which are backed by this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I am really pleased to be able to take a
call or two in the Committee stage of the C onservation (Natural He ritage Protection)
Bill. Can I begin by commending the member Jacqui Dean, in whose name the bill
stands before the House, and say that it is a very good bill. I appreciate the way that she
engaged with the Local Government and En vironment Committee, and I particularly
appreciate the fact that she acknowledged my  colleague Maryan Street for her work. I
think that is a very good attitude and a very good basis on which to progress the bill.
Labour will certainly be giving its support to th e bill. It does things that are sensible.
Even though it was a good bill to start wit h, it was substantially improved and it was
made even better at the select committee. I thi nk that is also a trib ute to all the select
committee members.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: It’s like peace is breaking out.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Yes, perhaps we could quit now . Peace seems to have broken
out, as my colleagues say. [ Interruption] No, I am enjoying it. It is a good bill and the
select committee did good work as well. So, as I say, it is a pleasure to support this bill.
I wonder what went through the minds of the members or the leaders of the House—
the Hon Gerry Brownlee, the Hon Anne Tolle y, and the Hon Steven Joyce—when this
bill was due to come up on this particular ni ght. Well, I am sure that they would have
seen the title of the bill and thought “Conservation? Actually, I think we’ve had enough
discussion about conservation in the House in th e last little while.”, because, of course,
the Minister of Conservation, the Hon Nick Smith, has been figuring quite highly in the
last 2 weeks as a result of his inconsistent representati ons to the House and to the
public. So it is good that this bill—even  though it deals with the Minister of
Conservation’s legislation—is going to be  so well supported, and that comments that
are made about it are going to be consistent rather than highly questionable.
The member Jacqui Dean went through the bill  in quite some detail. I think that if
you go from the starting point of the fact that  this is a member’s bill rather than a
Government bill, and look at what the member Jacqui Dean sought to do, it is a really
sensible place to start, because the penalt ies regime was clearly outdated and clearly
inconsistent. This bill brings it into a much more realistic state, where the penalties that
are imposed on people will serve the purpose.  The penalties will give those people a
wake-up call. They will make them pay the price for any damage that they have done.
13730 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 25 Sep 2013
We can go into the details of what the pena lties might do later, but for any of the
penalties that are incurred, they now have a penalty that is considered relevant by this
Parliament to the damage that has been done. I think that is a very good thing.
At the select committee, Maryan Street pr oposed that a new Part 6 be added to the
penalty regime, so that the Marine Mamm als Protection Act 1978 was also updated in
the same way as the other pieces of legislat ion. As Jacqui Dean has noted, that was a
move that was innovative. So I think th at the Hon Maryan Street should be
congratulated on that forethought, but also  that the select committee should be
congratulated on supporting it.
There is a frustration that is often shared in  this Parliament about the framing of the
conservation debate. I think it is one that is worthy of mention at the moment, given that
this is the topic before us. It is certainly topical in a number of other areas where the
current Government has seen conservation and the environment, actually, as being
something that needs to be ba lanced off against proposals an d against things that might
give us economic gain. In my view, that is not the appropriate way to view the
environment, conservation, and the economy, becau se if you lose some  of the value of
the conservation estate, it is gone for ever . The overall value to the economy of our
conservation estate is very high. New Zeala nd has a lot of things to offer, but our
biggest attraction is our natural environmen t. People come to New Zealand because of
that. They enjoy it, they go back home and tell other people about it, and it is something
that many other countries envy. We enjoy so much in New Zealand because of the land,
the environment that we have around us, and these are often things that can be enjoyed
at no cost, which, again, is something that other countries are very envious of.
So we need to do our best to always offer protection. If you start your frame of
thinking with “Well, we have got some cons ervation values here, but we have got some
potential economic gain there, and those need to be balanced off.”, then I think you are
likely to get the wrong answer. In my view, yo u need to say that there are some things
that are so precious that it is our responsibil ity, whether in law or just from a moral
standpoint, to protect those values and thos e precious parts of our country—whether it
is the water, whether it is the land, or whether it is other landscapes and fauna and flora.
That is the frame that I think we need to bring to the conservation debate.
This bill actually contributes in many ways, because it comes from the starting point
of saying that people who break the law, pe ople who do damage, should actually have a
penalty attached to that actio n that reflects the upset that New Zealand society feels at
their action. The previous penalties were w ildly out of date and also inconsistent,
depending on what action was taken and also wh ere it was taken. So that did not give a
strong message about the value of the conservation estate, in the same way as the
National Party’s frame of balancing up c onservation versus economic development
sends the wrong message to the public of Ne w Zealand. The message that we should be
giving is that we are the guard ians of our land and of our sea. We are responsible for
what future generations will have to enjoy, a nd that is a responsibility that we should
take very seriously.
I want to conclude by also noting the fant astic work that the officials did on the
committee. It is often, I think, a pretty frustrating task being an official who is dedicated
to the work that they are doing. They are,  in the main, and I have seen very few
exceptions to this, high quality public servan ts—oh, they should be sitting down here in
the Chamber. There are some really nice gr een seats down the front that officials are
able to use sometimes, but these particular officials are shy and they are getting more
embarrassed by the minute, as they are clearl y in the range. We cannot refer to where
they are, of course, because that is against Standing Orders, but they are certainly within
earshot of this.
25 Sep 2013 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 13731
On this bill I want to commend the quality of the work from the officials. I know that
officials can often get frustrated by what they see as game-playing with important
pieces of legislation that they might have worked very hard on. This bill would have
come as a surprise to them because it was a member’s bill, not a Government bill. I
think that the thought they gave to it and the contribution that they made really allowed,
as I said earlier, quite substantial changes to be made during the select committee
process, which were unanimously agreed and which will now be progressed through the
Committee. I know that the Department of Conservation officials, particularly, have had
a really hard time in the last  little while. The department ’s funding has been cut back
over the last 4 years. It has had big restruct uring, and for the staff who are there, these
have been pretty stressful and trying times . The most recent incident was where there
had been a whistleblower who—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! That is not part of the bill.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: —raised the issue of the submission from the Department of
Conservation on the Ruataniwha Dam.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Concentrate on the bill.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Of course, there will be further uncertainty within the
department, so for those officials to come to the select committee to look at this bill, and
to support us in the way they did, is not ju st a commendation for their professionalism
but also a recognition of what else is happening in their lives.
With those highly relevant comments, I wa nt to again commend the member for her
vision in introducing this bill and to th ank the select committee members for their
substantive work on it.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I too am very happy to
support this Conservation (Natural Heritage  Protection) Bill, brought to the House by
my colleague Jacqui Dean. It is a very timely bill. As the Hon Ruth Dyson said,
everyone on the Local Government and Envi ronment Committee worked hard to make
sure that we got a good outcome, and it was fully supported. As has already been stated,
the purpose of the bill is to update penalties across conservation legislation in order to
better protect conservation land and protect native species. The bill increases the
penalties for offences across six pieces of le gislation administered by the Department of
Conservation.
It was the smuggling of jewelled geckos from the Waitaki Basin that raised the issue
for Jacqui Dean. Smugglers we re very active in her electo rate, and the penalties for
stealing these very beautifu l and very valuable geckos—they are worth up to $25,000
each on the international market—were la ughably low. We know that the smugglers
were very active in her electorate because we managed to catch some of them at
customs. We had one smuggler who had nearly a dozen geckos secreted around his
person. We also know that there were many smugglers who were spending time in
Jacqui’s electorate and getting away w ith smuggling. Jewelled geckos have unique
markings on their bodies, and we knew where so me of them were liv ing. One day they
would be in the Waitaki Basin; the next day you would see their pictures on the internet.
They were being marketed to collectors in Europe. We did catch some of those
smugglers, but when we caught them, the penalties were nothing to write home about.
In fact, they did not punish and they did not deter.
There has been other serious conservation o ffending in recent ye ars. We have all
been disturbed by the killing of marine ma mmals. We do not like the illegal hunting of
protected species and illegal, commercia lly motivated activities, including the
smuggling of animals and plants, the draini ng of wetlands, and the logging of native
trees.
13732 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 25 Sep 2013
It is very important to have significant penalties for illegal, commercially motivated
activities because they can be  highly lucrative. These new penalties respond in part to
the comment by judges when sentencing thos e very gecko smugglers that the current
penalties were not sufficient to punish or de ter offenders. These penalties will not affect
legitimate operators, such as tourism conce ssionaires, if they play fair. Increased
penalties are also proposed for non-commerci al offences and for breaches of by-laws
and regulations across all six Acts.
I too would like to thank the officials. They did a lot of work on this bill. They did it
with assiduous care. They worked very hard with us, and I think we are all very pleased
to see this legislation coming out at the other end. We were unanimous in our support
around the table. We all believ e that there should be stronge r penalties for conservation
offending. We want to protect our natural heritage. Thank you, Jacqui Dean.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: It gives me great pleas ure to rise to support
this Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection)  Bill in the name of Jacqui Dean at the
Committee stage. I too would like to join the wave of unanimity and harmony and peace
that has broken out in the Committee over this bill and say that it gives me great
pleasure, indeed, to support it. In fact, I want to thank Jacqui Dean for her gracious
acknowledgment of the contribution I was able  to make on this bi ll by extending it to
cover the Marine Mammals Protection Act 1978. I will come back to that in a moment,
because the purpose of the inclusion of that Act in this bill will become clear.
But I have to say that in the course of  thinking about whether or not there was
something more that could be done with this bill, there were a number of recent cases of
harm to marine mammals that had come to  public attention. I must confess that I
approached the Minister of Conservation, Dr Nick Smith, and asked him whether he
would oppose or be averse to the inclusion of the Marine Mammals Protection Act and
penalties under that Act in this bill, so that  in the process of making penalties consistent
across a range of Acts, we could include ha rm done to marine mammals. He was very
enthusiastic about that incorporation and, in fact, signalled a review of marine mammals
legislation and marine Acts in general, wh ich I understand he is pursuing. He was very
gracious, and I want to give him credit for that. Notwithstanding the difficulties he is
facing currently, I believe cred it should go where credit is du e, and, after all, every dog
has his day.
As far as this bill is concerned, the purpose that J acqui Dean brought to the Local
Government and Environment Committee was to  ensure that New Zealand’s wildlife
and natural and historic resources would be  better protected. This was her motivation. I
applaud her for that. It was a worthwhile effort, and, in the course of the select
committee, I think we have jointly made some constructive improvements around the
table at the select committee that have streng thened even further the capability of this
legislation.
The problem had been that across a range of pieces of legislation the penalties
differed. It was entirely possible to commit an  offence and have it receive a negligible
penalty under one piece of legislation and a different penalty under another—for
example, if someone were to release a stoat on to a nature reserve, the highest penalty
would be $500 or 1 month’s imprisonment. Under the National Parks Act 1980, if a bit
of a national park was carved off and converted  to pasture or a stand of trees milled, the
highest penalty would have been a maximum fine of $2,500 or 3 months’ imprisonment.
However, if the same offences happened in a conservation area, then the maximum
penalty would be $10,000 or 12 months’ jail.
Typically, the national parks’ protected areas  were of higher value than conservation
areas. But when it came to the creatures that  inhabit these, for us, special areas, the
range of penalties made no sense—made abso lutely no sense. Obviously, the situation
25 Sep 2013 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 13733
that my colleague Nicky Wagner referred to a moment ago, arising out of the member
Jacqui Dean’s own electorate  of Waitaki, where the smuggl ing of jewelled geckos was
becoming rife and hugely lucrative for the people who were engaged in it, was impetus
enough for this bill.
But what we have done in this bill, which I think is highly commendable, is that we
have taken the Conservation Act 1987, the National Parks Act 1980, the Reserves Act
1977, the Wildlife Act 1953, the Wild Animal Control Act 1977, and, added to that, the
Marine Mammals Protection Act 1978, and we  have brought them all under the same
penalty regime. So there can be no more  obfuscation around damage to, harm to,
stealing of, or smuggling of creatures that ar e precious to us, whether they be eggs or
whether they be live specimens.
Now we have changed that—or at least we will with the passage of this legislation
currently in its Committee stage. Most penalties are increased to up to $100,000 for
individuals and $200,000 for individuals who are acting for commercial reasons or for a
company. Ongoing daily penalties are increased to up to $10,000 and $20,000,
respectively, for individuals and those working on behalf of a company. Breaches of by-
laws incur up to $5,000 or $10,000 penalties. Th is two-tiered kind of regime will make
not only the monitoring but the implementati on and the prosecution of  this legislation
consistent.
So at the moment we have—without wi shing to comment unduly on a case before
the court—a case of a Blenheim man in front  of the Nelson court currently on charges
of killing 13 female breeding s eals at a seal colony on the Kaik ōura coast, two bulls,
and eight seal pups. Because of the differen ce in the regimes under different pieces of
legislation, he is being tried under a piece of  legislation that will have far lesser
consequences for him than if he were be ing tried under another piece of legislation.
That was then, and he will be tried according to the law in place at the time of the
alleged crime, so that is happening as we speak. But no more after this; once this bill
gets to its third reading, people will not be able to pick and choose which piece of
legislation they will contest their crime under.
The police will have an easier job of pros ecuting under different pieces of legislation
because the penalties will be comparable. So it will be easier for the police to make sure
that the actions will be dealt with consistently  in terms of penalties, regardless of the
particular piece of legislation they are ch arging a person under. That has got to be
helpful. We need to protect our special fauna in this country, and that extends to marine
mammals.
I would also like to add my congratulations to the offi cials on the work they did.
They advised us in a way that was impartial but very committed. They were very
committed to what they were doing. I recognise  this as a feature of staff who work in
the Department of Conservation and I thank them for it. There are fewer and fewer of
them as the days go by, but the ones who stil l remain are absolutely committed to the
conservation of our endangered species and our special species in our jurisdictional
area. I thank the officials for their advice and for the way they made sure that what we
were doing in this bill was consistent throughout. I commend the bill to the Committee.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: It is with great pleasure that I talk to
the Conservation (Natural Heritage Protec tion) Bill. As many have said, it is a
member’s bill with enormous merit. It is an omnibus bill, which will be heard in one
part, of course, and its purpose is to increa se the penalties in the main enactments
administered by the Department of Conserva tion. It is all about, as many have said
already in other readings, c onsistency. It is about making people aware of the problems
and making, through the various Acts, a clear picture of what will happen if you do the
wrong thing by our flora and fauna, and now, I should say, marine mammals as well.
13734 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 25 Sep 2013
I think, as others have mentioned, that th is bill has been a particularly harmonious
bill at the Local Government and Envir onment Committee. There were no changes,
really, that were put through that were not ag reed to. That sort of harmony, if you like,
was also evident in the submissions we  heard. We heard only one, from the New
Zealand Law Society, and eight submissions we re received in support. The submissions
were very helpful and very useful. They talk ed about the value of higher penalty levels,
the need for a consistent approach—all of th e things, effectively, that came out in the
ultimate bill that we have.
I must say that one of the submissions that stood out for me was from Te R ūnanga o
Ngāi Tahu, the board of Ngāi Tahu. It talked about the need to have consistency and the
need to put some money into some positiv e steps towards entrenching kaitiakitanga
from a Crown perspective and also into public education and behaviours within the
community. Its point, I thought, was very well made in its written submission to us: that
it is certainly about th e carrot and stick approach. The stic k is that the penalties had to
increase—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the honourable
member. The time has come for me to leave the Chair for the dinner break.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: I am pleased to take a call on the Conservation (Natural
Heritage Protection) Bill. The Green Party su pports this bill and congratulates Jacqui
Dean on her work in bringing it to the H ouse, because it will encourage compliance
with conservation legislation, and by doing this it better protects our natural and historic
resources and our wildlife. Jacqui Dean provided a very comprehensive summary of the
bill’s purpose and its contents, so I will not repeat that, but I will just say that it does not
create any new offences or have any new powers, and that may account for the small
number of submissions. There were eight submissions to the Local Government and
Environment Committee, and all of those subm issions supported the bill. None of those
submissions opposed it. Submitters certainly stressed the value of higher penalties and
the need for a much more consistent appr oach across the five pieces of legislation—
including the National Parks Act, the Conservation Act, and the Wildlife Act, which the
bill originally dealt with. Now there are six pieces of legislation, with the addition of the
Marine Mammals Protection Act. Submitters stressed the need for effective penalties to
encourage compliance and they also highlighted the value of having some flexibility in
terms of sentencing options.
So we certainly welcome the legislati on, but we do wish Jacqui Dean would
encourage Government members to have a ra ther more consistent approach to the
protection of our distinctive plants and wildlif e. If you look at clause 4C of the bill,
which inserts new section 43C, that has penalties in relation to “unlawful acts in respect
of spawning fish:”, and, in section 26ZR of the principal Act—the Conservation Act—
to “the use of a substance or  electric device to take or de stroy freshwater fish:”. Under
the principal Act, because of this bill, the c ourts will be able to impose a sentence of
imprisonment of up to 2 years or a fine of  $100,000 if you do anythi ng to interfere with
spawning fish or if you put a hazardous substa nce or a narcotic substance in the water
with the intention of killing fish. Yet the very same department, the Department of
Conservation, which is able to prosecute thos e offences with those penalties, is not able
to put evidence in front of the board of inquiry on the Tukituki catchment proposal,
which would show how the intensive agricu lture and irrigation that that catchment
proposal enables could kill about 18 species of native fish in the Tukituki River,
because when the nutrient runoff—the nitrog en that is associated with intensive
25 Sep 2013 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 13735
agriculture—seeps into waterways, you get more al gal blooms and you get conditions
that are toxic to fish.
This bill increases the penalties for harming fish. Yet when the very same department
with the very same statutory responsibilities to advocate for conservation, to preserve as
far as practicable all indigenous freshwater fi sheries, to protect recreational freshwater
fisheries—the purposes that this bill is base d on—tries to carry out  that same statutory
responsibility in relation to the Tukituki ca tchment and in relation to the Government
Ruataniwha irrigation proposal, it is not allowed to do it, because a Minister of
Conservation who has been as slippery as an eel in relation to his denials of having
anything to do with suppressing that Depa rtment of Conservation submission has not
allowed the department to put forward evidence of how irrigation can make rivers toxic.
Yet this bill is increasing the penalties fo r an individual who does that. So we desire
more consistency across Government.
We welcome this bill, but we think that the department should also be allowed to
carry out its statutory responsibilities for fr eshwater fish and for conservation advocacy
in a wider sphere under the Resource Mana gement Act, not just relating it to
individuals. So we will be supporting it but it is a very great pity that the board of
inquiry will not have any contestable evidence  from a Government department in front
of it when it considers the Tukituki catchment proposal. It will have evidence from the
Ministry for Primary Industries but not from the department. Yet this bill is right on
point in terms of recognising the department’s responsibilit ies for the protection of
freshwater fish and for increasing the penalties for killing fish. Thank you.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: That was a very good choice of yours, Mr
Chair. I am taking a call on behalf of New Zealand First on Jacqui Dean’s Conservation
(Natural Heritage Protection) Bill. We have said in the previous reading that we would
be supporting this bill. We believe  that it has a lot of merit in  terms of what it tries to
achieve.
I have mentioned in this Chamber before  that we have had many instances where
there was smuggling of some of our endangered and precious creatures, including a case
where a German tourist tried to smuggle 44 No rthland green geckos out of the country
and was caught. That was in 2010. There wa s another case where some Czech botanists
were convicted in 2004 for attempting to smuggle 363 wild plants, including 93
endemic orchids. This sort of thing goes on a ll the time. Of course, for all the cases that
we do hear about and where we do appreh end the culprits, obviously, there are many
that go unnoticed and where people are get ting away with it. Worldwide, Interpol
estimates that the smuggling of wildlife and precious species is wo rth in the order of
$10 billion to $20 billion. So worldwide smuggli ng of precious flora and fauna is quite
a big trade.
In New Zealand’s case we do have some uni que species that are found only here in
Aotearoa because of our isolation and because of the way we separated from
Gondwanaland and the rest of the continents. As a result, we have some species that
people in other parts of the world would very dearly love to get their hands on. So this is
a good piece of legislation to increase the surv eillance of that and to ensure that there
are increased penalties for those who ar e caught and apprehended. Some of those
penalties are quite hefty, going from 1 to 5 years’ imprisonment, and, particularly for
those who are caught doing it for commercial gain or co mmercial reward, penalties
going up to 5 years’ imprisonment, a $300,000 fine, or $20,000 per day. That sends a
very strong message to anybody who feels that they wish to partic ipate in the illicit
trade in flora or fauna that this is getting into fairly serious money.
But sometimes it is not always done for commercial gain. Sometimes it is done
perhaps somewhat negligently, but, again, people need to be aware that there are
13736 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 25 Sep 2013
penalties if they are negligent when it comes to New Zealand’s precious fauna and flora.
So there is the ability within this bill for people to be sentenced to community work and
other smaller penalties if they are caught offending perhaps unwittingly in this manner.
We do have concerns, like some of the ot her Opposition parties, that although it is a
good move on behalf of one National member to bring this bill to the Committee to help
protect our environment, there are many other things that this National Government is
doing that are flying in the face of the envi ronment. When we look at some of the
reforms in regard to the Resource Manageme nt Act, and now, part icularly as we are
moving towards Part 2 and clauses 6 and 7 of the Conservation (Natural Heritage
Protection) Bill, we have some grave concerns  in that area of the environment. So we
would hope that we are not seeing a double standard here from the Government in terms
of a good member, and a member on our Local Government and Environment
Committee, doing a good job bringing this Cons ervation (Natural Heritage Protection)
Bill to the Committee to improve the standards.
We certainly do not like the idea that on the other side of the ledger the same
Government is perhaps pulling the rug out fr om other aspects of the environment. We
do stand by our pride in havi ng a “100% Pure New Zealand” image and branding, and
trying to be internationally respected for that , so it is important that we maintain that
high level. In that respect we do have some concerns about what is  occurring this very
week in terms of the Minister of Conserva tion, Nick Smith, and wh at is happening in
that whole saga. Therefore, we are pe rhaps seeing some double standards coming
through, which we certainly do not condone and we do not wish to see.
However, we do applaud the member Jacqui Dean for bringing this bill to the House.
It is overdue. There have been now quite a considerable number of years where things
have occurred and where people have got away  with various things. Just to conclude,
we think as a result that this bill can serve only to further the good work that has been
done in the area of conservation and the envi ronment, and we certainly support it. New
Zealand First will be following this through.

items.speaker: CLAUDETTE HAUITI
items.text: The Conservation (Natural Heritage
Protection) Bill sets out to better protect our w āhi tapu and taong a by increasing
penalties for non-compliance with laws administered by the Department of
Conservation. It also implements a consistent  approach to penalties across the amended
laws. The bill proposes bigger fines and longe r jail sentences for people who endanger
our wildlife or damage our pr otected natural habitats. Some penalties currently in place
are far too low, and there are other inconsistencies that need to be addressed.
But this bill is more than a technical bill. This bill is safeguarding our intimate
relationship between us, the people of Aot earoa New Zealand, and our natural world—
all that is between Ranginui and Papat ūānuku and including Tangaroa. This is about
kaitiakitanga, the very thing that Te R ūnanganui o Ng āi Tahu pinpointed in its
submission. This is about cultural guardians hip, the system of law and lore through
which we are obliged to nurture and care.
This bill is relevant and responsible to a changing and demanding world. We are
continuing to improve the environment and bu ild a cleaner, greener, brighter future for
all New Zealanders. This bill upholds our  kaitiakitanga in law. Amendments are
proposed to the Conservation Act, the Nati onal Parks Act, the Reserves Act, the
Wildlife Act, and the Wild Animal Control Ac t. The bill will also apply to the Marine
Mammals Protection Act.
This bill upholds our kaitiakitanga in lo re—as an example, keeping the two species
of tuatara safe. It is helping protect the only surviving members of its order, which
flourished around 200 million years ago. To M āori, tuatara are arik i and thought to be
messengers of Whiro, the god of death and disast er. To some, tuatara also indicate tapu.
25 Sep 2013 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 13737
Māori women would sometimes tattoo images of  lizards, some of which may represent
tuatara, near their whare tangata, or genitals , and this was in celeb ration of Hine-nui-te-
po and her power to bring lif e and death to mankind, as M āui Tikitiki-a-Taranga
discovered when she squashed him between her legs. The whakapapa of tuatara is just
one history of a species we are protecting.
This bill sends a strong message that we take protection of New Zealand’s wildlife
and natural areas very seriously. What this bill does is send a strong message to
ourselves that we take seriously our role as kaitiakitanga.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I rise to take a short call on the Conservation
(Natural Heritage Protection) Bill—[Interruption]—and I want to make just a few brief
points when the follicly challenged one over ther e is quiet. Firstly, I observe that Part 6,
which was inserted at the Local Government and Environment Committee, is a victory
for the process of public input—for this nation’s citizens being able to make
submissions on legislation and to improve a bill. I have been one to condemn this
Government for the way it has had to put amendments to amendments to amendments
and rushed because of its policy of rushing through bills, but it is great to see the
democratic process working with this bill.

items.speaker: The select committee reported
items.text: “We recommen d inserting new Part 6 to reflect the
intention of bringing consistency to the pe nalties administered by the Department of
Conservation.” The committee went on to re fer to Standing Order 288(1), which states
that “a select committee may recommend only amendments that are relevant to the
subject-matter of the bill, are consistent with  the principles and objects of the bill …”.
The Local Government and Environment Committee went on to say that it was
confident that Part 6, which amends the Ma rine Mammals Protection Act, meets that
requirement.
I suggest that it would be useful for the select committee report to record why this
particular change came about—that reason bein g that a member of the public asked for
the change in a submission. Only eight subm issions were received, including a learned
one from the New Zealand Law Society—and I will touch on that one shortly. One
person asked for the change to the marine  mammals law and put in just a short
submission of 300 words or more. The submitte r did so, firstly, because of a report on
Radio New Zealand National in January this year entitled “Claim of illegal fishing in
marine sanctuary”, and, secondly, because, at the time, submissions were being received
on this bill. To cut a long story short, th e select committee was convinced by the power
of the argument, which spoke for itself. It  was an overnight success, which we are
debating just 8 months later. That is a good-news story for the public of New Zealand—
that input by New Zealanders into our nation’s legislation can be brought to fruition.
The next point I would like to touch on is the process that has brought us to where
we are today, debating the Committee stage of the Conservation (Natural Heritage
Protection) Bill and its Parts 1 to 6 and pr eliminary clauses. We are doing this on a
members’ day because the bill has been brought forward by the honourable Jacqui Dean
as a member’s bill. I say good on her for doin g that, but she has done  it because it has
not been brought forward as a Government b ill by successive Governments led by the
last four Prime Ministers.
Let us look, for example, at clause 4B in Part 1 of the bill. It updates the penalties in
section 39 of the Conservation Act for a pers on who, in the words of  section 39(4) of
that Act: “disturbs, injures, poisons, kill s, or detrimentally affects any freshwater
fishery, fish spawning ground, or food of freshwat er fish in any river, stream, lake, or
any other water, by allowing any contaminant to enter into any such water or refuses to
remove as much as may be practicable of the contaminant”. Well, it is a mouthful, but it
defines a specific offence. The provision  was added to the law in 1990 by the
13738 Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill 25 Sep 2013
Conservation Law Reform Act 1990, with pe nalties of up to $30,000 and a further fine
of $3,000 a day for a continuing offence. In th e intervening 23 years the quantum of the
maximum penalty has not changed. The dollar amounts are the same today as they were
23 years ago, yet the value of  $30,000 in 1990 was obviously fa r greater than the same
amount today.
I frequently hear members in  debate observing the importa nce of this House getting
the regulatory framework right and of setting good policy parameters, yet too often they
do not get revisited, and so we have a massive catch-up, as we see today in clause 4B of
this bill, as brought forward by Jacqui D ean. The Law Society, whose submission I
alluded to earlier, made four recommendati ons. One of the recommendations was that a
review should be undertaken to  ensure that the bill’s pena lties are consistent with the
penalties specified in other enactments that protect or manage aspects of the natural
environment. The Law Society suggested it  would be desirable for there to be a
consistent approach to penalties in all enact ments that protect or manage aspects of the
natural environment.
Perhaps another useful step would be for Pa rliament to have a process for bills to
specifically revise and update  penalties contained in st atute, as it is important
constitutionally that this House sets out pe nalties and maximums in primary legislation.
But it would do little harm for one bill in each Parliament, an omnibus bill, to be
introduced to keep the penalties up to da te and, as desired by the Law Society,
consistent across the statute book. The Law Society suggested that it would be desirable
for there to be a consistent approach to penalties in all enactme nts that protect or
manage aspects of this national environment.
Finally, I turn to clause 2, which sets out  the commencement date. The clause is a
good one, and I commend the honourable member  Jacqui Dean for specifying a fixed
date. I will support this bill.
Parts 1 to 6 and clauses 1 and 2 agreed to.
Bill reported without amendment.
Report adopted.

bringing this bill to the House. I know that the Airline Pilots’ Association will be very

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Well, it is a pleasure to take a call on the Summary
Offences (Possession of Hand-held Lasers ) Amendment Bill. In my introductory
comments I do want to congratul ate Dr Cam Calder for bringi ng the bill to the House. I
will be remaining on the Transport and Indus trial Relations Committee. What is more, I
am going to be flying the flag for Labour in the transport portfolio, which is fantastic. I
am very excited about it. I am sure we will get round to talking about the Hamilton
expressway at some stage, Mr Bennett.
I want to start first of all by acknowledging the pilots of th ese aircraft—you know,
the wonderful pilots who work for our wonderful national carrier, Air New Zealand. But
they must be not only worrying about lasers at the moment; they would probably also be
dreadfully worried about the Government’s plans to partially privatise or further
privatise Air New Zealand. That is probably a far greater risk to their sense of job
security and safety than anything that some larrikins may do with lasers. So as I say, I
want to acknowledge them and acknowledge all the people, such as the flight crew, who
fly on Air New Zealand, who are feeling some  uncertainty at this stage as this
Government progresses its crazy asset sales programme.
Although I have congratulated Dr Cam Calder , it is tempting to say that I have to
wonder why we are doing this on a members’ day—I do. I really have to. I have gone
back—and in one of my previous portfolio s I was the transport safety spokesperson—
and this is not something that is new. In  2010 someone said: “Larrikins shining lasers
into the cockpits of aircraft might need to  experience the full penalties of the law to
remind them of the seriousness of their [ac tions].” That was me. In 2010 I was calling
on the Government to do something about it.
In February 2012 someone else said: “The unlawful targeting of aircraft by reckless
laser users is endangering the safety of both pilots and travellers,”. Who said that? That
was Iain Lees-Galloway. It was in 2012 he was saying that. That is 2 years after I
started this crusade about lasers with genuine  concern, so I am really pleased that Dr
Cam Calder has followed the lead of the La bour members on this side who have been
calling for something to be done about this.
We are very pleased to support the bill, al though, as I have said, I believe it should
be a Government bill. The Government rea lly needs to not waste members’ days on
things it could do itself. It could easily, eas ily put this into a transport bill—easily—or
an omnibus bill. It could easily do that, and instead we could be dealing with some
issues in this House that actually need to  be addressed by members—particularly those
members on this side of the House who do not get the opportuni ty to put forward
Government bills.
Having made those comments, congratulate d the member, and said he has done a
good job in doing this, we all know this is a growing problem, and it has been growing
since 2010 at least—at least. We know it is a growing problem, and it does need to be
dealt with. We are talking about  people’s lives. It is a hi ghly dangerous situation. I do
feel very concerned, however, that the Mini ster of Transport has fobbed this off to a
backbencher. He has fobbed it off to a bac kbencher to use up a members’ day. David
Bennett is now threatening me with a laser.  He is now threatening me with a laser—
forgive my croaky voice, but I have got the lurgy.
25 Sep 2013 Summary Offences (Ha nd-held Lasers) Amdt Bill 13741
We do accept this is a serious issue. I am looking forward to discussing this in the
Transport and Industrial Relations Committ ee and seeing more demonstrations—seeing
some more demonstrations. I am sure Dr Cam Calder, as I know the member really
well, will have done his research  and will have a variety of lasers to demonstrate to the
select committee.
I am also looking forward to hearing from  the pilots and ot her members of the
public, because it is a se rious issue. It is highly dangerous . It is madness, actually, to be

flying over and above. It does put  people’s lives at risk, so we will support the bill. I
look forward to some interesting discussion in the select committee. I just wish that the
Government was doing this rather than the member, but, however, good on him for
doing this.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I am pleased to take a brief call on this Summary
Offences (Possession of Hand-held Lasers) Amendment Bill. I have to say that when
the Greens first sighted this bill, we were so mewhat ambivalent about it because of its
inclusiveness. This point has been touched on—the fact that  it does, indeed, make it an
offence to possess any laser pointer means th at even people carryi ng them would have
to rely on fairly thin defe nces based on reasonable ground s and reasonable cause. We
found that slightly less than pe rsuasive in terms of the way the bill is worded. So, as I
say, we are ambivalent about it. The inclusiveness is counting against it. It does, in
some way, reflect Dr Calder’s personality. He is a very inclusive so rt of fellow—not at
all of the prophylactic sort of nature that Mr Benne tt referred to. I was rather surprised
to hear that.
But, more seriously, I guess I was somewhat more persuaded to support this bill,
albeit we see it as flawed, when I learnt that there are something like 100 incidents a
year—twice a week, effectively—where airc raft are endangered by misuse of these
instruments, these items. I would not suggest  for a minute that anybody in this House
would vote according to self-interest, but it must be recognised that as MPs we all spend
an awful lot of time at airports and in the air,  so of all people we are quite sensitive to
the safety of air travel in New Zealand. If this is occurrin g twice a week—and, of
course, I take Dr Calder at his word; I am sure it is well-grounded information—then
that is a very serious problem. It is almost inevitable, if it is happening a couple of times
a week, that at some point a pilot will lose control thr ough being blasted with light,
losing his night vision, or whatever it might be, and we will see a tragedy occur.
Having said that, we do, nevertheless, feel that clearly the regulations are going to be
put in place, and given some  work through the Ministry of  Health and elsewhere, to
restrict the import of the high- powered instruments that are, inevitably—well, they are
invariably going to present some danger if they are in the wrong hands. That was part of
our objection initially—that the bill was fo cused at the wrong place, to restrict the
import of these. As I understa nd it, I could purchase myse lf online tonight a very high-
powered laser, and wave it about willy-nilly with very little risk of being prosecuted
unless I actively sought to disrup t an aircraft or a vehicle or  whatever it might be. But I
do think that now it seems that regulations will be in place perhaps this year to put some
serious controls around the import of these things.
They do have legitimate uses, and astronomer s are mentioned in this. I had the very
fortunate experience about 2 years ago of  visiting the Mount John Observatory in
Tekapō on a very dark, very cold  night. In the midst of an  extraordinary experience,
which I would recommend to anybody who has not done it, I saw those lasers being
used appropriately by astronomers and people presenting to tourists and visitors to
indicate constellations. They do have legitim ate uses, and I see that researchers and the
Defence Force also have a reason to use these high-powered things.
13742 Summary Offences (Hand-held  Lasers) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
The notion, as the bill is drafted, is th at anyone owning even  a very, very low-
powered, very inoffensive instrument could be liable to prosecution if they could not
demonstrate reasonable cause. I think we  have common ground with our Labour
colleagues here. We would like to see some ti ghtening up of the drafting, and I am sure
that the Transport and Industrial Relati ons Committee will do some creative work. I
accept Dr Calder’s analogy about possessing knives. Nobody is offended by someone
carrying a pocket knife, but walking through an  urban environment with a large hunting
knife in your pocket clearly would raise some questions about your purpose.
But, essentially, we see that the intention of this bill is clear—and we respect that—
to protect air travel, drivers, people w ho ought to be protected from the potential
dangers inherent in these very, very high- powered instruments. We do expect, and we
would like to see, some redrafting of the bill,  just to perhaps put some clarity about the
class 1 lasers, for example, which could be ex empt perhaps, but I w ill leave that to the
select committee. So for the moment, we are su pporting this bill’s refe rral to the select
committee. We look forward to being part of the debate about making it a better bill,
and achieving the ultimate goal of it, whic h is about protecting people from the
malicious use of these things. Kia ora.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak to
the first reading of the Summary Offen ces (Possession of Hand-held Lasers)
Amendment Bill. New Zealand First supports this bill.
I was discussing this bill with a colleague  of mine last month, and my colleague
remarked: “What a shame it is that we have to legislate, that we have to pass laws,
because of people’s stupidity.” Yet that is what we are doing. It is a great thing that Dr
Calder has brought this bill to  the House and we are please d to be able to support it,
because it will address an issue of safety that is of genuine concern, but at the same time
it is a very great shame that he has had to  draft a bill to addr ess the matter at hand,
because the need for it has come about wholly  and solely thanks to the stupidity of a
few individuals.
Lasers are a fascinating invention. I have b een fascinated by them since learning the
theory and workings of them in physic s in high school. Li ght amplification by
stimulated emission of radiation is what the acronym LASER stands for, and a truly
wonderful process that is. The principle of wave-particle duality, the fact that light can
exist as either a wave form or a particle but not at the same time, has been employed by
mankind to his great benefit si nce the invention of the laser in 1960. Today lasers are
common in industry, medicine, and science. La sers are used for precise and accurate
measuring, cutting, reading and recording, engraving, incising, ex cising, and aligning
and levelling. Everything from dumpy levels  to DVD players have lasers in them. Of
course, they have other uses , such as the hunter using a laser sight to pinpoint the
hapless bunny in his crosshairs, to a lecturer or presenter highlighting elements of his or
her presentation on a screen or a whiteboard for the benefit of the audience, and to
driving one’s cat into a frenzy as it chases  the impossible-to-catch  little red dot all
around the house. Indeed, they have many practical and legiti mate uses. They have less
legitimate uses as well, and it is one of thes e in particular that has been the reason for
the good Dr Calder to bring this bill before us.
Laser pointers—hand-held lasers in particular—have evolved rapidly in recent years,
and their availability has increased as pr ices have fallen e xponentially. Once the
preserve of fictional characters in futurist ic movies and TV programmes, the hand-held
laser has become an easily accessible realit y, powered by ordinary torch batteries, and
capable of great feats such as igniting matches and bursting balloons over a great
distance. I would have loved one as a boy, and with hindsight in some ways I think it is
just as well that I never did have one. Bu t boys today do have them, and some of those
25 Sep 2013 Summary Offences (Ha nd-held Lasers) Amdt Bill 13743
boys choose to do stupid things  with them, which is why we are here debating this fine
member’s bill, from the very fine member i ndeed, if I may say so, with the intention of
making it into an equally fine law.
I do own a laser pointer—I should confess that  at this point. In one of my previous
lives I was involved with the manufacture of colloidal silver, which is a broad-spectrum
germicide consisting of the suspension of micros copic silver particles in distilled water.
One of the tools that is used to confirm the presence of the silver particles in colloidal
suspension and solution is a laser beam. Wh en it is shone through the brew, the laser
produces what it known as the Tyndall effect, which is the scattering of light by very
small particles diffused in suspension. The la ser pointer that I used for this purpose was
a very small device that I purchased from a well-known chain of red shops for the
princely sum of $2. It has a power output of  about zero-point-nothing of a milliwatt,
but, that said, it will still illuminate a reflective road sign some 2 kilometres away.
The hand-held lasers that the silly boys I referred to earlier seek to own and misuse,
however, are a different animal altogether. Th ey are advertised online as being of great
power and effect, many hundreds and even thou sands of times more powerful than my
own little key ring device, which, despite its ut ility, is really little more than a toy—a
toy that could still blind somebody, mind. But these powerful lasers are in a different
league, and use them to blind they do. Foolis h boys have taken to using these devices to
blind the pilots of aircraft approaching our airports, putting literally hundreds of lives in
the air and on the ground at risk. It is only a matter of time before some clown decides
that drivers on the motorway are an equally hilarious target and fair game for their
stupidity.
Dr Calder’s bill will remove these devices from temptation’s reach and that is why
we are happy to stand alongside him, shoulder to shoulder, in suppor t of it. We despair
that this bill has become necessary and that, as my erstwhile colleague said, we have to
legislate because of people’s stupidity. But it appears that we do, and here we are. New
Zealand First congratulates Dr Calder on ha ving his bill drawn fr om the ballot. We
thank him for his motivation and his reasoning.  We support this bill,  and I commend it
to the House.

It has been discussed that although the Labour Pa rty will be suppor ting it, it is a

measure the strength of the lasers and make it an offence only if they are over a certain

knife. That is a very similar type  of offence, in the sense that  a knife, in itself, is not an

has an unlawful intent. In that offence, it is not a case that the length of the knife is the
issue, because if anyone has ever been conf ronted with a knife, as I was as a police

the length of an arm if it is used in the right  place. I would liken that to the situation in
this bill, and put it in the sa me category. It is not about th e scale or the calibre of the

When all is said and done, most people will  have lasers for various reasons and most

As we take this matter forward to the select committee, as I say, I want to commend
