SENTENCING (PROTECTION OF CHILDREN FROM CRIMINAL
OFFENDING) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : I move, That the
Sentencing (Protection of Children from Crim inal Offending) Ame ndment Bill be now
read a first time.  I nominate the Law and Order Committee to consider this bill. Talofa
lava, greetings, t ēnā koutou katoa, and thank you for the opportunity to introduce this
bill to the House for its first reading. In introducing this bill to the House I would like to
acknowledge the late Brian Donnelly QSM,  a former New Zealand First MP, who
strongly advocated for a bill like this to be de veloped in order to tackle the issues that
this bill intends to address.
Jim Rohn said that “Happiness is not so mething you postpone for the future; it is
something you design for the present.” Our young children deserve happiness with good
education and secure homes. It is impo ssible to postpone happiness for our younger
generation, for they need to plan for prosperi ty and stable lives t oday. So in order for
our future generations to have stability, we  ought to carefully engineer their current
environment and ensure that we design the be st platform to counter the risks and evils
that could harm and cause more damage to them and our nation in years to come.
The bill brings a unique focus to the way in  which New Zealand deals with criminals
who continue to ignore the rights of our children to a safe r and secure environment—an
environment where they can grow up to b ecome good citizens with aspirations to be
great leaders of our future ge nerations instead of professiona ls in criminal activity or
leaders of some gang-affiliated organisation. I ask that we put as ide our politics and
come together and be united for the sake of our vulnerable children.
The Sentencing (Protection of Children fr om Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill
seeks to make criminal offending in the pres ence of a minor an a ggravating factor at
sentencing. Criminal offending by adults often exposes minors to serious harm. That is
why this bill aims to enable the legal syst em in New Zealand to view such criminal
activities and give appropriate sentences that are reflective of this harm. I say: let the
punishment fit the crime. There is a need for more emphasis to be placed on the well-
being of minors or our children who witness, and are exposed and unfairly subjected to,
25 Sep 2013 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 13749
criminal activity. At the same time criminal s who ignore these children should be held
accountable.
The bill will make criminal offending in the presence of a minor an aggravating
factor at sentencing. It is a crackdown on indi viduals who engage in criminal activity in
the presence of young minors, and a minor would include anyone under the age of 17
years. The intention is to send a clear message  to others in New Zealand that we will no
longer tolerate crime being w itnessed by children, and that we can no longer allow our
children to be abused in such a way that they become emotionally and psychologically
affected.
Another important aspect of this bill in cludes strengthening judges’ powers when
sentencing offenders where minors have been exposed to potential serious harm. A
primary example of serious harm is the production of illicit drugs in homes where
children are living. Honourable members, this bill sends a clear message that this is
unacceptable. It has become too common for young children to be living in homes
where drugs are produced and so ld. The reality is that drug s are often associated with
other forms of illegal activity, from theft to  gang associations and violence, and with
this comes the abuse. Young children are far too often the innocent parties to criminal
offending by adults. There have been numerous  media reports of children being placed
in danger where crimes are committed, which shows a real need for this bill to be
passed into law.
On 3 September or earlier this month I re ad a media release by the New Zealand
Police saying that young children were present at some addresses that were the subject
of a search executed on several Mongrel M ob addresses, and that  the police had made
three referrals to Child, Youth and Family. Children living in  P labs suffer the risk of
harm from living amongst toxic waste, e xplosive chemicals, and drug-manufacturing
debris. Living in such a dangerous environm ent, children are exposed to immediate
danger from chemical poisoning, contamin ation, and the high chance of fire and
explosions. Children found in P labs are likel y to be inhaling and absorbing the same
levels of methamphetamine as adult drug users.
Senior lecturer in psychological medicine  at the University of Auckland Dr Trecia
Wouldes said that although there was no re search on the long-term effects of P on
children, what was known about the effects of passive smoking could be indicative. The
effects range from allergies to irritations  from the drug, with the worst coming from
breathing the fumes daily and physical trauma or burns that could occur if the labs
exploded. In 2010-11 more than 460 children we re found in 37 percent of all clan-labs
and 73 percent of all drug-dealing houses iden tified by the police. This is up from 26
percent and 65 percent, respectively, in 2009.
If the direct harm from the drugs th emselves is not enough, children are often
neglected because of the natu re of the trade. In many cas es, children are subjected to
and witness violence. A High Court judge last year was appalled at the number of
women he saw in court for neglecting th eir children while using methamphetamine.
Justice Williams reported that cases like these only create a generation stuck in the same
drug-addicted cycle. In other words, children pick up bad habits.
I worked in the Department of Correcti ons where I came across offenders who were
in prison with their father and grandfathers. Studies have shown that children learn from
adults. Parents’ criminality strongly correla tes with an increased chance of a child
developing conduct problems and, later on, criminal activity. Children in environments
where crime takes place are taught at a young age to accept this certain lifestyle.
Offending is an indirect consequence of the offence.
Several jurisdictions in the United Stat es have passed legi slation where drug
manufacturing in a residence occupied by a minor is an aggravating factor at sentencing.
13750 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
In the state of New South Wales in Australi a, sentencing procedure legislation makes it
clear that an offence committed in the presence of a child under the age of 18 is an
aggravating factor. Why, then, is New Zealan d turning a blind eye? It is time that
sentencing takes into account the safety of the children. A situation where children have
been exposed to dangerous criminal activity cannot and must not be taken lightly.
The National Government’s White Paper for Vulnerable Children introduced in
recent years, although well intended, unfort unately, gave New Zealand no assurance
that the problem of children in crime-operating environments will be addressed. So let
us hope that the Vulnerable Children Bill will enhance our combined efforts in this area.
New Zealand First has brought forward before  Parliament a solution to this serious
problem. The bill recognises that children will slip under the radar. Just because harm to
children occurs behind closed doors, it does not  mean that we should turn a blind eye
when it comes to sentencing those guilty of the actions that have created such
unfortunate consequences.
The current legislation does not go far e nough to provide results in sentencing that
properly take into account the safety of children and their e xposure to dangerous
criminal activity. This bill defines minors as “under the age of 17 years”, and covers
both mental and emotional harm, as well as physical harm, to minors. Furthermore,
children need only to be present to trigger this as an aggravating factor.
If this Government is going to take a serious stance on vulnerable children and tackle
the negative issue of child abuse, this bill paves a way in the right direction. Let us not
seek the answer from the right, the left, or the centre, but seek the answer that is right. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: National does support this bill, the
Sentencing (Protection of Children from Cr iminal Offending) Amen dment Bill, at its
first reading. We will be very interested to consider this bill. National does support this
bill because it aligns pretty fair and square w ith the work that this National Government
has been doing in, first of all, putting the vi ctims of crime first, but also in its very
strong cross-ministerial work  programme looking after the interests of all children,
including vulnerable children.
I commend the member Asenati Lole-Taylor for bringing this bill to  the House. It is
a simple bill. It proposes to amend sec tion 9 of the Sentencing Act to add a new
aggravating factor at the time of senten cing. As I understand the bill, the judge
presiding must take into account whether or  not the child, who is to be under 16 years
old, has had a crime committed in their presence by somebody over the age of 17
years—so it concerns an adult, albeit a young adult, having committed a crime in the
presence of a young person or child under the age of 16. So the judge, at the time of
sentencing, is to take the fact  that that young person or child was present at the time of
the offence into consideration when sentencing that offender.
The member will be very aware that this Government passed legislation earlier this
year to make it an aggravating factor at sentencing offences against corrections officers,
police officers, ambulance officers—and I might be forgetting—
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: Fire, ambulance.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: The Fire Service. We did that  with the support of the House
because we recognised that t hose service providers did no t ever have the option of
running away from an incident. So the fire man cannot run away from a fire. If that
fireman is prevented from going about their business, as happens, and as happens to
ambulance officers on a not infrequent basis,  and to prison officers, they have no
choice. They have to stand their ground. They have to deal not only with the emergency
that they face, like the prison riot we had recently, but also with perpetrators committing
offences or attempting to commit offences on them.
25 Sep 2013 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 13751
So you can very well argue—and I think it is very true to say—that young people
under the age of 16 can find themselves in ci rcumstances, through no fault of their own,
such as being in the midst of a crime scene,  be it, as I think the member Asenati Lole-
Taylor cited, being seen in a P lab and having the toxic fumes and the very danger of
explosion around them, be it family violence, or being sat in a vehicle that is the subject
of a police pursuit. All of those scenarios ar e similar in that the child does not have the
choice. They are children. Th ey are in the control—one wo uld hope, in our society—of
responsible adults. So I commend the member for bringing this bill to the House for its
first reading, and we will have a good look at it in the Law and Order Committee. It
aligns very well—very well—with the policie s of this National G overnment and with a
lot of the work that this  Government has done alread y in our first 5 years in
Government.
I will talk about some of the more detailed aspects of the bill. It refers to “in the
presence of a minor”, and that means in a place or a building where a minor is present
or could reasonably be expected  to be present, or in clos e proximity to a place or a
building where a minor is present or could re asonably be expected to be present. In
other words, I think the member is saying he re that they do not ha ve any choice. They
are kids. They have got to do what they are told. They are minors. They get placed in
these circumstances, and here we have a bill  that makes the presence of a minor an
aggravating factor in the sentencing of the perpetrator of a crime. Well, good on you,
Asenati Lole-Taylor, for bringing this bill to the House.
I just want to go through a few of the initia tives that are complementary to this bill,
and they are around the protecting of vulnerabl e children. I do have to disagree with the
member that the Children’s Action Plan is not going far enough. I believe it is. I believe
it is putting the interests of vulnerable childre n first, and I think so me of the provisions
in that policy are going to be quite crunc hy for people. But we are unapologetic in
putting the interests of vulnerable children first. Why? To keep them safe. Why?
Because they cannot choose the homes that they are born into or the si tuations that they
find themselves in. They do not have that choice. We as adults have that choice;
children do not have that choice. So I am unapologetic and I am proud of the Hon Paula
Bennett’s Children’s Action Plan. I look fo rward to seeing the roll-out of the
implementation of that plan and keeping our young children safe in New Zealand.
Under National, we have already toughened sentences for crimes against children.
We have already done work in that area. It is now a crime to stay silent if you know that
a child or a vulnerable adult is  at risk. We removed the parole eligibility for the worst
repeat violent offenders and for offenders who commit the worst murders. We did that
with the three-strikes law, thanks to our coalition partner the ACT Party. We introduced
screening of parole applications, to allow the Parole Board to reduce the number of
unnecessary hearings. Again, this was putting the interests of the victims first, be they
adults or children. Of course, there are alwa ys children associated with victims. We are
all mothers, we are all grandmothers, we are all aunties, and we are all family members.
Every crime that is committed in New Zealand has a number of victims and a number of
those victims are children.
I could go through a number of initiatives, and I know my colleagues will. I just want
to talk about the Victims’ Orders Against Violent Offenders Bill, which is newly
introduced into the House and is now going through scrutiny in the Law and Order
Committee. Again, this is another complement ary piece of legislation that puts the
interests of the victim first. It is about prot ecting the victim as much as is possible from
crime and criminals in New Zealand. It might be  adults, but in this case it is children.
This Sentencing (Protection of Children from Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill is a
13752 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
good bill. We will support this bill through its first reading. I commend the bill to the
House, and thank Asenati Lole-Taylor for bringing it to this House.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to take the first call from Labour
on the Sentencing (Protection of Children from Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill,
brought by the New Zealand First member Asen ati Lole-Taylor, and to say that Labour
is supporting this bill to the Law and Order Committee so it can be given further
consideration, both by the public and by member s of this House. But we do have some
reservations, and I want to share and outline those with the House now.
We absolutely agree with the member that it is incumbent upon us to protect the most
vulnerable from harm. Our argument would be: wh at is the best point of intervention to
try to ensure that those layers  of protection exist? How do we best ensure that a child is
kept distant from harm? How, when they ar e found to be in harm’s way, can we best
ensure that they are supported and remove d from that harm? Our question is whether
adding an extra bit of criteria for when an offender comes to be sentenced is the best
way to do that, keeping in mind that, as it is, most judges would probably keep in mind
or factor in the presence of  children, when they come to sentence. But what we are
relying upon for this bill to take effect is, first, for a criminal to be charged—for enough
evidence to exist for them to be charged—s econd, for them to be convicted, and then,
third, for the sentencing to take place.
I want to use the example that the member has used, around the presence of children
in methamphetamine labs, because it is a very good example that the member is right to
raise. There are a number of vulnerable ch ildren in this country  who are currently
exposed to the dangers of methamphetamin e manufacturing. In 2010  alone, 44 children
were found living in laborator ies, physically liv ing in the environment in which
equipment and drugs were manufactured—a pot entially explosive environment, not to
mention the fact that they were absorbing thos e toxins into their skin. That was in just 1
year. It is a growing trend, and that is dow n to police records. Police records have
demonstrated the presence of almost 200 children since they started measuring that.
The issue is that you would assume that the police, who, for instance, then report to
Child, Youth and Family when they go into a home where there is methamphetamine—
they will tell Child, Youth and Family that there is a child in the home where they have
done a drug raid. We would assume, as fai r-minded New Zealanders, that any parent
raising their child in that ki nd of risk environment would ha ve their child removed. It is
a fair assessment, a fair judgment, to make. Th at is not the case. In some cases we have
parents who are being charged, convicted, and sentenced, but their spouse is still caring
for the child and they go back into the hom e with that child. They may sometimes even
return to manufacturing methamphetamine. The police have found this to be the case.
Why is that? Well, it is simply because the threshold for abus e and neglect implies
that you are removing the necessities of life from a child, and there is, at least in the
minds of Child, Youth and Family, a thre shold that is not met through drug
manufacturing. There is apparently not enough evidence to demonstrate that that is the
removal of the necessities of life. Well, in  my mind, when you find t oxins equivalent to
that of a methamphetamine user in the hair  follicles of a child, that is enough. That
should be enough. Simply the fact that you cons ider it acceptable to  raise your child in
that environment, that should be enough.
So the point that we want to make is this. If we really want to protect children,
should we be considering the fact that it should be a separate offence in itself rather than
an aggravating factor? Should we be consid ering that at least our child protection
agency considers it neglect and abuse for thos e children to be in that environment? And
why do we not do that first? That is what we know we are crying out for now. Putting
any child back into a home where this is occu rring says to me that a hole exists, and if
25 Sep 2013 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 13753
we are waiting until someone is convicted, that does not fix the hole. So we have got to
look at some of those other issues.
But, as I have said, we support this bill to  the select committee so that we can debate
some of these issues. As I say, some of our reservations are about whether or not it is
directed in the right place and whether or not judges already have this power, but that is
something we look forward to considering. I thank the member Asenati Lole-Taylor for
bringing this debate to this House.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I too want to congratulate Asenati Lole-
Taylor on bringing this Sentencing (Protec tion of Children from Criminal Offending)
Bill to the House—I guess, on having it drawn by  what I should term the process of the
roulette wheel. It is quite an achievement , as I understand it. Many have sat here for
years with no success at all in getting a bill drawn. It is a bit like going to the Skycity
Casino and leaving with nothing, which, of course, can happen.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Not by this Government. They’v e got plenty out of the Skycity
Casino.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: Have you worked that out?
The bill—[ Interruption] They are rather noisy, Mr Assistant Speaker—they are
rather noisy. This bill has the potentia l to complement Nati onal’s law and order
legislative programme, which, I think, is having spectacular success. Aside from
significant reductions in crime at almost all le vels, particularly in the youth crime area,
we have also, of course, seen recently in the youth crime area a great reduction in road
deaths amongst young people. That is a pretty extraordinary achievement.
My brief time in this Parliament has been spent on the Law and Order Committee,
and I have seen and learnt a lot about the outstanding ro le our police play in our
communities, keeping our communities and our  young people safe. I want to briefly
mention the work of our youth aid officers in our communities, particularly in our rural
communities. They really are the key to our policing success, and, of course, to some
extent this bill sets out to deal with th e harm that comes to young people from their
association with crime. Our youth aid officers pl ay a critical part in  the success that we
have in keeping those young people safe and keeping them out of crime and those sorts
of things.
I also want to talk briefly about the work of the Department of Corrections and about
what are, at times, testing, intimidating, and even dangerous conditions. I think the
corrections department does a pretty amazing job. We have had the opportunity in the
last 18 months to visit a number of New Z ealand prisons to look at what goes on there
and to see the efforts that ha ve been made to repatriate those prisoners and re-educate
them and get them back into the workforce. I think, again, that we are making
significant progress in that area.
This bill seeks to, I guess, impose tougher penalties on those people who, by
association, involve young people in their criminal efforts. There is no doubt that young
people associating with crime leads to them  being much more likely to have a life
involved in crime. So I think that the bill from that perspective has some great potential.
There are already, of course, some opport unities for tougher penalties for people who
involve young people in crime, but this bill certainly clears it up.
I want to talk briefly about this Governme nt’s targets for reducing crime. We have a
target of reducing reoffending by 25 percen t by 2017. We want to reduce the overall
crime rate by 15 percent, and, of course, those results are signi ficant already. I would
have to say that some of the legislat ion that has gone thr ough the Law and Order
Committee in the last 18 months has certainly contributed to the improvement in those
targets, and no doubt the legislation that wa s put through in the previous 3 years had
made a huge difference to those targets.
13754 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
The other area that the Government has fi rmly concentrated on is putting victims
first. As the previous speaker Jacqui Dean said, we have a bill currently before the
select committee that aims to improve the opportunity for victims to protect themselves,
once those criminals who have done them the da mage get out of prison. That is a pretty
good start, I think. There are also numerous other means by which the Government has
moved to improve the lot of victims. I think th at is a great bit of work. It is currently a
work in progress, of course. As Jacqui Dean said, the bill that I am talking about is the
Victims’ Orders Against Violent Offenders Bill, which is currently in the House.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: This is the silliest piece of legisl ation the House has seen in a long
time.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: Those of us who have the oppor tunity to serve on the Law and
Order Committee have a greater understandi ng of these things, and clearly we do not
need to engage in this kind of discussion.
Finally, I want to congratulate the member  on bringing this bill to the House and I
commend it to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. The first line of the
explanatory note of this Sentencing (Protec tion of Children from Criminal Offending)
Amendment Bill essentially spells out the motiv ation for it, I think. It simply says that
“Criminal offending by adults often exposes  minors to serious harm.” Undoubtedly it
does. To those of us who are parents or even who have the ca re of other people’s
children, it is inexplicable, in a sense, th at people would willingly expose children often
to quite serious harm, but, sadly, that is the reality. It is something that this bill seeks to
address, and the Greens are happy to support the progress of this bill. It is appropriate.
The bill goes on to mention, too, that crim inal offending by adults does cause harm
to children, who deserve protection from adu lt offending that puts them at risk. It is
opportune, or, perhaps, it is ce rtainly appropriate, that we are debating this bill in its
first reading this week, which is, of course , Children of Prisoners Week. I was very
happy yesterday to host a brief celebration, a la unch, of that week and of a display from
PILLARS, Ng ā Pou Whakahou. I do acknowledge my parliamentary colleagues from
across the House who cooperated and enable d that brief launch, that celebration, to
occur in the parliamentary pr ecincts. I would just like al so—if I may diverge slightly—
to mention and acknowledge Verna McFelin,  the founder and current director of
PILLARS, who has 25 years of work protecting and doing her very level best to protect
the well-being of the children of prisoners. She was recognised a couple of days ago
with an award from the Department of Corr ections. Twenty-five years is an extremely
long time to be committed and devoted to a very tough call around protecting children
from the consequences of adult offending.
So with those comments, I will talk more sp ecifically to the bill. In a sense, we see
this as a belts and braces bill. We believe that clearly the intention is that having
children exposed to criminal offending—and th e specifics, talking a bout P labs and the
like—should be treated as an aggravating fa ctor at sentencing. We note that in 2005
Justice Winkelmann, in sentencing an offender who was involved in the manufacture of
methamphetamine, said this: “it is a consider able aggravating factor  that one of these
operations was in the garage at the prope rty where you lived with  your children”. She
went on to say to the offender: “you exposed your children to toxic chemicals in a
dangerous environment.” So, in a sense, we have got some confidence that judges at
sentencing would already treat the presence of  children as an aggravating factor, but
clearly this bill would make it, perhaps, easier for judges to make that call and more
likely that they would indeed consider that  an aggravating fact or. Certainly, it does no
harm; it may do good. It is kind of a belts and braces approach, and there is no harm in
that.
25 Sep 2013 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 13755
It is a very short bill, and none the worse fo r that. It is very clear in its purpose. We
respect that purpose—to protect  children from the very poor judgment, clearly, of adult
offenders who may put those kids at risk. We compliment our colleague on bringing this
bill to the House. We will be pleased to support it. Kia ora.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak to the first reading of
the Sentencing (Protection of Children from Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill. Can
I, at the outset, congratulate Asenati Lole -Taylor on bringing this bill forward and on
having the good fortune to have it drawn out  of the ballot—well done. In a previous
speech I made on a Government MP bringi ng forward a piece of  legislation, I was
critical, of course, that it had not been turn ed into a Government bill. On this occasion I
will not afford that same criticism to this bill, because, of course, the member has no
option but to bring it forward as a member’s bill, and that is the right and proper use of
the members’ ballot, in my humble view. So congratulations.
It is an important issue that Asenati Lole -Taylor puts before this Parliament, because
what more worthy cause of this Parliament is there than to be protecting children from
harm and to be putting children at the centre of what we do? The Labour Party made a
deliberate decision some 4 years ago that at the heart of all of its policy development
would be the impact on children. So of course it is supporting this bill at its first reading
and referral to the Law and Order Committee.
I will personally be very interested to h ear submissions on this bill because I have a
bill that is a little similar to this, but with quite different implications and different
motivations behind it, going into the member s’ ballot. It is about having domestic
violence as an aggravating f actor at sentencing. I think th ere are some real synergies
with this bill because, of course, one of th e circumstances in whic h this bill would be
brought to bear is in a situation where chil dren are present during a criminal offence
of—I am going to call it “dom estic violence” but, of course , there is no actual criminal
offence of domestic violence; possibly it would be an assault, male versus female, or
however it is described in the Sentencing Act.
Those situations are often—and far too of ten—occurring in homes, and frequently
children who are present are harmed when they  are party to that type of offending. One
of the stories I still recall—an d it resonates with me when ever I think about the work
our police do in this country—is the story I heard from a community constable about
how important it was for him to do work in th e local schools. He relayed to me a story
about the fact that becaus e children knew him and he ha d visited their school, the
children would come straight to him when , sadly, he was attending domestic violence
situations in their homes. The children w ould come out of hidi ng—that is often what
children do in these situations; they hide—a nd come straight to him. When the police
knock at the door, the children ar e even more terrified than they are of the events
happening around them. But this particular  police officer was telling me of the
importance of having a relationship with the children in his community so that they
knew that when he appeared at their door, he was there to provide them with safety.
So I think it is going to be quite instructive for us to see what submitters make of this
bill. I agree with my colleague Jacinda Ardern—that is probably no surprise to
anyone—in that I would much rather we were working at the front e nd of this and in a
way whereby children are never put in this situation, because, sadly, by the time this bill
is brought to bear, the harm has actually already occurred. The ha rm for an innocent
child—who has no other option but to be party to  a crime and to be in the vicinity of
that crime—has already happened by the time a judge is considering an aggravating
factor at sentencing. That is the saddest th ing about the bill that we are debating here
this evening. Having said that, it is one measure that I hope will make some difference. I
congratulate the member on bringing it to the House.
13756 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I will pick up where the member Sue
Moroney left off in acknowledging the New Zealand First member Asenati Lole-Taylor
for bringing this bill, the Sentencing (Protection of Children from Criminal Offending)
Amendment Bill, forward. Members’ days are a good opportunity for backbenchers to
contribute to the work of Parliament. Some bills have merit; some bills do not. They all
get debated if they are fortunate enough to be  pulled from the ballot. I am actually very
pleased to be debating this particular bill.
Most in the House will be aware, but I am sure for the three or four people who are
now watching me at home—

items.speaker: Hon Chris Tremain
items.text: Come on—thousands.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Possibly five, if they have not turned off already. As a former
detective I worked on electr onics, undercover operations, surv eillance, all the “ninja
turtle” stuff, at the time when methamphetamine—I was hiding behind trees; large ones,
obviously. I was working in th e police at the ti me when methamphetamine went from
being really a very little-known issue to New Zealand having one of the worst problems
in the world with that particular drug. It is the only hard drug that can be made in the
kitchen from readily available retail chemicals.
New Zealand was quite captured by that dr ug. I was one of th e first clandestine
laboratory officers trained. The clandestine drug laboratory officers were trained to
work alongside the Institute of Environmenta l Science and Research scientists, go in
and dismantle the labs, gather the evidence, and prosecute in respect of these things.
During that process I came to learn of the immense dangers that the manufacture of this
drug actually created. Sure, members w ill talk about issues other than
methamphetamine, but if we look at that part icular drug and the im plication of that on
children, it will give a very good  example, I guess, of wher e this bill may indeed have
its place, and that is in the significant a ggravation that is caused when someone is
manufacturing methamphetamine in the proxim ity of children. Sadly, all too often that
is exactly the case.
Here is a drug that is made from readily av ailable retail chemicals. It can be made in
a plastic bag, it can be made in a soft drink bottle, and it is often made in the lounges,
kitchens, and bathrooms of homes all around this country—it has been. There have been
thousands of labs—many, many hundreds of  labs—that have been dismantled, of
significant size and scale. We are talking a bout chemicals such as  hydrochloric acid,
sulphuric acid, and solvents of all manne r that are highly flammable but toxic in
themselves, such as red phosphorus, which will self-ignite without any rhyme or reason.
These are chemicals that in combination become incredibly toxic. They are not visible
and often cannot be detected  by the senses. They will emit during the manufacturing
process. They absorb into the wall linings. They go through the wall linings and into the
stud timber. They go through the floor, down into the substrate beneath the floor linings.
They go up into the rangehoods and all throughout the plumbing of the house. For every
kilogram of methamphetamine, 9.5 kilograms of waste is created, and often that is
tipped down drains or tipped out over the back lawn.
When I looked at a lot of the analysis on the implications of the ticking time bombs
that meth labs become, what became very apparent is that children in those
environments, by simply crawling around, w ould actually pick up those chemicals.
They are, typically, putting a lot of things in  their mouths, so trace elements of those
volatile insolvents and acids, drain cleaner , and so forth, are being ingested by the
children. Then, of course, those chemical s are producing methamphetamine, which is
often smoked in that environment as well. So  the children are ingesting that smoke, and
the residue from the smoke also falls and they ingest that. Not only are they being
poisoned but also they are ingesting the methamphetamine.
25 Sep 2013 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 13757
It is abhorrent when one considers what  goes on. Admittedly, most people who are
manufacturing in that circumstance are doing so  to feed an addiction. They are addicted
to drugs because they cannot not take them. But when children are in that environment,
and the parents can turn a blind eye to it, it is almost someth ing that I think is contrary
to human nature. It is so abhorrent, and the implications for the children are so severe.
So on that basis alone I am happy to support the bill to be considered by the Law and
Order Committee.
The one note of caution that we  may signal is the fact that  judges do, of course, have
discretionary ability to apply an aggravating factor in terms of se ntencing, and that will
always have to be weighed off against an arbi trary legal status such  as this. I think the
bill has merit and I commend the member for bringing it forward.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First): The Government has introduced a number of bills
that put the interests of children as param ount. An example, of course, is the Family
Courts Amendment Bill, which was recen tly passed. New Zealand First actually
opposed that bill because we felt it had too many serious faults. Although it made the
interests of children paramount, in fact it le ssened the circumstances in which a lawyer
for the child would be appointed. So we fe lt that the Government had reneged on its
own declaration about the paramountcy of th e interests of children in that bill. But
although New Zealand First did not support that bill, we di d support the principle of
putting the interests of children first, and we know that there is also cross-party support
for this important principle.
The Sentencing (Protection of Children fr om Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill
will increase sentences for offenders as a mean s of bringing home to them the need to
protect children from the effects of their offending. That puts this principle into practice.
So it is no surprise that all parties want this bill at least to go to the appropriate select
committee for examination. All parties, I am sure, want to see something done about the
problem that the bill seeks to address, wh ich is the exposure of children to criminal
offending and to the psychological effect that this has on their whole lives, one of which
is to drag those children into criminal offe nding themselves in later life. Another recent
piece of legislation is the Victims of Crim e Reform Bill. This is supported by New
Zealand First for the same reasons.
New Zealand First and Asenati Lole-Taylo r are promoting this bill to protect
children from the effects of criminal offendi ng. For too long victims’ rights have been
ignored. The current Government legislation to reverse that situ ation will be well
augmented by Mrs Lole-Taylor’s bill, the Sentencing (Protection of Children from
Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill, because although the victims’ rights are
extremely important generally, there is a co nsiderable gap in the need to emphasise
children’s rights in these areas. The particular focus of this bill is to deal with a by-
product of offending, being the effects on mi nors when crimes are committed in their
presence and when they live in unhealthy homes because of the effects of crime,
especially the production and sell ing of drugs. So the bill, in fact, targets that area, and
especially where methamphetamine is invol ved. Offenders who allow their criminal
activities to cause harm to children must have a much higher degree of deterrence by the
imposition of much harsher penalties. Such criminals must get a sharp wake-up call that
not only is the offending itself going to be puni shed but also if it harms children, then
that will cause a significant increase in the penalty. That is the purpose of this bill. It is a
simple and straightforward measure. Even  the dumbest criminal will understand it.
Accordingly, the bill will help to attack one  of the worst-affected sectors of the victims
of crime—New Zealand’s children.
We in this House have a sacred duty to do all we can to protect children, and this bill
is one way of doing just that. Th e essence of the bill is in cl ause 5, which says that it is
13758 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
“an aggravating factor in the consideration of  sentencing of an offender aged 17 or over
for the crime to have been committed in the presence of a minor if the actions
undertaken to commit the offence put the mi nor at risk of harm.” Although there is
nothing in the law currently that would prevent a court from taking that into
consideration as an aggravating factor, they too often do not do so. So it would be much
better if they are required to do so as a mandatory measure. This would advert the
courts’ attention to the issue so that they do consider this consistently in sentencing. I
congratulate Asenati Lole-Taylor on bringing the bill before the H ouse. It is a small
measure, but it is likely to have considerab le impact on the prot ection of children and I
trust it will get the support it deserves.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I rise to speak on this important piece of legislation,
Asenati Lole-Taylor’s Sentencing (Protec tion of Children from Criminal Offending)
Amendment Bill. I want to say, as many others in this House have said tonight, that we
are duty bound to ensure that the laws that this House passes afford proper and real
protection to the most vulne rable in our society, and ch ildren are foremost amongst
those.
However, now I want to be the fly in the ointment, or the jeremiah, and say that I
have some concerns about this bill. I ha ve concerns on the basis of longstanding
principles of criminal justic e and the drafting of criminal legislation. We all understand
the need for an appropriate penalty to be  in place when a crime involving violence
and/or harm to others has been committed. There are important principles when it
comes to our criminal statutes. One is that  crimes, because they attract the coercive
powers of the State through i nvestigation, detection, pros ecution, enforcement, and
sometimes incarceration or other forms of puni shment, are expected to be very clearly
and unequivocally defined, so that people know what the boundary is that they have to
cross before they attract the label of crimin al or before they have committed a crime.
That is fundamental.
What I see in this bill is some vague language, some uncertainty, and some
equivocation. When it says that a minor is put at risk, what does that mean? What is the
nature of the risk? And what is the extent of  the risk, especially if there has been no
material impact or effect on the minor? Given the definition in  the bill of “the presence
of a minor”, what does it mean to say “whe re a minor … could re asonably be expected
to be present;”? Well, if the minor was not present and has not suffered harm, what is
the basis of attracting a criminal sanction and punishing the person?
Let us punish the wrongdoers. Let us punish those who do wrong things and who
cause harm and danger to others. Let us not try to criminalise a w hole bunch of activity
that in the absence of anythi ng else would not be criminal. That is one point. Let us not
have wishy-washy, vague terms as the basis of  our criminal statutes. We live in a time
and, sadly, in a Parliament where it is very appealing and attractive to create more
crimes and create more criminals and all the rest of it. We should be very cautious about
doing that.
The second point I want to make is whether or not this bill will actually add anything
to what is already there. If you have a l ook at section 9 of the Sentencing Act 2002, it
lists 15—actually more than that because  some of them are broken down into
subsections—aggravating factors that a judge has to take into account. Five of them—at
least five of them—would c over the very situa tion that the member who has sponsored
this bill, Le’aufa’amulia Asen ati Lole-Taylor, is trying to cover. If we have a look at
section 9(1)(d) of the Sentencing Act, one of  the factors that a j udge could take into
account is “the extent of any loss, damage , or harm resulting from the offence:”.
Paragraph (f) is “that the offender was abusing a position of trust or authority in relation
to the victim:”—that includes a parent not using the house for the proper reason for
25 Sep 2013 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 13759
which it ought to be used. Paragraph (g) is “that the victim was pa rticularly vulnerable
because of his or her age or health or because of any other factor known to the
offender:”. There are some other ones there.
Then you go on to subsection (3), which stat es some things that the court must not
take into account, including whether or not the offender was under the influence of
drugs or alcohol. And then subsection (4) is  very clear that not hing in those earlier
subsections “prevents the court from taki ng into account any ot her aggravating or
mitigating factor that the court thinks fit;”, and it goes on to say that that provision does
not imply that any particular fa ctor is any less or more im portant and that they ought to
be taken together.
The real question, when this bill goes to the Law and Order Comm ittee, is what it is
actually adding to our present law. Although we will support this bill going to the select
committee, we do not want to continue the trend of crimin alising ever mo re behaviour
and adding ever more to our criminal statutes when it may, in fact, be totally pointless.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Timothy Macindoe.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: So does my mother when I am in
trouble. May I begin, as other speakers ha ve done, by congratulating Le’aufa’amulia
Asenati Lole-Taylor on having her membe r’s bill, the Sentencing (Protection of
Children from Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill, drawn and brought to the House.
It is an exciting time.
I have to say to Mrs Lole-Taylor that I am a little bit jealous, as I have been here
longer than she has and I too have a bill in the members’ ballot that has never looked
like being drawn. If it is, it will make a signifi cant difference, I think, to dealing with an
aspect of criminal behaviour in our community. But, anyway, I will not be churlish.
I congratulate her and I want to acknowledge Denis O’Rourke, who mentioned at the
start of his address that National has had a focus since we came into office on building a
safer New Zealand. It has, after all, been one  of our key Better Publ ic Services targets.
We have had a huge number of justice-relate d and criminal justice - related measures
that have come through Parliament, and we are seeing results, with a lower crime rate.
In fact, crime is at its lowest level in 30 years, and that is a fantastic achievement. Youth
crime is down significantly—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Get the figures right. Why doesn’t the member get the figures right?
Doesn’t have an argument. Doesn’t have an answer.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: —and I think that Mrs Lole-Taylor is bringing something
forward that is a thoughtful contribution to perhaps making another step in the right
direction. I hear Mr Little ch irping away. He needs to be reminded that before we came
into office in 2008, crime was increasing, gangs were on the rampage, courts were
overcrowded, and our prisons were particularly overcrowded and had a chronic shortage
of beds—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why can’t this member get the facts right?

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I am giving him all the facts. He does not like it. He will not
correct me, because he knows that I am right. He will simply continue to barrack. Well,
that is fine. I expect that sort of fairly churlish behaviour, but I will just carry on.
In recent times we have put 600 extra front-line police on the beat—that is a good
measure. We have got a 70 percent increase in  police foot patrols as  of the end of last
year—that is a fantastic achievement. These are some of the reasons why we are getting
these major improvements. I have no doubt that these will continue, and at any stage we
cannot let up on our focus.
13760 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
This particular bill amends the Sentencing Ac t. As I am one of the final speakers, it
may be that some people have only just t uned in. The bill will amend the Sentencing
Act “to make criminal offending in the presen ce of a minor an aggravating factor at
sentencing. Where the offending endangers or  exposes a minor to potential adverse
effects from that offending, the sentence must reflect this.” I am sure we all shudder at
the prospect of children being exposed to violent crime or perhaps being brought up in a
P lab or seeing some appalling gang activity. What an appalling impact that must be
having on these children. There is, sadly, huge  evidence that children who grow up in
that sort of environment go on to be at risk  of committing that sort of criminal activity
themselves, and therefore everything we can do to try to prevent that from happening
has to be a good thing.
I do, however, want to reassure the public who may be listening that the presence of
a child and the risk of harm to them are al ready aggravating factors that can be taken
into account by the courts in sentencing, even though they are not specifically listed at
the moment in the Sentencing Act. Furtherm ore, where the offending has involved the
presence of children alongside the manufact ure of drugs, offenders have also already
been charged with neglect offences, and so it  should be, because, as I say, the prospect
of this happening is so damaging for those children.
So, as has been indicated by my colleagues, Na tional is supporting this bill at its first
reading so that it can go to the Law and Order Committee so that submissions can be
made on it and it can be given due attention.
Colleagues have also mentioned the Children’ s Action Plan. I am a particular fan of,
and advocate for, that, because it is part of dealing with the real problem we have with
vulnerable children in our community growin g up in some dreadful circumstances and
being subjected to the most a ppalling abuse. Sadly, we have  one of the worst rates of
child murder in the Western World. As I say, this issue is a passion of mine. I
acknowledge all those who work in our communiti es to deal with that issue, and, again,
I hope that this bill will make another co ntribution in that dir ection, because although
we have made some progress, there is still a long way to go.
I was glad that Mrs Lole-Taylor acknowledge d the late Brian Donnelly and the work
that he did in this area, and I too echo that. He was a fine member of Parliament.
We know that a key to reducing crime long te rm is to stop children from entering the
criminal justice system. This is a bill that may well contribute to that end. It will, I am
sure, play a constructive role.
So for these reasons I too support its introduction and the fact that it should be sent to
the select committee. It sounds, from the way speakers have talked, as if it will be. I
again congratulate Mrs Lole-Taylor on her achievement. I will follow the bill’s progress
through the select committee and beyond with interest.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First): Talofa lava. Malo lava le
soifua. I want to acknowledge the contributions by various honourable members
tonight. I am reminded of H Jackson Brown Jnr’s words: “Live so that when your
children think of fairness, caring, and integrity, they think of you.”—they think of you.
During the development of this bill, the Sentencing (Protection of Children from
Criminal Offending) Amendment Bill, the memories of my dear eldest nephew
reminded me of the difficulties he faced in his first 17 years. If you are listening now,
Ioane, I just want you to know that I do l ove you. Your experience encouraged me to
ensure that this bill came to the House.
I am encouraged by the contributions and support shown by various members in the
House tonight. I also want to acknowledge the comments by David Clendon here with
regard to prisons and the fact that this week is celebrating PILLARS’ contribution to
fathers in prison and their children. Ian McKelvie also mentioned the visits he has made
25 Sep 2013 Sentencing (Protection of Children etc.) Amdt Bill 13761
to some of the prisons. I can assure you that I have spent 6 years in the prison
environment. I can assure you that I have spent 6 years in the Department of Corrections
looking after or catering for the top part of the northern regi on in this area.
Rehabilitation and reintegration is something that is very dear to me. During that time I
came across a lot of different generations from the same families. They happen to be the
families who come from the same kinds of pr oblems. If it is not domestic violence, it is
abuse, rape, or, of course, drug dealing.
This bill takes a clear stand that it is not OK for children to w itness and be innocent
bystanders to crime. We need to send a cl ear message that we will no longer sit back
and ignore children who are innocently caught up in high-level criminal offending and
ongoing crime that leaves them in the path of harm. Children are too often the innocent
parties in criminal offending by adults.
I acknowledge the comments that were rais ed by Jacinda Ardern tonight about the
judges that often they do not take it into acc ount, or often they do take it into account,
and they should. I suppose the response I can gi ve to that is that judges often forget that
the children were involved by the time the se ntencing happens. By then they often just
give a lenient sentence based on the actual cr iminal, forgetting that there were children
involved and, in addition to that, forgetting th e mental and the psychol ogical effect that
has on our children in those situations. I do hope that the Law and Order Committee,
though, will give that some serious consid eration in order to  incorporate those
comments that were raised by Jacinda Ardern . I sincerely hope that Andrew Little’s
concerns will also be addressed, and any of  the loopholes that he considered to be
missing from this bill.
Where offending endangers minors or exposes them to potentially adverse effects,
the sentence imposed should reflect that. Criminals should have no right to endanger
innocent children. The people of New Zeala nd expect us to fix this problem. Our
children are the future of this nation, and if the individuals around them are not taking
responsibility to protect them from harm and a cycle of abuse, and, plus, are initiating
them into a life of crime, then surely it is time they are held accountable for their
actions. Punishment is not for revenge but to lessen crime and reform the criminal.
Decisions in this House should be made base d on what is in the best interests of our
nation and our people, not on individuals’ needs or person al agenda. I duly commend
this bill to the House. Thank you.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Law and Order Committee.
SOCIAL SECURITY (CLOTHING ALLOWANCES FOR ORPHANS AND
UNSUPPORTED CHILDREN) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. I move, That the
Social Security (Clothing Allowances  for Orphans and Unsupported Children)
Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Social Services Committee to
consider the bill.
There is a story behind this bill, and I beg the indulgence of the House to explain the
personal connection that has been one of the drivers behind this member’s bill. In the
1940s my mother, Anne, was 2 years old and liv ing in Christchurch with her 5-year-old
brother, Barry, and their mother, Beverley. Th eir father, Jim, was away at war. One day
Beverley took the kids to the next-door neighbour’s. Nobody knows what she told them,
but she left the kids there and that was the last time they ever saw their mother. It would
13762 Social Security (Clo thing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
be 45 years later that Anne would be able to make contact with people who would speak
about Beverley and what had happened to  her after the day that she abandoned her
children. We now know that Beverley went on to live a completely new life, never
mentioning her children to her new workmates or friends until her passing from
toxaemia in the 1950s.
Some months after Beverley left, my mother’s paternal grandmother finally became
aware of her grandchildren’s circumstances and showed up at that door. Originally, she
took only Barry with her, beca use Grandfather had said th at she could bring the boy
home because he could work, but to leave the girl. Thankfully, a few months later,
Granny could stand it no longer and she came ba ck to collect little Anne. As life would
have it, Anne and Barry were loved and car ed for by their granny for approximately the
next 8 years. The army deducted a shilling from the children’s father’s pay and paid this
to their grandmother. When the war was ove r their father came home. He took time to
readjust to life on Civvy Street. He ente red a common-law marriage with Maude Mohi,
and it was another traumatic time for these ch ildren when their fath er arrived to take
them to live with him and his new wife in  Hastings. My great-g randmother shifted to
Napier to follow the children.
I recognise today that although each circum stance might be different, grandparents
are still grandparents and kids are still kids. Nothing has changed but the times we find
ourselves in. It is this personal connection and an innate sense of fa irness that has been
the driver behind this member’s bill under my name.
This bill does one thing and one  thing only. Bluntly and in a nutshell, it says that if a
child has been identified as an orphan or an unsupported child, then with regard to the
clothing allowance eligibility, it makes no difference who is caring for them. A child
being cared for by kin carers requires no less clothing than a child being cared for by an
unrelated adult. However, orphans and unsuppor ted children are not e ligible to receive
the clothing allowance.
This member’s bill proposes to give or phans and unsupported children clothing
allowance parity with a foster child. Its goal is  to have a single section inserted into the
Social Security Act, new section 29B: “A person who receives an orphan’s or
unsupported child’s benefit in re spect of a child is also en titled to receive a clothing
allowance for that child at the same rate as  is determined by the chief executive from
time to time under section 363 of the Child ren, Young Persons, and Their Families Act
1989.” That is it. That is all this little bill does, but what a difference it will make to the
lives of these children and their kin carers.
Before I enter into the substantive content of this speech, I w ould like to take a
moment to acknowledge the previous and cu rrent work by the Minister for Social
Development in this area. In 2009 it was the Hon Paula Bennett who took the steps
required to raise the main payment that caregivers received to match the orphans benefit
and the unsupported child’s benefit to those made  to foster carers. This Minister also
provided 500 respite care places per year for these childr en in week-long holiday health
camps, and I know that the kin carers were grateful for this support.
I also wish to acknowledge th at the Minister and I have  had positive interactions
around our mutual desire to recognise and s upport these kin carers, who are very often
grandparents raising grandchild ren. I am grateful to have recently been a member of a
ministerial reference group around the al location of $35 million over the next 4
financial years. That has been set aside in contingency for extended family members
caring for children and in recognition of the difficult job that they do. The Minister,
however, will also concede that if all ch ildren are not recognised as equal inside
legislation, then there is a r eal danger that at the end of that 4-y ear period, kin carers
will once again find themselves back at square one.
25 Sep 2013 Social Security (Clothin g Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 13763
I also want to recognise that  we are, as a nation, in restrictive financial times, and
that the select committee will have to take these factors into consideration. However,
there are times and there are issues wher e fairness and equity, particularly where
children are concerned, must be the drivers of  decision making in the first instance, and
then a can-do lens around funding should be applied.
I want to reiterate what this bill seeks to achieve. The intention of this bill is to
recognise in statute that an orphan is an or phan, whether placed with foster parents or
caregivers, and that all State support shou ld be based upon the circumstances of the
child, not the circumstances of the adult. This must be one of the only pieces of
legislation where a distinction is based upon blood and not on any other criteria.
For a variety of reasons, more and more children are finding themselves in the
unenviable position of being declared an orph an or an unsupported child by the State.
Kin carers are being targeted by social services to step up and take in these children,
which they do. We should recognise that th e majority of kin carers looking after the
day-to-day needs of these orphans and unsupported childre n tend to be grandparents
who are now raising their grandchildren.
So these kin carers step up, only to fi nd that these children are deliberately
disadvantaged through lower support, due to this very kin relationship. Children are
being discriminated against by the State due to circumstances beyond their control. I do
not believe that there is a member in this House who would argue that if you are raised
by your grandparents or auntie, you therefor e wear fewer clothes than a child placed
with people to whom they are not related. So if we do not argue that, then upon what
does this discrimination stand?
Just to make sure we are all clear on how  these children find themselves in these
circumstances, I would like to outline the criteria for the two separate categories. A
child is considered an orphan by the State if their parents have died or cannot be found,
or when they cannot look after their child because they have a long-term illness or
incapacity. A child is consid ered an unsupported child when their parents cannot
support them because of a family breakdown. Children must be expected to be in
caregivers’ care for 12 months or more for support even to be accessed. These criteria
have raised their own set of issues for those children  whose parents are imprisoned for
sentences of 3, 6, or 9 months and who are placed with caregivers. These children are
not eligible even for the base support outlined here, but that is for another day.
It is worth noting at this poi nt that when a child is suppor ted by the State in either of
these circumstances, the natural parents are required to pay child support through the
Inland Revenue Department child support sc heme, should they be earning. I would
request that the Social Services Committ ee take this revenue into account when
considering this bill and its expenditure.
I would also request that the select committ ee recognise that more than half of these
children are reported as having serious physic al and psychological problems as a result
of the abuse and neglect they experienced prior to coming into their grandparents’ or kin
carers’ homes. However, research shows us that 86 percent of th ese children report
significant improvement over time, and that this is directly attributed to the stability of
care, the resilience, and the commitment of these caregivers. We ask the select
committee to consider the cost savings these kin carers facilitate for the State by
stepping up to the proverbial plate. It is becau se these individuals do step up that we as
a State are not looki ng at creating orphanage s up and down New Zealand, in which to
house these close to 10,000 children.
Reports have also revealed alarming statis tics that show that for 40 percent of
caregivers, their tota l family income was less th an $30,000 per annum. Almost 39
percent were solo carers, weighted heav ily towards women, who were particularly
13764 Social Security (Clo thing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
financially compromised. Several described their struggle to feed and clothe themselves
and the children adequately. One stated a wish not to go to bed hungry and for clothes
that fit. The incidence of kinship care va ries across cultures, with 53 percent of M āori
children in need of care placed with wh ānau and 59 percent of Pacific Island children
placed with fono, compared with 31 percent of P ākehā children placed with extended
family.
This study evidenced that the children in wh ānau or family care do well, but that the
lack of parity around the application of th e clothing allowance is contributing to the
difficulties their children and their caregivers experience. The State has calculated the
rate at which the clothing allowance is required inside certain age brackets for children,
but the Act creates a situatio n where, if you are related to  the person who steps up to
look after you, then you apparently no longer need that support. There are no other
criteria that affect this decision. It is completely based on blood relationship.
A Labour Government acknowledged this  issue. A National Government has
acknowledged this issue. It is  time to stop talking about it  and time to ta ke action. On
behalf of these children and carers, I implor e all parties in this House to support this
bill’s referral to the select committee. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Malo le soifua. It is a real
privilege tonight to speak on the Social Secu rity (Clothing Allowances for Orphans and
Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill. May I first commend the member in charge of
the bill, Tracey Martin—first, for sharing your personal story with us and with the
nation in terms of why it is important to you, and, second, for bringing  this bill to the
House. National will support this bill in its first reading.
It is about equity, as you have outlined in your speech. It is about aligning the rights
of orphans and unsupported children to those of foster children. For that I certainly
commend you. It is also about supporting childr en in need. As the member has stated,
our Government, this National Government, ha s put in place a number of measures to
support young children, vulnerable children, in need. But there is much more to be done
in this area, and, certainly, this bill goe s some way to addressing the needs of our
children.
Thirdly, this bill assists kin carers, those grandparents and those wh ānau members
who are looking after childre n, sometimes through no c hoice of their own and
sometimes to support a parent, as the member has said, who may be incarcerated, may
be missing, or may be taking a break. It suppor ts those family members who take up the
challenge of looking after these children in need. I think many people out there and
many members here will appreciate the work that kin carers and grandparents do. I have
seen it, certainly, in my own family. Ha ving been raised by my grandmother for a
number of months in the very early stages  of my life, I appreci ate those moments and
the support that I received personally. Bu t other members here will certainly have
stories in their own personal lives and their own families that can relate to this bill
specifically. I have also seen the needs of c onstituents in my electorate office who have
come in very much in need and very much wanting to support their whānau with limited
resources. This bill goes some way to ad dressing the needs of those people who are
looking after these children.
But, as the member has already stated, we live in fiscally constrained times.
Certainly, it is about using taxpayers’ money in a wise way and in an orderly fashion
that is targeted to those kids who need th ese resources the most. But, above all, it is
about addressing the needs of those individu al children and what is in their best
interests, what their needs are, and how the State can, through the Government, support
those children.
25 Sep 2013 Social Security (Clothin g Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 13765
As Ms Martin has stated, negotiations have  been going on to address some of these
needs and to ask how we can better target the spending in this area. The Minister for
Social Development has set up a ministerial re ference group, of which Tracey Martin is
a member, along with our own colleague Alfred  Ngaro, as well as representatives from
foster care and iwi and of  Grandparents Raising Grandc hildren. They all have
representatives on this group, which is work ing towards putting together a package of
options in order to better give extra fina ncial assistance to, and ideas towards better
ways of spending the money on, these children who require it most. That is part of the
Children’s Action Plan, which the Minister, th e Hon Paula Bennett, is in the process of
implementing.
I look forward to the deliberations in front of the Social Services Committee, which I
chair, because we will be looking at some  of the options. We will be looking in good
faith at building on the work that has alr eady been under way. I certainly look forward
to working across the aisle as well, with a newly appointed spokesperson for the Labour
Party, Sue Moroney. I am sure Labour will join other parties across this Chamber
tonight to support this bill.
It also supports the White Paper for Vulnerable Children, which was announced and
where this funding—$10 million worth of additional kin carers’ costs—will be covered.
Certainly, it is part of an overall regime whereby we are implementing laws to address
the needs of vulnerable children. We have ju st heard earlier toni ght about another bill
looking at sentencing that the honourable  member Le’au Asenati Lole-Taylor
introduced. That bill is another part of th e jigsaw puzzle that will go towards mitigating
just some of the factors involved in cari ng for our vulnerable children. Also, as the
member in charge of this bill stated, in 2009 National en sured that kin carers got the
same weekly amount as foster carers. Again, it was about equity in terms of the weekly
amounts that these kids received. It was a bout addressing a need in the community, and
this Government again responded swiftly to that upon coming into Government to
address those inequities in the system.
I just want to touch briefly on other pa renting support that is out there in our
communities. This Government, in partnership with Grandparents Raising
Grandchildren, as well as The Parenting Pl ace, which is an organisation that does
wonderful work in our communities, has developed a tailored tool box programme
specifically for kin caregivers, at a cost  of $600,000 per year. It acts as a refresher
course for grandparents who are, for whatev er reason, returning to  front-line parenting
duties, maybe many years after having raised their own children a nd after having taken
a break. The course gives a li ttle bit of insight into how  children’s early experiences
might affect them now and into the future. They are useful tools,  and it is part of
providing not just the resources like direct funding but also the tools to allow kin carers
to better look after the kids who are within their guidance and their care.
So this bill, as I said at the outset, is a commendable bill. It is a bill that really does
focus on those kids who are in need. I still be lieve that much work needs to be done in
terms of targeting some of those dollars  to the needs of children and their wh ānau, and
when we talk about these kids , in particular, we are talki ng about kids whose carers are
predominantly from low socio-economic groups. You know, every dollar that is
dedicated to the kids’ upbringing  is certainly valued by those wh ānau and the families
who are looking after these young kids. So this bill is commendable. It is a bill that we
are certainly looking forward to assessing in  the select committee.  It will help those
many thousands of children out there who need assistance. I certainly commend this bill
to the House and look forward to its process through the select committee.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I am just so desperate to get my opportunity to put
Labour’s perspective on this bill, the Social  Security (Clothing Allowances for Orphans
13766 Social Security (Clo thing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 25 Sep 2013
and Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill, on the table before we finish for the
evening. I want to start by adding my tha nks to the member Tracey Martin of New
Zealand First for bringing this really important piece of legislation to this House. We do
not often get the opportunity to discuss the really important work that carers in New
Zealand do, and this is an opportunity not only to raise that but also to highlight the fact
that there are some inequities in the way th at our system works. So I thank the member
for bringing in this bill. I thank her for sharing her personal e xperiences. I am looking
forward to the chance at the Social Servi ces Committee, for all of the other members—
although I have recently departed that sele ct committee—to start looking at some of
those inequities, and I wanted to touch on some of that just quickly.
There has already been some discussion over the support that exists  for foster carers
through the Ministry of Social Developmen t. Obviously, they receive some basic
boarding assistance. But, alongside that, fost er carers do receive the clothing allowance
that this bill confers on other carers. They  receive some assistance for birthdays and
Christmas. That may seem surprising to members of this House, but I can tell members
that I come across families who are living in  impoverished situations where children
know only one birthday in the household because the family can afford to celebrate only
once. So the children think that they were al l born on the same day. That is the kind of
circumstance some children grow up in. So I th ink it is entirely correct that some of our
nation’s most deprived children, who often e nd up in foster care, are supported to have
things that New Zealanders consider are a normal part of a ch ild’s upbringing. They
also get support for pocket money, education, and medical needs.
The thing I want to highlight is that fost er carers do not raise children for money.
They get a very basic allowance that almo st entirely across the board does not even
cover the cost of taking on that child. They do it for love, generosity of spirit, and their
sense of duty to New Zealand. There are 5,000 children at any one time who are in the
care of the State and who may be in the care  of foster carers. They might be in a
residential facility, or they might still have Child, Youth and Family oversight for
kinship care. It is a discrepa ncy, in my view and in La bour’s view, that we do not
provide that kind of assist ance to groups like th e Grandparents Raising Grandchildren
Trust.
But our contention is that rather than just applying one element of what foster carers
are able to receive to those who are kins hip carers, why do we not treat all kinship
carers as we do foster carers? Why do we not remove that discrepancy altogether?
These are often family members themselves who do not have the resources but do have
the desire to support the ch ildren of their wider fam ily members in whatever
circumstances they find themselves in, part icularly grandparents raising grandchildren,
who are often living on a pension and findi ng themselves dealing with not only legal
expenses that come with looking after these children but much, much more.
There is a distinction I want to make, because some people ask what the difference is
between a foster carer and someone who is classified as having an unsupported child or
orphan. Well, actually, to qualify, if you are a grandparent, you cannot be a foster carer,
because you are a grandparent. It is the same with a kinship carer, so that is where there
is a distinction there. But the way that it is  defined by Work and Income is that it is
looking for family breakdown. It will be looki ng to see whether or not there are reasons
that mean that child cannot be with their family. Some grandparents, therefore, do not
even get the unsupported child’s benefit. There might not be a technical breakdown, but
the grandparent knows that the environmen t the child is living in is not a good
environment for that child to be in, but they themselves are often deprived of that
support because of the strict criteria that exist. I would hope that  the select committee
would look at that as well in its considerations, because it is a significant issue.
25 Sep 2013 Social Security (Clothin g Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 13767
I am glad that Tracey Martin has the ability to work with the Government on some of
these issues. We would have liked to help too, but I have great faith, given that the
member is there, that she is carrying over so me of the views that we have. We need to
look more generally at foster care in this country. We need to have a look at the fact that
foster carers do not receive a lot of support fr om the State. We need to look at kinship
care. Those are all things that Labour will do when in Government.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Ahn nyung has se yo. It is a great pleasure to rise to
support the first reading of this Social Secu rity (Clothing Allowances for Orphans and
Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill. Li ke previous speakers I would like to
congratulate Tracey Martin on bringing this b ill to the House. I w ould also like to bid
my farewell to Jacinda Ardern from the Social Services Committee. She has actually
often brought a very clear view of the La bour position on the bills that we have
discussed in the select committee. I look forward to working with the new spokesperson
from the Labour Party, Sue Moroney.
The purpose of the bill is to increase fina ncial support to kin car ers who are looking
after children, such as gra ndparents raising gran dchildren. Many members have talked
about the issues earlier and, I guess, I l ook forward to the select committee process
because often members are exposed to more in formation about issues that they may not
necessarily be familiar with. This particul ar issue about children being raised by
grandparents—orphans and unsupported childre n—are important issues that we must
consider, and I am seriously looking forwar d to the submission pr ocess in the select
committee.
Just to bring a little  bit of ethnic pers pective into this, grandparents often raise
children. Even my own mother is, I feel, raising my child, because often as members of
Parliament we do leave our homes for long periods of time. Often I am not at home
enough to look after my t eenage son. My son has just celebrated his 15 th birthday and
often I do feel very, very guilty that he is at the most important time of his life and his
mum is actually not at home. And being a sing le mum is also very difficult as well, so
having my mother, his grandmother, at hom e raising him to provide the emotional
support—
Debate interrupted.
